Sports.title: Gabriel and Mac Allister's cheating is not just embarrassing, it's malevolent and wicked... players need the threat of red cards for such dishonesty and if that fails punishments after review, writes IAN LADYMAN
Sports.content:
Gabriel and Mac Allister's cheating is not just embarrassing, it's malevolent and wicked... players need the threat of red cards for such dishonesty and if that fails punishments after review, writes IAN LADYMAN

Football’s law makers like to meddle. The problem is they do it in areas that tend not to need any meddling. Like around handball and offside and other places that were doing just fine as they were.

So here’s a tip for the meddlers at the International Football Association Board. Meddle somewhere that needs it. Meddle in a way that would be meaningful and important and in a way that would actually help the game.

Please meddle with cheating. Please do something that would spare us from the embarrassment of grown men behaving like children in a bid to get other players booked and sent off. Yes, please meddle there.

Because football at the top level really needs it.

It needs a route through which players such as Alexis Mac Allister and Gabriel Magalhaes can be properly punished, shamed and embarrassed for what they did during Sunday’s otherwise fabulous Premier League game between Liverpool and Arsenal at Anfield.

It needs a deterrent. It needs greater power to match referees and greater leeway for retrospective punishment.

Alexis Mac Allister drops to the floor holding his face after his forehead is slightly brushed

The Liverpool man tried to get Noni Madueke sent off during Arsenal's 1-0 victory at Anfield

In a way, it is handy that there was one from each team this time. That way, we can be spared the usual accusations of bias that tend to come when footballers are called out for their sins.

Here, live on TV, Gabriel and Mac Allister were both as bad as each other. One in each half, clear as day.

Arsenal defender Gabriel was poked in the chest early on by Aleksandar Isak and went down holding his face. Then, much later, Liverpool’s Mac Allister was brushed by the forehead of Noni Madueke and did likewise.

Neither fooled referee Andy Madley. Both were told to get up and get on with the game. On TV, Sky Sports analysts Gary Neville and Jamie Carragher didn’t hold back.

‘Embarrassing’ was the word they both chose. Neville to describe Gabriel and Carragher as a way of calling out Mac Allister.

But this type of chicanery is more than that. We see it from lots of players and we see it all the time. It’s not just embarrassing. It goes much deeper. It’s malevolent. It’s low. It’s pre-meditated. It’s wicked.

Short of dark subjects such as spitting and leg-breaking tackles, I can’t think of much worse things on a football field than pretending to have a head or facial injury when you actually haven’t.

So where IFAB need to get involved – where they need to ‘meddle’ – is simple. They must increase football’s powers to punish.

On the field and in the moment, referees can issue yellow cards for simulation and for cheating. Players can be booked for exaggerating contact (Mac Allister) or pretending contact has been made with a certain area of the body when it hasn’t (Gabriel).

Arsenal defender Gabriel Magalhaes performed a similar act of cheating in the first half

The Brazilian fell down clutching his face after Alexander Isak brushed his neck and chest

But why is there no power – at least in occasional and exceptional circumstances - to issue a red card?

Gabriel and Mac Allister appeared to be trying to get their opponents sent off. Would they do it if they knew the match referee at least had the option of showing them the red card instead?

Very probably not.

So, yes, IFAB could have a meddle there.

Retrospectively, meanwhile, we need greater leeway for action.

Under a law passed a decade ago, a player can theoretically be banned by a review panel for two-games for ‘successful deception of a match official’. However the reality is that the initiative has largely been superseded by VAR and was only really used for players diving to try and win penalties anyway.

In terms of the nonsense we witnessed at Anfield on Sunday – and indeed see on a reasonably regular basis around the country – there is very little recourse once the game is over so once again a possible deterrent has been removed from the equation.

Cheating of this nature currently looks and feels like a risk worth taking and that is what must change.

Alexander Isak was not given a penalty despite being blatantly pulled back by Jurrien Timber

Here, it was interesting to hear Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola suggest afterwards that he must start telling his players to go down under contact. He was talking about Isak’s refusal to buckle under a clear penalty area shirt tug from Jurrien Timber.

That’s an important issue, too. Players should not be punished for their honesty. A foul is a foul, regardless of the reaction. VAR should have awarded a penalty.

But here on an otherwise fine day for the Premier League, another known and rather ugly blot on the landscape grew larger.

The threat of red cards for cheating and – if that fails - punishments handed down by review. That’s the kind of meddling we should all be on board with.

Sports.title: Kimi Antonelli becomes youngest champion in F1 history! Third-place finish at Mexico Grand Prix secures title triumph for 20-year-old superstar in race won by Max Verstappen
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli becomes youngest champion in F1 history! Third-place finish at Mexico Grand Prix secures title triumph for 20-year-old superstar in race won by Max Verstappen

Sobs and tears and you could hardly believe it. ‘Champion of the World,’ Kimi Antonelli was told over the Mercedes radio by his race engineer Peter Bonnington. And the crying and bawling started.

For once the tension, he admitted, had got to him this weekend. That is how Antonelli felt going into this Mexico City Grand Prix, an incident-laden one, a controversial one, but one from which he emerged emotional as the youngest winner of the Formula One title in history, at 20 years and 68 days.

But he was, agonisingly, made to wait here on Sunday after a high-speed crash involving Valtteri Bottas delayed his route in the hot sunshine and thin air of this sprawling city, the honking horns of its roads so different from the calm he has exhibited all season.

The serenity he had shown, that is, until his triumph was done and he broke down and then hugged his dad Marc and mother Veronica.

As Ferrari squabbled – more of which later – and Max Verstappen won, with Lewis Hamilton second and Antonelli third, the Italian’s coronation was punctuated by 33 minutes when Bottas’ front left wheel was suddenly half torn away from its hinges, still attached yet askew, and his Cadillac was suddenly transporting him as a passenger, a big snap. It looked like a suspension failure. The race was suspended as the Finn received treatment and the fencing was mended. He hobbled away.

So, a red flag was waved and Antonelli prepared to go through a second dose of lights-out torture from fourth place at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez.

Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton lift the new champion Kimi Antonelli on their shoulders after his third-place finish secured the title at the Mexico GP

Antonelli celebrates becoming the youngest world champion in F1 history

Antonelli embraces his team having secured the title with a third-place finish in Mexico

A further delay followed when Racing Bull’s Arvid Lindblad was punted into the air in a tussle with McLaren’s Oscar Piastri. A safety car was deployed.

Even from the original start, long before the Bottas mishap, the drama had been set up in the most intriguing way. Antonelli started on the second row alongside Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc with the only two men who could possibly delay his elevation to champion status in front of him, Hamilton and George Russell.

For Hamilton, no matter what was to come in the race, his first pole for Ferrari, and indeed his first for three years, demonstrated his enduring gifts, however tempered they may slightly be by his 41 years.

Anyway, this was a perfectly choreographed line-up. One of the front-two pair had to win or Antonelli was champion. And even then only if he finished outside the top nine in the case of Russell winning, or outside the top ten if Hamilton were victorious.

But what about the opening seconds?

It is a massive 1,000 yards into the first corner and experience suggests that pole here is not always the advantage it usually is. Slipstreaming from pursuers had been key in the past, and highly dramatic, and it raised the question whether Antonelli would try to impose himself at this early point. Or sit back.

He had, as it were, a three-foot putt to win The Open, but in this case a mighty right-hander waited to test his race craft and nerve.

He looked calm on the grid in the immediate build-up, chatting to his dad under a black umbrella protecting them from the intense heat. He kissed his mother on the cheek. His little sister Maggie was also in attendance.

Antonelli, pictured during the Mexico GP, did enough on the day with a composed drive

Antonelli's family embraces him after he crossed the finish line to complete his ambition

The good news for Antonelli is that he was not snared at that opening corner. He held on to fourth position. Verstappen, a past master at that very place and already a five-time winner here, was the big bolter.

Russell fell back to sixth, an emblem of his miserable season. But the real drama was at the front as the two Ferraris tangled at Turn 4, after Leclerc used Russell’s slipstream down the opening straight to press his claims.

They were wheel-to-wheel going into Turn 4. Leclerc went down the outside. The Monegasque could not make the corner and cut across the grass into the lead. They did not quite touch.

Hamilton, who made it around the bend, albeit with a slight wobble, fell back to third. Verstappen cashed in on the internecine squabble to go second. ‘Pushed off by my team-mate,’ complained Hamilton.

The stewards opened their investigation. ‘What is happening about Charles?’ asked Hamilton.

A five-second penalty came Leclerc’s way. When this was announced 12 laps in, his lead over Verstappen stood at 3.5sec.

Antonelli is draped in the Italian flag as he takes in the magnitude of his accomplishment

The new world champion receives adulation from the crowd in Mexico CIty

Hamilton thought this unfair. He had a point. Leclerc’s questionable lunge had granted him free air at the front. He asked his pit wall for them to be switched around. This was not so easy because Verstappen was sandwiched between them.

By lap 20 of the 71, Leclerc’s lead stood at five seconds, his sanction negated. Hamilton fumed: ‘The stewards have basically handed Charles this win. We agreed this (rules of engagement) in the drivers’ meeting.’

Yes, there was self-interest in Hamilton’s comments but it is hard to argue with his logic. Though, as it turned out, once Leclerc had served his penalty Verstappen just jumped him in the pits for the lead.

Russell, meanwhile, had run into Isack Hadjar on the eventful opening lap and sent the Red Bull No2 to the back of the grid. The stewards’ prosecution workload doubled. He was landed with a ten-second penalty while running fifth. It never rains on George’s side of the garage.

Ha, but meanwhile, the boy prince Kimi was running fourth, and Russell, his bag man, was going to fall further behind once he had served his punishment, finishing sixth.

A brittle cocoon of calm was created around the likely-to-be champion.

From error-prone rookie to history maker: How Antonelli became F1's youngest-ever champion Kimi Antonelli came from the shadows to take the title, having started the year with question marks that arose last season not over his pace, which was never in doubt, but about errors that punctuated his rookie campaign. He had been significantly outgunned by George Russell in the other Mercedes. There was also a feeling that he was overexposed too early in a top seat rather than given time to learn his craft at a less visible team, an accusation that was probably true. The alternative of a year or two at, say, Williams, might have been kinder on his young mind. He was, after all, just 18, and to take up the place vacated by no less than Sir Lewis Hamilton was surely a task for an older head. Would he bounce back from the pounding? Could he rein in the extravagant ebullience that was the extreme edge of his electric speed? In fairness, Toto Wolff was his ever-supportive boss and put an arm around his slender shoulders to emollient effect. Antonelli and Russell have been managed by Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff (left) Wolff, who enlisted Antonelli to Mercedes' young driver programme aged 12, never wavered in his belief that he had unearthed Hamilton's rightful heir. He conveyed this conviction to Kimi both privately and publicly. Still, there were doubts in the paddock. One team principal told me at the start of the season when I asked him for his assessment of Antonelli: 'Undoubtedly quick but prone to too many mistakes.' But he has shown himself to be serene in 2026, and especially so for a driver of 20. Think about that. Only 20. There are only a few examples from the past of this kind of precocious brilliance. Stirling Moss secured his landmark win at Goodwood on his 19th birthday in 1948, announcing his gifts to the world. Max Verstappen won his first F1 race in Spain at 18 in 2016. Well, Antonelli can be satisfied at living in that sort of society. He frankly blew away Russell, who started the season as favourite and full of confidence that his time had come. He duly started in spectacular style in Melbourne with a win there and it looked as if he had only to stay alive to take the title. It was all his for the taking. A pivotal moment, the most significant of all in my estimation, came in China with Antonelli's first victory a week after Russell's Australia. A door opened, just as Russell needed to keep it slammed shut in Antonelli's face, and from there impetus swung the Italian's way. I think Russell, who had won the sprint in China, was psychologically damaged by trailing Antonelli home the next day - five seconds the margin. The usurper had done it from pole, again a first for him. He was to keep his foot to the floor for weeks on end, helped by the good fortune to be driving the grid's dominant car for the early part of the season. Other teams later caught up. Antonelli's first win of the season, in China, may have done the psychological damage to Russell, who trailed him by five seconds Wins in the next four races - Japan, Miami, Canada and Monaco - poleaxed Russell, who was at a loss over how best to drive his machine. Poor George began by talking a good game, but he gradually realised the dream of a lifetime was slipping away from him. Yes, he suffered the bigger slices of bad luck, and perhaps there was a slight bias in the team towards Antonelli, not to the extent of sabotage or ill-intent towards Russell, but a natural inclination towards the star they saw as their future hero. The damage was done by now and Antonelli, skilfully tutored by Lewis Hamilton's old race engineer Peter 'Bono' Bonnington, was always busily aggregating points, there or thereabouts even on his off days. After three races without a win - including Hamilton's maiden victory for Ferrari in Barcelona, something of a false dawn - Antonelli triumphed again in Spa. This represented a big swing. Russell and Hamilton collided on the first lap, with Russell eliminated and Hamilton given a five-second penalty. Antonelli held off Charles Leclerc to stretch his lead over Hamilton to 45 points and over Russell to 50. Antonelli inherited Lewis Hamilton's former race engineer Peter 'Bono' Bonnington when he came in at Mercedes following the seven-time world champion's move to Ferrrari Other highlights? Probably the best was Antonelli's home win in Monza from the back of the grid after taking a penalty for a change of engine. The car was quick, his new power unit strong, and he was favoured by an agreeable strategy, but it was still a fine comeback drive. Most of those in the stands would have preferred a Ferrari victory. Their red tops and their banners signified that. There was barely a Mercedes shirt in sight. But, still, this win helped lift Kimi on to a pedestal in his homeland he had yet to reach. Another milestone in his remarkable championship journey was Russell's engine blowing up in the closing stages of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia at the start of last month. That sealed it, basically, even though Antonelli finished second to a resurgent Red Bull of Max Verstappen. Still, the points were ticking up all the time. And his victory in Austin last weekend was a remarkably commanding one. Now he has clinched the title with four rounds remaining depending on whether the planned concluding races in the Middle East, in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, survive the vicissitudes of war. If they are off, the planned alternative is a finale in Imola. It would be some party to toast the boy born just 20 miles away in Bologna.

READ: Inside the rise of Kimi Antonelli: How a shock conversation with Mercedes boss Toto Wolff, a close relationship with Bono and hand washing cars at home propelled Italian to F1 history

Sports.title: Inside the rise of Kimi Antonelli: How a shock conversation with Mercedes boss Toto Wolff, a close relationship with Bono and hand washing cars at home propelled Italian to F1 history
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton had just sprung the surprise of his life on Mercedes. He was off to Ferrari, and so Kimi Antonelli was called in by Toto Wolff, the Austrian team principal who had supported his talent like a second father since he was 12.

One insider remembers the moment vividly. Antonelli was 17-and-a-half at this stage and sitting intently in the team’s factory at Brackley after completing a Formula Three test at Silverstone. He had not even competed in Formula Two, Formula One’s feeder series.

‘Toto told him it could be him in the F1 seat in 2025, and you saw his eyes light up,’ revealed a member of the small group of individuals in the room that day in early February 2024.

‘He was trying to keep it cool all at the same time. He couldn’t quite believe it and at the same instant couldn’t wait to get started.’

So that is how it began in the Midlands of England and has taken Andrea Kimi Antonelli to the madness of Mexico City to become the youngest world champion in history, aged 20, in his second season.

Nine wins transported him to the cusp. He has barely made a mistake, no signs of yips, and, even on days when he has not dominated, a little luck and a lot of discipline have allowed him to tot up the points, so that he was 123 up with only 125 on the table.

But what is he like? Little is known of him to the outside world. He has become Formula One’s most anonymous champion ever. He is young and fresh on the scene and rewriting the script of the sport: you can’t win in your second year, barely out of school, a teenager until a few months ago!

Antonelli was born in Bologna on August 25, 2006, a few weeks after Michael Schumacher announced his retirement from Ferrari

George Russell, Antonelli's nearest challenger 123 points back, has had to deal with a gravitational pull towards his rival

He is, to underline the case, three years younger than Sebastian Vettel, still for a few hours at least the youngest title-holder, having triumphed with Red Bull in 2010 – and Seb had the look of a grungy gap-year student existing on $20 a day.

Antonelli was born in Bologna on August 25, 2006. For context, Michael Schumacher had a few weeks earlier announced his retirement from Ferrari. A few months later McLaren confirmed that Hamilton would race for them the next season. By then, Fernando Alonso was on his way to win his second and final title.

Kimi’s father Marco, here with him in Mexico as a quiet support, was a sports car racing driver and is now owner of the AKM Motorsport racing team, based in San Marino, where Antonelli lives. His mother Veronica Pomaro, who once worked for the Italian postal service, helps Marco run his business. Kimi has a younger sister, Maggie.

He was a glitteringly successful karter as a kid and spotted by Mercedes. They got in there fast, just beating Ferrari to his signature because he was officially too young for the Italian team’s academy scheme.

His father had wanted him to be a footballer but he was drawn to motorsport from an early age and idolised Ayrton Senna, watching DVD videos of the great Brazilian. Lionel Messi is another idol.

Aged nine, he first drove a Lamborghini Super Trofeo while his dad operated the pedals. The die was cast. He learned English, motorsport’s lingua franca, during his race weekends, and he now speaks it very well, and added German to his repertoire when he joined Mercedes.

He brings an infectious enthusiasm to the team and there has been a gravitational pull towards him. Poor George Russell, his nearest challenger those 123 points back before Sunday's race, has had to deal with that, admired though he is within Mercedes with him also being a protege they enlisted at a young age and invested in.

‘Kimi is a character who needs people around him,’ a Mercedes friend of his told Daily Mail Sport. ‘He drapes himself across whichever colleague is close by. He is very close to his race engineer Bono (Peter Bonnington).

'He is also a people’s person and has brought a real sense of fun and mischief to the team. It’s impish fun,' a source said of Antonelli

‘He has one of those personalities that draws people in. He’s simpatico and has a photographic memory for people’s names. He enjoys spending time in the garage and with the car. He treats the car like a living being – touching it and talking to it.

‘But he is also a people’s person and has brought a real sense of fun and mischief to the team. It’s impish fun.’

Since splitting in February after a two-year relationship with Czech Eliska Babickova, a one-time karter, he is single. He is also teetotal.

When he goes back to San Marino, he has a ritual that helps sustain him away from the swirl of high-pressure sport. He hand washes his car, an AMG GT63 Mercedes, which he crashed last year. ‘It is a meditation for him,’ I was told. ‘He does that when he can on a Monday after a race.’

It is a gruelling life in some ways for one so young, with so much of it being spent in the air, getting to and from races. He reckoned that he spent a month on planes last year, albeit a problem alleviated by taking private jets when he can.

The toll was perhaps evident on Thursday when he was excused from media duties due to a virus, a bit of which is going around the paddock. He required a ninth-place finish to end all doubts he will become the first Italian since Alberto Ascari in 1953 to be crowned champion. He claimed third on Sunday as Max Verstappen won in Mexico.

‘There can be challenging moments, times when you lose your privacy because someone has a camera phone and wants to record you when you are out, but I love what I do and I want to keep on in the sport for many years to come,’ he said.

Antonelli smiled, as he is wont to do, a reliable trademark of the ‘impish’ champion presumptive.

Sports.title: Virgil van Dijk and Andoni Iraola hit out after Liverpool denied 'clear penalty' against Arsenal - as Reds boss reveals he will tell Alexander Isak to 'dive on floor' in future
Sports.content:
Andoni Iraola has revealed he will now tell Alexander Isak to 'dive on the floor' as he and Virgil van Dijk hit out at VAR after Liverpool were denied a 'clear penalty' during Sunday's 1-0 defeat by Arsenal. The Gunners ended their 14-year wait for a Premier League victory at Anfield to return to the top of the table, keeping Liverpool at bay with a superb defensive performance after Kai Havertz opened the scoring in the 16th minute. Just minutes after the German's opener, Liverpool striker Isak looked to have a golden opportunity to equalise when he rose to meet Bradley Barcola's cross, only to miss the ball after having his shirt pulled back by Arsenal defender Jurrien Timber. Despite clearly tugging the Swede's shirt, Timber escaped punishment from referee Andy Madley, while VAR opted not to intervene and award Liverpool a penalty despite protests from Iraola and his players. Sky Sports pundits Jamie Carragher, Daniel Sturridge and Ian Wright unanimously agreed Liverpool should have been awarded a penalty at half-time and suggested that Isak was denied the spot-kick because he failed to make more of the incident. Andoni Iraola (right) and Virgil van Dijk (left) hit out at VAR after Liverpool were denied a 'clear penalty' during Arsenal's 1-0 win at Anfield on Sunday Alexander Isak was blatantly pulled back by Jurrien Timber but was not awarded a penalty Iraola thinks the game could have gone differently had Madley not missed Timber's shirt pull. The Liverpool boss said after the match: ‘There are two situations and they are a little bit related. The Isak one is a clear penalty. ‘He's gonna head the ball in front of the goal, and they grab him where everyone sees the shirt. You don't need a lot, just to avoid Alex, because the ball just goes in front of him, and I don't see the reason why, probably because he doesn't dive or he doesn't go to the floor. It shouldn't be a reason not to concede a penalty. Iraola also pointed to a similar situation where Cody Gakpo was tugged back, but the officials said the Dutchman would not get to the ball. ‘They say the ball was too long and Cody wouldn't have arrived to the ball, but then you're basically accepting that the first one is, is a pen, no?’ added Iraola. ‘So you cannot use the argument in both ways differently. So I think it's a, yes, it's a pen, the Alex one is.’ Speaking to Sky Sports after the match, the manager said: 'It's a problem we have with the game. Because he doesn't dive and go to the floor. The fact that you are even asking me if he should go to the floor, if he goes to the floor, they call the penalty 100 per cent. 'It should be like this but it is what it is. Next time, the managers should tell Alex to go to the floor, otherwise they won't call it.' Van Dijk insisted it should not be on his team-mate Isak to make more of the incident Asked if he will tell Isak to do that in future, the Spaniard replied: 'Yes, definitely.' Reds captain Virgil van Dijk took aim at VAR too after the match, expressing his disappointment at the defeat. 'I think it was a clear penalty. I've seen it back and I've seen it being given. Today it wasn't meant to be,' he said. Asked if Isak should have reacted more, the Dutchman added: 'We have 50 cameras. Why does he have to complain when there are so many cameras? 'Everyone has seen it. In the end it wasn't given and we lose the game unfortunately, so well done to Arsenal.' Former Liverpool defender Carragher was furious that VAR had not intervened as he analysed the incident at half-time. 'One of the best goal-scorers in the league is pulled back seven yards from goal, and the pull back stops him heading the ball. Why does he need to make a meal of it? VAR, do your job,' he said bluntly. Arsenal moved to the top of the table on 24 points with victory at Anfield, while Liverpool remained fifth after Brighton and Chelsea, who are third and fourth respectively, both won on Saturday. Mikel Arteta hailed his side’s resilience to win at Anfield. Asked if it feels better to do so as a player or manager, he said: ‘Now it feels better as a manager, it has been such a long time without this feeling. We are extremely proud, especially the conditions we arrived in after the defeat against Fleetwood looked like the end of the world. ‘But then you have to pick yourself up. Four days later you have to come to Anfield against this manager and this team.’

Sports.title: European 1500-metre champion and two-time Olympian, 34, who married her partner last month dies after cancer battle
Sports.content:
European 1500-metre champion and two-time Olympian Ciara Mageean has died aged 34 following a battle with bowel cancer.

The Northern Irish athlete, who represented Ireland at two Olympic Games and claimed European gold in 2024, died on Sunday morning surrounded by her loved ones.

Mageean, from Portaferry in County Down, was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer in May 2025.

Her death comes just weeks after she married her long-term partner Thomas Moran in an intimate civil ceremony in Belfast.

A statement shared on her social media accounts confirmed the news on Sunday. It read: 'At 6.30am this morning, Ciara lost her battle with cancer surrounded by her loved ones.

'A beloved daughter, sister, wife, friend and inspiration to so many, she will be deeply missed. Ar dheis Dé go raibh a hanam [may her soul rest in peace].'

Tributes have poured in for the celebrated middle-distance runner, who became one of Ireland's most successful athletes after overcoming years of injuries and sporting setbacks.

European 1500-metre champion and two-time Olympian Ciara Mageean has died aged 34 following a battle with bowel cancer

Her death comes just weeks after she married her long-term partner Thomas Moran in an intimate civil ceremony in Belfast

Athletics Ireland said in a statement: 'We are heartbroken. An inspiration to so many, Ciara will be remembered for her courage, kindness and incredible spirit.

'Our deepest sympathies are with her family, friends and loved ones at this difficult time. Rest in peace, Ciara.'

Mageean's crowning achievement came at the European Athletics Championships in Rome in June 2024, when she stormed to victory in the women's 1500m final to claim the first major title of her career.

In a dramatic race, she found herself trapped behind British runners Georgia Bell and Jemma Reekie before finding a gap and surging down the home straight to take gold in four minutes 4.66 seconds.

The emotional victory followed years of near-misses on the international stage and cemented her reputation as one of Europe's finest middle-distance runners.

An ecstatic Mageean later admitted that 'words can't even come close' to describing her feelings after finally securing the coveted title.

But her hopes of adding an Olympic medal to her collection were cruelly dashed just weeks later when an Achilles injury forced her to withdraw from the Paris Games on the eve of her opening heat.

It was the latest in a series of injury setbacks that had repeatedly threatened to derail her career.

Mageean had previously represented Ireland at the Rio Olympics in 2016, where she reached the 1500m semi-finals, and the delayed Tokyo Games in 2021, where a calf injury hampered her preparations and she was eliminated in the heats.

Her sporting talent had been evident from childhood, when she played camogie for Portaferry GAC before turning her attention to athletics in pursuit of her Olympic ambitions.

She enjoyed a glittering junior career, winning silver medals over 1500m at the 2010 World Junior Championships and the 2011 European Junior Championships.

At just 18, she also reached the 1500m final at the 2010 Commonwealth Games.

The Northern Irish athlete, who represented Ireland at two Olympic Games and claimed European gold in 2024, passed away on Sunday morning surrounded by her loved ones

However, a serious ankle injury subsequently ended her hopes of competing at London 2012 and required surgery in 2013.

She fought her way back to win the Irish 1500m title in 2014 before claiming European bronze in Amsterdam two years later.

In 2017, she moved from Dublin to Manchester to join Steve Vernon's Team New Balance after parting ways with coach Jerry Kiernan.

Her career continued to flourish, with a European Indoor bronze medal in 2019 followed by a series of record-breaking performances.

In 2020, she shattered Sonia O'Sullivan's 27-year-old Irish 1,000m record at the Diamond League meeting in Monaco.

Two years later, under the guidance of former British Olympian Helen Clitheroe, Mageean won silver medals at both the European Championships and the Commonwealth Games in Birmingham, finishing behind Britain's Laura Muir.

She subsequently defeated Muir and a world-class field at the Brussels Diamond League meeting, breaking O'Sullivan's Irish 1500m record with a time of 3:56.63.

In 2023, she narrowly missed out on a World Championships medal after finishing fourth in Budapest, but broke the Irish mile record and was named BBC Northern Ireland Sports Personality of the Year.

Her long-awaited European triumph in Rome the following summer was the pinnacle of a career defined by extraordinary resilience.

Following her cancer diagnosis, Mageean spoke movingly about her gratitude for the life she had enjoyed and the opportunities athletics had given her.

Earlier this year, she said she was 'continuing to find the joy in every day' as she thanked supporters for their messages.

Speaking to the BBC in June, she said she was 'grateful' for having a career 'that many others didn't get to have'.

In a poignant interview with The Irish Times in June, Mageean had spoken candidly about her terminal diagnosis and the prospect of leaving her partner behind.

She revealed that doctors had warned she might have just two or three years left to live, admitting she feared she would not reach her 40th birthday.

Despite the devastating prognosis, she remained determined to make the most of her remaining time, publishing a memoir, My Greatest Race, and going ahead with her wedding plans.

Just days before her death, Mageean and her husband celebrated their marriage with family and friends at Darver Castle in County Louth, following their earlier civil ceremony in Belfast.

The couple's celebrations marked a final joyful chapter in the life of an athlete whose determination and achievements had inspired thousands across Ireland and beyond.

Taoiseach Micheal Martin said he was deeply saddened by the news.

'My heartfelt sympathies go to her husband Thomas, all her family and friends,' he said in a statement on the social media network X.

Tanaiste Simon Harris described the news as heartbreaking.

He said on X: 'She was a European champion, two-time Olympian, a proud Irish athlete and an extraordinary person.'

Northern Ireland's First Minister Michelle O'Neill said Mageean demonstrated 'extraordinary talent, determination and dedication'.

'From representing Ireland at two Olympic Games to winning European Championship gold in Rome in 2024, Ciara demonstrated extraordinary talent, determination and dedication,' she said.

'However, beyond the medals, records and sporting accolades, Ciara will be remembered for her warmth, courage and tremendous strength of character.

'Throughout her illness, she showed a remarkable spirit and an incredible ability to find hope and joy in life, even in the most difficult circumstances. Her courage touched countless people and will leave a lasting legacy.

'For a community like Portaferry, this loss will be deeply felt. Ciara was one of our own, and the pride she brought to her community and beyond will never be forgotten.'

Sports.title: First Anfield victory for 14 years was vindication for Mikel Arteta after Fleetwood humbling. His Arsenal look the finished article - Liverpool were authors of their own downfall, writes OLIVER HOLT
Sports.content:
Five nights ago, 40 miles to the north of Anfield at a remote outpost of English football, Arsenal fell to one of the most humiliating reverses of their long and august history. In the teeth of a gale that blew in off the Irish Sea, they were knocked out of the League Cup by Fleetwood Town, a team 18th in League Two.

They left with their tails between their legs, their teenage prodigy Max Dowman sent off in a melee, their heart questioned, their quality debated, their discipline an issue. Mikel Arteta and his side knew that just a few days later, at the other end of the Fylde Coast and across the Ribble Estuary, they would have to swap running the gauntlet of the Cod Army for the challenge of facing down the roar of the Kop.

They did not shirk it. If Tuesday night was a humbling, their gritty 1-0 victory in an Anfield that was a cauldron once more felt like a significant triumph. It was a defensive masterclass from the champions, an exercise in indomitability. It was their first victory here since 2012 and it took them above Manchester City so that they sit, once more, at the top of the table. Liverpool could not summon a single shot on target.

‘It felt like the end of the world when we were knocked out at Fleetwood,’ Arteta said after this win. ‘You look so silly. I was thinking “How can I lift these players up?” You have to dig deep. This was a mission to win here and it is something that we have not done for 14 years for a variety of reasons. We knew we would have to navigate some difficult moments.’

If Arteta left Fleetwood answering questions about his management of Dowman, he finished this game by striding on to the pitch after the final whistle, pumping his fists in front of the Arsenal fans celebrating in the Anfield Road end, and beating his hand on his chest. This was a vindication for him and his team. Five nights is a long time in football.

He had talked about the harsh realities of this sport after Tuesday’s loss. He had reminded everyone that playing at this level was not like ‘Disneyland’. And this victory was not like Disneyland, either. It was less a theme park and more an assault course. It was rough and it was unforgiving and Arsenal were equal to it.

Liverpool, improving under the management of Andoni Iraola, had been talked up as title contenders ahead of this match on a dank evening on Merseyside where the streets around the ground were decorated with the toothless grimaces of rotting pumpkins on doorsteps. The home team showed exhilarating signs of their re-emergence as an attacking force.

They dominated much of the game, too, but they looked like an emerging team, a team that is still evolving. Arsenal, marshalled imperiously by Declan Rice, looked like the finished article. They created one outstanding chance and Kai Havertz converted it. That was all they needed.

Their defence stayed rock-solid, although there was some puzzlement that Liverpool were not awarded a penalty for Jurrien Timber’s blatant shirt-pull on Alexander Isak. After the interval, Liverpool rarely looked like drawing level.

Kai Havertz gave the Gunners a lead to defend after finishing off a well worked move early on

The German slotted home after Declan Rice fizzed a dangerous ball across the six-yard box

Winning at Anfield was vindication for Mikel Arteta after Arsenal's defeat by Fleetwood Town

The opening had been predictably frenetic. Neither team forged a chance but Trey Nyoni, who has forced his way into the first team with a series of excellent performances in midfield, could have been booked twice inside the first quarter of an hour.

The initial infringement was a nasty tackle on Martin Odegaard inside the first minute where he planted his studs in Odegaard’s ankle. The second was a spiteful tackle on Kai Havertz. Neither received a yellow card, which gave yet more pause for thought about the red card shown to Dowman at Fleetwood, and its aftermath.

Let’s get one thing straight – the criticism of Arteta for his ‘treatment’ of Dowman was absurd. It has come to something when a manager giving a player a hard stare is interpreted by some as a disproportionate response.

Nobody is necessarily hankering after a return to the days of Sir Alex Ferguson’s hairdrier or Joe Kinnear’s rants that broke records for expletives but if a boss is attracting censure because he looked at a player a bit funny, we are in big trouble.

Arteta is not there to indulge Dowman. He is there to coach him and to teach him and to help him grow up in the context of a Premier League football club. His actions in Fleetwood on Tuesday fulfilled his obligations in all of those criteria.

Arsenal survived the initial frenzy here and took the lead after 16 minutes. Liverpool were the authors of their own downfall. They gave the ball away from a goal kick, it was worked to Noni Madueke on the right, and when Madueke fed it to Declan Rice on the overlap, Rice crossed beautifully for Havertz, who touched it home at the back post.

Arsenal nearly returned the favour a minute later when they played themselves into trouble at the back. Bradley Barcola found himself through on David Raya but his first touch let him down and Rice moved across to clear the danger.

Alexis Mac Allister was left with his head in his hands after missing a glorious chance to score

Liverpool's 19-year-old talent Trey Nyoni started the match but was replaced in the second half

Liverpool recovered and began to dominate the game. Barcola’s pace began to cause Arsenal all sorts of problems down their right flank and Liverpool came close to an equaliser when Virgil van Dijk flicked on a corner and Alexander Isak was denied by the brave intervention of Raya.

Arsenal were still threatening on the counter. Christos Tzolis chipped a ball to the back post and, as Liverpool scrambled to clear it, Madueke turned it back across goal. The ball was intended for Havertz, who was unmarked in the middle, but Timber could not get out of the way of it and it bounced off him into touch.

The atmosphere was febrile. Liverpool had three appeals for penalties, first for Timber’s shirt pull on Isak, then for challenges on Alexis Mac Allister and Cody Gakpo, turned down in quick succession. Tempers began to flare on the benches.

The breathlessness of the match was relentless. Florian Wirtz drove a free kick against the face of the crossbar with Raya beaten and then, three minutes before the interval, Mac Allister ran on to a cross from Milos Kerkez and, with the goal at his mercy, directed his free header too high.

Liverpool laid siege to the Arsenal goal after the break but the openings just would not come. Isak blazed high over the bar from an angle, Wirtz had a shot on the turn blocked and then, just before the hour, Dominik Szoboszlai replaced Nyoni and, to more acclaim, Rio Ngumoha came on for Gakpo.

Still Liverpool could not prise Arsenal open. Arsenal began to grow in confidence and threat. The home team The home team were grateful to Jeremy Jacquet for a clearance that prevented Odegaard turning Tzolis’s cross into an open goal, for Van Dijk’s brilliant interception to deny Havertz and, most of all, for a quite magnificent one-handed save from Alisson that diverted a Tzolis shot round the post. It will stand the test of time as one of the saves of the season.

Arsenal put in another excellent defensive display to frustrate and keep Liverpool at bay

Liverpool’s frustration boiled over. Mac Allister was booked for his part in an ugly fracas with Odegaard and Madueke. The stands became a mass of pointing fingers and shouts of protest and anger. Time-wasting and play-acting peppered the match. Liverpool felt the game slipping away in the angst.

Liverpool threw everything at it in the final minutes. Lewis Koumas flung himself at a bouncing ball but could not get enough power on his header, Ngumoha had a shot charged down, Barcola desperately searched for pockets of space but could not find them. There were six minutes of time added on but there was no way through. Arsenal’s defence would not yield.

Sports.title: After Robbie Fowler claimed the moon landing is 'bulls***' and dubious Joe Cole said he has 'questions' for Neil Armstrong... who makes our ultimate XI of football conspiracy theorists?
Sports.content:
Robbie Fowler certainly helped to draw attention to his new podcast with his former Liverpool and England team-mate Steve McManaman this week by airing his views on the 1969 moon landing. After answering fan questions ranging from favourite films, comedians and useless talents, Fowler responded to McManaman's prompt of the moon landing as a conspiracy theory. 'I think the moon landing is bulls*** to be fair,' with an excited McManaman declaring 'that is a massive one,' before declaring his subsequent reasoning made 'perfect sense'. He is far from the only footballer to have doubts, with another ex-England international Joe Cole declaring he would like to sit down with Neil Armstrong – who died in 2012 – to get to the bottom of it. Fowler later quipped he is 'not a flat earther' having been up on a plane. However, some former footballers are, while others have raised a wide range of conspiracies, ranging from the small scale to the more wild. Here, Daily Mail Sport puts together our ultimate XI of football's conspiracy theorists. Former Liverpool forward Robbie Fowler admitted this week he believes the moon landing is 'bulls***' Source: YouTube - We'll have a look podcast GK: David Icke For many, David Icke is football's original conspiracy theorist – so entrenched in his off-the-wall beliefs and so willing to share them publicly that he is more widely known as a crackpot than a goalkeeper. Nevertheless, Icke turned out for Coventry City's youth set-up between the sticks in the late 1960s, and later played for semi-professional outfit Hereford United before hanging up his boots and pivoting to sports journalism. While his playing career might have been small-fry, his commitment to conspiracy theories is Premier League. Among his often-cited beliefs is the idea that an inter-dimensional race of reptile-like shape-shifters – the 'Babylon Brotherhood' have infiltrated the upper echelons of global society. Among the accused are the late Queen Mother, the Rockefeller and Rothschild families, and former Prime Minister Edward Heath, whose eyes, Icke alleged, he saw turn 'jet black' when the pair met in 1989. Icke also believes that the 'Illuminati' at the top of the global food chain organised world events including Dunblane, 9/11, the assassination of John F Kennedy, the death of Princess Diana to prompt their subsequent responses. Less laughable is the thick seam of anti-Semitism which critics believe runs through his thinking, although Icke has denied this. For many, David Icke is football's original conspiracy theorist, with one of his cited beliefs is the idea that reptile-like shape-shifters have infiltrated the upper echelons of global society RB: Javi Poves Javi Poves endured a similarly unmemorable professional playing career in Spain, but did at least register one La Liga appearance with Sporting Gijon. Then, he quit. It was a matter of principle: he had grown to believe that 'professional football is only money and corruption'. Not an unreasonable view point, from some perspectives, but years on from his 2011 resignation things become somewhat more surreal. Poves joined lower-division Madrid club Mostoles Balompie in 2016 and later became the club's president. In 2019, he renamed the club Flat Earth FC, to draw attention to his primary cause. 'Football is the most popular sport and has the most impact worldwide, so creating a club dedicated to the flat earth movement is the best way to have a constant presence in the media,' he said that year. 'Flat Earth FC is the first football club whose followers are united by the most important thing, which is an idea.' Although Poves has since moved to fellow amateur side CDC Moscardo, he remains passionately committed to the idea that the earth is flat and not round, and other environmentally-rooted conspiracy theories. These include viewing 'chemtrails' as a deployment of toxic chemicals, and refusing to believe that suncream can help prevent skin cancer. CB: Dejan Lovren One thread which runs through a number of players included in the XI is a scepticism of Covid-19. Some, like Sol Campbell, have suggested that the pandemic was in some way man-made. Icke is in the camp which believes that the lockdown and vaccination scheme was akin to governmental 'facism'. Lovren was firmly in team Icke during the lockdown years, posting a number of his videos on social media. He also used social media to attack Microsoft billionaire Bill Gates, implying some kind of conspiracy with his comment: 'Game over Bill. People are not blind' on Gates's online tribute to health workers. The Croatian defender seemed particularly swayed by Icke's theories around the links between Covid-19 and 5G technology in 'controlling' populations, with Lovren resharing clips with the caption 'we will not be censored'. Dejan Lovren supported Icke's views during the pandemic and hit out at Bill Gates Lovren took to Instagram to promote an interview with Icke during the pandemic CB: Sol Campbell As mentioned in Lovren's section, Campbell also had his suspicions during the Covid-19 pandemic. Then managing Southend United, in May 2020, Campbell appeared to suggest that he believed the disease was made deliberately and designed to target certain population groups. 'Was this virus a natural mistake or a designed mistake...?' he posted on social media. 'I wonder does this virus deliberately attacks a certain blood type.....?' Campbell shared his idea alongside a screenshot of an article citing an ONS report that showed Black people were four times more likely to die from Covid-19 than any other ethnic group. He later was widely derided for having no scientific evidence to support his argument. Sol Campbell appeared to suggest in 2020 he believed Covid-`9 was made deliberately and designed to target certain population groups Campbell shared his idea alongside a screenshot of an article citing an ONS report that showed Black people were four times more likely to die from Covid-19 than any other ethnic group LB: Fabian Delph The former Manchester City defender has previously admitted to a conspiracy theory that has more sympathetic readers nodding in approval: he believes in ghosts. Delph admitted in 2016 that he sees ghosts 'all the time', adding that 'genuinely' he had seen about 'four'. 'When I first signed for (Aston) Villa I stayed in a hotel there was lots of things moving in the room, a lot of bangs,' he told Man City's official YouTube channel. 'And about four months ago I saw, in my house in God's country (Yorkshire), I saw two ghosts in my bedroom.' 'I don't think they're there to harm me. But I've definitely seen them. It was just a split second and then they were gone. 'The one four months ago, that actually was carrying a body, it went out onto my balcony, then disappeared.' Joe Cole admitted he is open to having his head turnedabout the moon landings and would be keen to sit down with Neil Armstrong to 'get to the bottom of things' RM: Joe Cole Compared to how some of the other members of Daily Mail Sport's XI have at times risked public safety or aired unpleasant and divisive views, Cole's position on the 1969 Moon Landings feels somewhat milquetoast. Additionally, unlike many, he admitted that he is open to having his head turned, with Cole keen to sit down with Neil Armstrong, the first man on the moon, to 'get to the bottom' of things. 'I'm not sold either way and I need some convincing. I want to believe it, honestly,' Cole told FourFourTwo. 'But I've heard too much about it being fake - things like the flag waving and the footprints and all the rest of it. 'I would love to sit down with a man who actually went there and be convinced. I want him to tell me exactly how it all went down and some of the science behind my questions. 'I just want to put it to bed. If anyone could convince me, it's the first man to have apparently visited the moon. I don't mind being talked round to new ideas which is why I'd be more than happy for him to tell me how silly I'm being. 'That's what makes you evolve as a human being. You have to be open to different ideas in life.' CM: Marcos Llorente If Pove represents a distinctly Spanish-style conspiracy theorist, Marcos Llorente treads the well-beaten path, with his primary focus the benefits of sunlight – to the extent of snubbing suncream – and a suspicion of 'chemtrails'. Llorente takes his theories on natural light and the sun to the extreme, however. A staunch advocate of the blue light-blocking sunglasses also favoured by stars including Erling Haaland, the Atletico Madrid midfielder also eschews unnatural light sources in his house after dark. Instead, Llorente works on soaking up as much red light as possible. In the sun, Llorente takes it one step further, frequently sharing incorrect views on suncream's impact on Vitamin D and dismissing the connection between skin cancer and unprotected skin. Marcos Llorente is a committed wearer of blue light-blocking glasses in a bid to boost his melatonin Llorente has frequently endorsed the repeatedly debunked theory that 'chemtrails' are the result of government or corporate intervention Llorente often does so in a tongue-in-cheek way: in April, he dressed up as a bottle of suncream, but with a twist. Written on the bottle in Spanish were messages reading: 'Protect against your biology' and 'Blocking Vitamin D since 1985'. On the back of the bottle costume in lieu of ingredients, Llorente drew a graph of rising skin cancer rates and an accompanying message. 'Get in the shade when your body tells you, 'That's enough'. Get sun exposure year-round, not just three days in August,' the 'warning label' read. 'Use clothing as sun protection. Start in the morning and work your way up (don't start at 1pm). 'Build melanin gradually. Eat a balanced diet so your skin responds better. Stay hydrated and connect with nature.' More recently Llorente, a bon viveur and lover of rare steak, 'bulletproof' butter coffee and good wine, has intensified his stance on other medical theories, including alleging that high cholesterol or 'bad' cholesterol does not have an impact on health. CM: Matt Le Tissier Matt Le Tissier is no single-issue conspiracy theorist, with the Southampton icon borderline indiscriminate about the wide range of his causes. Like many, his outpourings amplified amid the pandemic, with Le Tissier frequently opining on the efficacy of vaccines and painting 'big pharma' as a bogeyman. Then, in 2022, he was stood down from his role as Saints ambassador after peddling Russian lies that the massacre at Bucha, in Ukraine, had been fabricated. This came despite the fact that there was video, satellite, and photographic evidence that Russia had murdered over 320 people in the town. Earlier this year, Le Tissier found himself in a spat with Grok, X's AI chatbot, over 'chemtrails', asking: 'Hey (Grok), why do some plane trails disperse quickly while others hang around and spread out to form grey blanket clouds?' The bot had responded that the contrails lingered or didn't due to atmospheric conditions, much to Le Tissier's displeasure, with the former midfielder grumbling that Grok was 'spouting government propaganda'. Matt Le Tissier, pictured taking a selfie at a Southampton game in February, has frequently raised conspiracy theories over social media

Your browser does not support iframes.

LM: David Cotterill Former Wales international David Cotterill sparked widespread backlash in 2022 when he referred to 'false flag events' using 'crisis actors' at the whim of 'controllers' within hours of a fatal school shooting in Texas. Cotterill said in the incendiary post that 'false flag events are one of their go to methods of manipulating the public opinion to bring about change'. He also alleged: 'America is the last major country that allows it's [sic] citizens to arm themselves. Which they can't really have with what they're planning to do in the coming months and years.' Cotterill later stressed that the post had not been related to the Texas massacre, instead stating that his post was 'just about recent articles when you see some of the stuff about the pandemic'. He similarly received intense criticism when he suggested that the retirement of Brighton's 24-year-old Enock Mwepu due to cardiac issues was linked to side effect of the Covid-19 vaccine. Cotterill remains unrepentant however, recently appearing on a podcast where he admitted that he supports 'everything' Le Tissier says, and revealed his belief in 2016's discredited Pizzagate conspiracy, among other conspiracy theories. 'I've gone into so many rabbit holes. If you see lots of things happening in the world with the number 33, which is obviously massive for Freemasonry and symbolism,' he told Made in Brum Podcast. 'If you see a lot of things that happen in the world, 33 is not far from that. Some people think I'm f***ing nuts. David Cotterill sparked widespread backlash in 2022 when he referred to 'false flag events' using 'crisis actors' at the whim of 'controllers' within hours of a fatal school shooting in Texas ST: Rickie Lambert Former Liverpool and Southampton star Rickie Lambert is among this cohort's Covid-19 conspiracy theorists, starting off on social media as a staunch vaccine sceptic - only to fall deeper into more fringe views. Unusually, in 2023, Lambert claimed that he believed that one can change the molecular structure of water based on speaking to a glass of the substance positively or negatively. 'The one word where water responds in the most beautiful way, with the most beautiful crystals, is showing gratitude to water,' Lambert said. More recently, Lambert has been an active supporter of the campaign against '15-minute cities', whose detractors believe is a government scheme to control the movement and rights of people, rather than an attempt to provide walkable goods and services. Ahead of attending a protest in Liverpool in September 2023, Lambert's call to arms to publicise the event stressed that the scheme was 'a controlled tactic being implemented across this country' and that Merseyside was set to be put under permanent surveillance. Rickie Lambert has claimed talking positively to water makes it clean ST: Robbie Fowler Like Cole, Fowler appears to have merely dipped a toe into the world of conspiratorial thinking, and has similarly alighted on the Moon Landing as the target of his suspicion. Unlike the former Chelsea star however, there seemed to be little that would change his mind when he discussed the topic with his We'll Have A Look podcast with co-host Steve McManaman. 'I think the Moon Landing is bulls***, to be fair,' Fowler said. 'Because there was a race in the Sixties, between the Americans and the USSR. 'All of a sudden, the USSR were ahead of the Americans (after Yuri Gagarin became the first man in space) and all of a sudden, the Americans got there first. 'I think it's a bit far-fetched. I don't know, that is the general gist of what I'm saying - I just don't think it was real.'
