World.title: Carney signals progress on Canada-US trade deal talks as midterms loom
World.content:
Canadian PM Carney announces progress in Canada-US trade deal talks ahead of US midterm elections on November 3.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced progress towards a future trade deal with the United States, which could help ease tensions between the two North American neighbours.

The Sunday announcement came just two days before the November 3 US midterm elections, which will determine control of the US Congress.

“Good conversation with US President Donald Trump on the future of Canada-U.S. trade,” Carney posted on X on Sunday.

Ties between Ottawa and Washington have been strained by an escalating trade war, with Canada and the US imposing billions of dollars in tariffs on each other’s goods in recent months.

“Teams from both countries will be working in the coming weeks to deliver that outcome,” Carney said. “This builds on recent constructive discussions on the outlines of a mutually beneficial trade deal.”

In his second term, Trump has upended global trade by imposing tariffs on many of the US’s allies, including Canada – one of the US’s biggest trading partners.

In August, high-level trade talks between Ottawa and Washington broke down, and Trump imposed a 50 percent levy on $20bn of Canadian goods, or 5.5 percent of its exports. Canada responded with equivalent tariffs on US steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.

Trump said last week that he expected a new trade agreement with Canada to be reached “pretty soon”, but offered no details.

The trade tensions with Canada have become an issue in the midterm elections, particularly in Michigan and Maine, where Republican candidates have faced pressure over tariffs that have hurt local businesses.



Canada has sought to diversify its trade options and recently welcomed a European Union offer to become an “associate member”.

Carney praised the proposal’s ambition, describing his goal as a “unique alliance” rather than conventional EU membership.

World.title: Why did Democrat Haley Stevens just endorse a Republican for US Senate?
World.content:
Stevens’s endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers comes after a bitter dispute with Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed.

Share Why did Democrat Haley Stevens just endorse a Republican for US Senate? on social media

A Democratic congresswoman has thrown her support behind a Republican in one of the most closely watched races of the US midterm elections, just two days before voters head to the polls.

Haley Stevens, who lost Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary in August, announced on Sunday that she was endorsing Republican Mike Rogers over her own party’s nominee, Abdul El-Sayed.

The decision follows weeks of tension between the two Democrats over Israel and has provoked a backlash within the party as it fights to win control of Congress and limit President Donald Trump’s power.

Here’s what we know.

Who is Haley Stevens?

Stevens is a Democratic congresswoman from Michigan who narrowly lost the party’s Senate primary to El-Sayed, a former public health official who could become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.

Despite a bitter primary battle, Stevens promised to support El-Sayed and said as recently as Wednesday that she still wanted him to win.

That was despite her fiance, Jason Turkish, a Jewish Democrat and civil rights lawyer, announcing that he would vote for Rogers. Turkish – who, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) reports, has donated nearly $250,000 to both Democrats and Republicans during this midterm cycle – accused El-Sayed of anti-Semitism, saying his rhetoric about Israel and its genocidal war in Gaza had made Jewish voters feel unsafe.

And on Sunday, Stevens changed her position.

Why did Stevens endorse Republican Mike Rogers?

The decision followed weeks of tension over Israel that became increasingly public in the final days of the campaign.



Stevens is a strong supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed has been an outspoken critic of Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza and US military aid to the country.

Their differences were also a major issue during the Democratic primary, when a super PAC affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) spent tens of millions of dollars to back Stevens.

But the latest dispute began last week, when an independent group backing El-Sayed, Rebellion PAC, released an  linking US military aid to Israel to Americans’ struggles with the cost of living.

The ad shows a couple shopping for groceries who decide to put back a carton of eggs because they need to save that money for “killing Palestinians”.

Stevens called the ad anti-Semitic and demanded that El-Sayed condemn it. She also accused him of making similar arguments by suggesting that money spent on Israel could instead go towards schools, healthcare and childcare.

El-Sayed said the ad was not produced by his campaign and that he disagreed with its message, adding that Stevens was trying to relitigate their primary rather than focusing on defeating Rogers.

The tensions came to a head on Sunday, when Stevens and El-Sayed were supposed to attend a church service together in a show of Democratic unity, but Stevens was uninvited.

“Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away,” she said in a video on X, announcing she was going to endorse Rogers.

“And he’s right. And that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today.”

But Democratic Congresswoman Debbie Dingell, who helped organise the event, said she was the one who asked Stevens not to attend, telling The Associated Press that “it had become way too distracting”.

Stevens also criticised El-Sayed’s association with political streamer Hasan Piker, whose uncle, Cenk Uygur, founded the PAC that released the ad.

Stevens told reporters on Sunday, with Rogers standing beside her: “We can’t stand with hate. We can’t stand with Hasan Piker”.

She insisted she was still a Democrat and planned to vote for Democratic candidates in 90 percent of the races on her ballot, but said her Senate vote would go to Rogers.

How have Democrats reacted?

Her decision has drawn an angry response from Democrats, including some of the party’s most senior figures.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called the endorsement a “despicable betrayal”, saying Senate Democrats remained united behind El-Sayed.



He brushed off questions about whether Stevens had betrayed the Democratic Party, saying he was more concerned about the issues facing Michigan voters.

“At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” he told reporters. “I’m just less interested in the politics of it all than I am in the policy of it all.”

He urged voters to focus instead on healthcare, civil rights and the differences between his campaign and that of Rogers, who is backed by Trump.

The Democratic National Committee (DNC) issued a blistering statement in response to what the organization described as Stevens’ “last-minute political stunts”.

“Haley Stevens’ disappointing decision to endorse Mike Rogers, a Trump ally who would join Republican efforts to sell out working families, is a betrayal of the values of the Democratic Party,” DNC Chair Ken Martin said. “At a moment when Democrats are united in fighting for Michigan families and standing up to Trump’s agenda, we reject these efforts to sow division within our party.”

The local arm of the DNC, the Michigan Democratic Party (MDP), also had strong words for Haley’s endorsement of Rogers.

“Haley Stevens’ decision to campaign with Rogers … shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about”, MDP Chair Curtis Hertel said. “We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum, and will not allow these eleventh-hour distractions deter us”.

Stevens’s decision also prompted resignations within her own team. Her chief of staff for eight years, Justin German, announced that he and several other staff members had stepped down over the endorsement.

“We are shocked and heartbroken by Congresswoman Stevens’s decision to support Mike Rogers,” German said in a statement first shared by CNN.

Trump, meanwhile, celebrated her decision.

“Wow, this is BIG!” he wrote in a social media post on Sunday before saying, during a rally in Iowa later in the day, he’d “love” if Stevens joined the Republican Party.

“Haley said what few people are willing to say,” Trump added. “It’s a thing called bravery.”

Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson, who flew with Trump to Iowa, also celebrated Stevens, telling reporters he sent the congresswoman a note after her “courageous” endorsement.

“Haley’s a good person. She’s always been very thoughtful”, Johnson said as he described Michigan’s Senate race as a “contrast” election. “She loves her state. She’s served it as best she could. She’s speaking the truth.”

Could Stevens’s endorsement affect the Michigan Senate race?

El-Sayed and Rogers are competing to replace retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters, in a closely contested race that could help determine which party controls the US Senate.

Republicans currently control both chambers of Congress, and Democrats are hoping to win enough seats to challenge Trump’s agenda and increase scrutiny of his administration.

Stevens defeated El-Sayed in Wayne County, which includes Detroit, and neighbouring Oakland County, drawing support from Black and Jewish Democratic voters. Both counties are Democratic strongholds where turnout could help determine Tuesday’s result.



The question now is whether Stevens’s endorsement could convince some of her supporters to back Rogers, or discourage them from voting altogether.

Polling suggests El-Sayed has largely consolidated Democratic support, according to Reuters.

Early voting began on October 24, before the latest dispute erupted.

World.title: Al Jazeera Director General hails 30 years of groundbreaking news
World.content:
NewsFeed Al Jazeera Director General hails 30 years of groundbreaking news

Al Jazeera has marked 30 years since its first broadcast in 1996, with a ceremony in Doha attended by Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani. Director General Sheikh Nasser bin Faisal Al Thani called for renewal, to protect the network’s independence and values.

World.title: Bulgaria’s acting President Iotova leads in run-off exit polls
World.content:
Iliana Iotova would become the nation’s first elected female president if results confirm her win on Monday.

Bulgaria’s acting President Iliana Iotova is leading the presidential election run-off, according to exit polls in the race overshadowed by drone attacks on ships off the country’s Black Sea coast.

Iotova, who advocates for dialogue with Moscow and opposes military aid to Ukraine, won just over half the vote in Sunday’s run-off, according to three exit polls, reported Bulgaria’s official news agency, BTA.

Iotova had 51 percent compared to about 44 percent for her rival, Andrey Gyurov, who is backed by the pro-Western opposition.

Exit polls put voter participation at about 27 to 29 percent, slightly higher ‌than the first-round race last week, which had a record-low turnout of 23 percent.

Official results are expected on Monday as ballots are counted for the presidency which is largely ceremonial.

If confirmed, Iotova would become Bulgaria’s first elected female president.

The 61-year-old took over as acting president in January, when her longtime ally Prime Minister Rumen Radev resigned to run in, and win, a parliamentary election.

“I don’t like either of the two candidates,” Krassimira Kostova, a 64-year-old teacher in the capital Sofia, who voted anyway, told the AFP news agency.

Petar Doitchinov, a 67-year-old retired engineer, said he had skipped the first round last week because he expected a run-off. He said he voted for “the lesser evil”, as neither candidate matched his “vision of democracy”.

The vote comes as 21 people remain missing following a series of drone attacks last month on commercial vessels off the country’s Black Sea coast. They are suspected to be spillover from the Russia-Ukraine war.



PM Radev has said that the attacks appear to serve Russian interests and summoned the Russian ambassador, though his government said there was no evidence directly linking them to Moscow.

Both presidential candidates have condemned the attacks and called for a diplomatic end to the war in Ukraine.

Gyurov, a banker and former caretaker prime minister, criticised Iotova in a television debate for not explicitly blaming Russia. “Russia must stop its aggression so that the next steps can be taken,” he said.

Iotova said “peace can come only through negotiations”. After voting, she said she wanted “Bulgaria to be strong in a strong Europe” and “sovereign in its decisions”.

In the first round of voting last week, Iotova won 35 percent, with Gyurov on 32 percent – a much narrower gap than the 20-point lead predicted by opinion polls for Iotova.

Political analyst Teodor Slavev told AFP that voters were passing judgement on “Iotova’s unconvincing response regarding Russian threats in the Black Sea”.

World.title: French officials eye social media’s role in promoting unrest.
World.content:
Pinned

Hundreds of thousands of protesters took to the streets in cities across France again on Saturday, the latest expression of national grievance that has led to clashes between protesters and the police and kept the country on edge.

As dusk fell and official rallies wound down, unauthorized marches splintered off in Paris, stoking fresh fears of chaos as night approached.

Adding to those fears: Halloween, which falls on Saturday. The French authorities, citing calls on social media for people to revolt that encouraged them to wear masks and costumes, warned that the risk of a new outbreak of violence was high.

In Paris, tensions began flaring between protesters and the police in the late afternoon, as officers fired tear gas at people who refused to disperse. The Paris police estimated that 70,000 people marched in the demonstration, compared with 110,000 last Saturday. After the main demonstration ended, hundreds of protesters, many masked and clad in black, formed an unauthorized procession in eastern Paris.

The interior ministry estimated that nationwide, 320,000 people demonstrated, compared with 410,000 last week. Protesters and the police also clashed in Marseille, Lyon, Toulouse, and Rennes.

Corentin Schnell, a 19-year-old engineering student, took part in the unauthorized march in Paris because, he said, he was angered by accounts of the police using tear gas and stun grenades against protesters in past weeks. “I’ve come to demonstrate and to try to provide medical care — to limit the damage, regardless of which side it’s on,” he said.

Earlier in the week, France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, promised to deploy 70,000 police officers, matching the numbers on Oct. 24. That operation helped keep a lid on outbreaks of arson and looting, although then, too, there were clashes as the police tried to disperse the crowds in the evening.

There was ample fuel for a repeat of those combustible scenes. Students, who are returning to school on Monday after a two-week break, were not mollified by the government’s initial response to their demands. The Education Ministry agreed to cap some class sizes, offer low-interest loans to rebuild school buildings and phase out an unpopular online college admissions platform.

The students vowed to go on protesting. Their two-month-old movement has grown to include university students, public workers and veterans of the “yellow vest” movement that convulsed France from 2018 to 2020.

The authorities have said they are most worried about trouble breaking out after nightfall.

“We are seeing numerous calls to gather coming from the far left, the radicalized extreme left, and from certain radicalized ‘yellow vests’ websites, which are urging people to attend rallies or public gatherings starting at 8 p.m. in many cities across France,” Mr. Nuñez said at a news conference.

Some of the messages were violent, Mr. Nuñez said, calling for “revolution” and “insurrection.” Those gatherings will be forbidden, and any attempt to gather despite the ban will lead to arrests, he said.

Demonstrators have been encouraged on social media to turn up wearing Halloween costumes. Mr. Nuñez warned that it was a criminal offense to conceal one’s face during a demonstration that disrupted public order.

Here’s what else to know.

Social media: French officials are increasingly concerned about social media’s role in attracting people and inciting violent behavior. Speculation that the government considered temporarily suspending several popular sites drew a denial from President Emmanuel Macron himself. Read more ›

Far-right activists: While the government has blamed far-left activists for much of the mayhem, officials confirmed that bands of young men with links to the far right have also infiltrated the demonstrations. They use the pretext of protecting shop owners but often clash with far-left groups.

Widening movement: The nationwide unrest in France began with a handful of student demonstrations at high schools in suburban Paris last month. Read more ›

Giulia Imbert contributed reporting.

World.title: Newly Freed American Describes His Years in Russian Prison
World.content:
Stephen James Hubbard, the 74-year-old retired American teacher freed last week by Russia after the intervention of President Trump, said he sometimes lost hope over the more than four years he was imprisoned on fabricated charges of being a Ukrainian mercenary. He read his mother’s Bible, which his captors let him keep. He spoke no Russian and barely communicated with anyone. Once, he was allowed to call one of his sons for about a minute.

But in mid-October, his Russian guard came and fitted him for a new coat. The guard leaned forward and whispered one English word into Mr. Hubbard’s ear: “Home.”

“I’ve been told many times I was going to be set free,” Mr. Hubbard said, describing his reaction to the news from the guard. “So I’m just waiting to see if it happens, and I can believe it if it happens. If it doesn’t, it’s OK.”

In his first interview since being freed on Oct. 21, Mr. Hubbard declined to make any political statements about Russia, Ukraine or the war. He did not want to talk about how he felt when Russian soldiers essentially abducted him from his home in Ukraine. Nor did he want to talk much about his treatment in Russia, adding that he did not want to jeopardize the release of any of the other Americans being held there.

World.title: Russian strikes cut power to thousands in Ukraine as Kherson ceasefire ends
World.content:
A rare humanitarian ceasefire in Ukraine's front-line Kherson region that allowed civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky has ended.

The localised ceasefire was due to end at 22:59 Ukrainian time (21:00 GMT) on Sunday. While the truce had held since it was implemented last week, fighting had continued elsewhere.

On Sunday evening, Ukraine's air alert system was apparently hacked, the country's air force said, warning of radiation over Kyiv - a reference to a possible nuclear attack.

The Air Force message read: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had struck energy infrastructure in four regions overnight on Saturday, leaving hundreds of thousands of homes without power. Some connections were restored on Sunday.

Another overnight strike killed two people, including a 13-year-old girl, in the Vinnytsia region, the State Emergency Service of Ukraine said.

Meanwhile, Ukraine hit a major missile fuel producer in Russia's Rostov region, which caused a fire and damaged four production facilities, Zelensky said.

In Ukraine, repair works to restore power continued throughout the day. Most customers in the Dnipropetrovsk region had their connections restored by early evening, but more than 60,000 were still without power, the governor said.

Because of regular attacks on energy infrastructure, emergency power cuts have been introduced across the country. Even in the capital Kyiv, electricity is cut off for most of the day, and water supplies are also disrupted.

Zelensky said in a social media post that the intensity of Russian strikes has been "extremely high" over the past week, adding that Russia was "trying to take maximum advantage of the shortage of ballistic missile interceptors".

He added that "every day" Ukraine communicated its need for Patriot missiles - the only effective weapon for downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles - to the US, Europe and other partners. He thanked countries for their support so far and longer-term commitments, but called again for more immediate aid.

World.title: Israeli strikes in Gaza kill eight including child, hospitals say
World.content:
Israeli strikes in Gaza have killed at least eight people, including a child, according to hospitals, despite a year-old ceasefire.

In Gaza City to the north, hospital officials said a missile attack hit a group of civilians next to Cairo School in the Al-Rimal neighbourhood, killing three people, including a four-year-old boy.

In the southern city of Khan Younis, the Hamas-run ministry of interior said a drone attack targeted a group of police officers in the Al-Mawasi area, killing five, as they were carrying out their routine duties.

The Israeli military said it had carried out two attacks on what it described as military operatives but has not yet provided evidence or further information.

Outside Gaza City's Shifa Hospital, video showed a crowd of men gathered to pray next to two body bags and the tiny body of the child, which was wrapped in a white towel.

"My son and his child were martyred. They were sitting in their tent, bothering no one, and nothing else was happening in the area when suddenly, a missile struck them, and they were martyred," Ali Oweis told AFP news agency. "There is no ceasefire; the war is ongoing, don't you see?"

At Nasser hospital in Khan Younis, women despaired as body bags lay on the floor, video showed. The interior ministry named the five police officers killed, who were between the ages of 23 and 53, and called the attack a "horrific massacre".

A ceasefire came into force in Gaza in October last year, but Israeli air strikes have continued almost every day.

Since then, 1,580 people have been killed, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. Israel says it is targeting Hamas, but often civilians are also killed.

Meanwhile, a peace plan for Gaza, brokered by the Trump administration, has stalled.

The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war.

The conflict was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage.

Since the war began, 74,594 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's health ministry.

Additional reporting by Jacob Phillips

World.title: University of Cambridge scientist among those who died in Spanish train crash
World.content:
An award-winning University of Cambridge researcher died in the Spanish train disaster while on her way to collect a prize for scientific excellence.

Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to an awards ceremony on Wednesday when the train she was on crashed into another near Urda, south of Madrid, killing 69 people.

The mother of two was an affiliate associate professor leading a group of researchers at MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) in Cambridge and had earned several awards for work on human embryos and cell biology.

In a statement, the LMB paid tribute to the "inspiring, talented and passionate scientist" and described her death as a "profound shock and a huge loss".

The expert in cell biology ran the Shahbazi Laboratory at the LMB, based on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus.

She had been announced as the winner of a Spanish Society for Developmental Biology award for her contributions to the study of early human development and was due to collect the award at a conference in El Rompido in Andalusia.

The LMB said: "As a wife and mother of two young children, Marta wrote eloquently about balancing her family and career, serving as a much-admired role model for a 'mother scientist', a term she used to describe herself.

"Marta was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist whose research shed light on the earliest steps in the development of human embryos and how errors occur that lead to failed pregnancies," the LMB said.

The institute said her death was "a profound shock and a huge loss for LMB".

Her work had been recognised with "many awards and prizes", the laboratory added.

World.title: Shops looted as German cost-of-living protests turn violent
World.content:
Rioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday as clashes erupted in German cities over the cost of living.

Besides Frankfurt - Germany's financial hub - there were incidents of violence in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, with police saying they used water cannon to disperse protesters who were targeting emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles.

Thousands joined largely peaceful demonstrations earlier in the day. They were organised by the campaign group Gen Z regelt - meaning "Gen Z takes charge" - to protest against underfunding in schools, the high cost of living, public spending cuts and military service.

The unrest in Germany follows similar youth-led mass protests in France, where more than 320,000 people also demonstrated on Saturday.

On Sunday, Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told Bild newspaper that overnight police had prevented "violence like that seen in Paris" in recent weeks and called for "harsh punishments" for rioters and looters.

Overnight, a large section of Frankfurt's main shopping street was closed off by police. A police spokesperson said many arrests were made in the city.

Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, roughly half of what the organisers had estimated on their website. German media say tens of thousands protested in German cities on Saturday.

Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said the demonstrations were "to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion".

She said: "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favour of a fairer distribution of the burden."

World.title: Armed police start patrols in Sydney after Bondi Beach attack
World.content:
Heavily-armed police officers have started patrolling Sydney's streets, as part of heightened security measures following last year's deadly shooting at Bondi Beach.

The Armed Response Command (ARC) will see specially trained officers in busy tourist areas carrying long-arm rifles â an unfamiliar sight for most residents.

New South Wales police say the officers will also patrol major events like sports matches and places of worship "to prevent, deter and rapidly respond to serious threats, including active armed offender incidents".

Fifteen people - including a 10-year-old girl â were killed in December when two gunmen opened fire on an event marking the Jewish festival of Hanukkah at the popular beach.

The attack was Australia's worst mass shooting in almost three decades and prompted sweeping gun law reforms and a crackdown on hate speech.

One resident told ABC news that the sight of armed police was "unnerving".

"They are just everywhere. Those guns are huge."

But another woman told the broadcaster that seeing police with weapons made her feel safe.

ARC is specifically designed to be "highly visible across Sydney, driving specialist vehicles and carrying rifles," New South Wales police said in a statement.

Its role "is built on a simple principle - preserving life," Detective Superintendent Andrew Evans said.

The shooting on 14 December put huge pressure on Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government, with calls for immediate action on antisemitism.

Jewish communities have welcomed the new police operation, which will eventually consist of 250 officers, but others have called for safeguards to protect human rights.

"No Australian wants to see officers with military weapons on our streets, but the sight of body bags is far worse," Alex Ryvchin, co-CEO of Executive Council of Australian Jewry, said.

But Amnesty International Australia said it was concerned about the "militarisation of policing", and asked for assurances from the state government that ARC will not be used to suppress peaceful protests.

"Any expansion of police powers and capabilities must be accompanied by clear, publicly accessible rules, robust independent oversight and accountability," said the organisation's Andrew Witheford.

The New South Wales administration defended the new measures.

"Our world changed forever. That's just the truth of it, right across this country. And I said it at the time, we will never be the same again," the state's Police Minister Yasmin Catley told the ABC.

One of the alleged gunmen, Naveed Akram, has been charged with 78 offences including 15 counts of murder, 40 counts of attempted murder, and one count of committing a terrorist act.

His father, Sajid Akram, 50 - who was also armed and shot at the crowd on Bondi Beach - was killed by police at the scene.

World.title: Democrat endorses Republican candidate in key Michigan Senate race as party spat erupts
World.content:
A Democrat in Michigan has endorsed the Republican candidate in the state's crucial US Senate contest, as a spat with her own party's candidate Abdul El-Sayed escalated just days before the vote.

Haley Stevens, a sitting congresswoman who lost out on the Democratic Senate nomination to El-Sayed, made a surprise appearance alongside the Republican candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday.

"I don't belong in Abdul's campaign," she said in a video posted to X shortly after that appearance. "Who we are as Michiganders is not hate and is not what we are getting out from our Democratic nominee right now."

"That's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers," Stevens said.

The move stunned many of Stevens' fellow Democrats who condemned her decision to break from the party and switch her support just two days before the election.

The public feud between Stevens, a centrist Democrat, and El-Sayed, who represents the party's left-wing, has boiled over in recent days.

Stevens called on El-Sayed to denounce a campaign advert from an outside liberal group that linked US support for Israel with high prices. El-Sayed criticised the advert and said he had nothing to do with its contents.

Stevens had been scheduled to appear at an event with El-Sayed on Sunday in an effort to display party unity, but he reportedly asked her not to come and she chose to attend a church service with his Republican opponent instead.

"This is a very close election, we all know that, but Abdul made clear that I was not welcome in his campaign, that he didn't need me there, that he didn't want me there," Stevens told reporters as she stood alongside Rogers outside the church.

When asked about Stevens' endorsement, El-Sayed told reporters he was focused on the problems Michiganders are facing.

"At the end of the day, I don't think about Haley Stevens," he said on Sunday. "None of this matters."

World.title: India's opposition holds mega rally seeking election chief's resignation
World.content:
Tens of thousands gathered in Delhi for a rally demanding the resignation of India's chief election commissioner over a controversial revision of voter lists.

Organised by the opposition INDIA bloc and led by Rahul Gandhi's Congress party, the protest drew many of the alliance's most prominent leaders in a show of strength against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.

Protesters waved flags and chanted "Save the vote, save the country" and "Vote thief, give up power".

It was the latest in a series of protests over electoral roll revision that the opposition says has removed eligible voters to benefit the Bharatiya Janata Party. The BJP and the Election Commission deny the allegations.

The crowds gathered at Ramlila Maidan, a sprawling ground in central Delhi known for hosting major political and cultural events. Some protesters sang and danced to patriotic Bollywood songs, while others waited beneath a large canopy in the colours of the Indian flag to hear opposition leaders speak.

Gandhi and several senior opposition leaders arrived at the venue in an open jeep, travelling through crowds of cheering supporters.

The event was also attended by Congress leaders Sonia Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge, alongside leaders of regional parties such as Mamata Banerjee, Akhilesh Yadav, Mehbooba Mufti, Supriya Sule and Tejashwi Yadav.

Addressing the crowds, Rahul Gandhi said those gathered had sent a message to Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

"This is not the voice of a single political party or of politicians. It is the voice of India's youth, women, farmers and workers," he said.

"We will not allow democracy to be destroyed in India. We will not allow the constitution to be destroyed."

Other opposition leaders echoed Gandhi's criticism of the Election Commission. Congress president Kharge said the alliance would continue its campaign until Kumar resigned, while Banerjee pledged to keep fighting against what she described as threats to democracy.

Speaking to reporters in Delhi on Sunday, senior BJP leader and federal minister JP Nadda accused the opposition of trying to create unrest and destabilise the government under the guise of defending democracy.

He described the rally as a "calculated conspiracy to plunge the nation into anarchy - in the name of democracy".

World.title: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
World.content:
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.

The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added.

Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so.

"Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.

In an update on Sunday, Binance said withdrawals had been restored on several of its networks, after they were suspended following the hack.

It previously said withdrawals would be resumed in phases.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the attack.

The FBI said it had observed hackers converting stolen assets into a type of cryptocurrency called Ethereum and that it is expected that the assets will then be converted again using decentralised finance and instant swap services.

Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits.

Speaking to reporters on Saturday night, US President Donald Trump said, external the US is still unsure who the culprits are.

"We're learning about it. We don't know if it's North Korea - but if it is, we'll talk to North Korea about it," he said.

Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury.

All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, Ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said.

The hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025 - for which the FBI also said North Korea was responsible.

North Korea has always denied involvement in these attacks.

World.title: Toluwanisings’ death and social media prosecutors, By Festus Adedayo
World.content:
My eyes are misty as I write this. I have spent the better part of the morning listening repeatedly to one of the tracks of that gifted Yoruba gospel musician, Olayemi Bayonile Bolaji, known on stage as Toluwanisings. The 34-year-old was nature’s human carving of an Àwòko for the listening pleasure of humanity. Toluwanisings was the nightingale, the mockingbird of sacred song. The nightingale holds a sacred placement in Yoruba avian symbolism. Àwòko is the peerless soloist of the forest, gifted with an unmatchable range of sweet cadence.

This human nightingale hailed from Ikirun, Osun State, the ancient town that houses Akinorun Grammar School, where I spent a memorable chapter of my secondary school education. Toluwanisings passed away suddenly a few weeks ago, on 14 October, after collapsing on the staircase of his Ibadan, Oyo State residence. He had just returned from an exhilarating worship concert titled In His Presence.

The palaver generated by his sudden departure is immense, disturbing, and deeply instructive. It calls to mind that timeless Swahili proverb which says, on the day a monkey is destined to be killed by a prowling wild cat, every tree it clings to becomes slippery. How does a man who sang so confidently about conquering postpartum human mockery and the conceit of hypocrites suddenly, barely a month after departing this mortal space, become the chief victim of these very wicked forces?

In that particular track that drew hot tears down my cheeks, he sang with prophetic defiance: “The machinations of the enemy will not triumph over me/Satan will never rejoice over my life/Heavens will not regret lifting me high/My sunlight will not be eclipsed by darkness/I saw Satan fall like lightning/The dragon was conquered by the power of our testimony/Satan will not celebrate the fall of a mighty man/My giant will not become a pygmy, as the Lord lives.”

I translated the above searing, tear-jerking lyrics from his verbatim Yoruba rendering that goes thus: “Ero ọta ko ni ṣe lẹ mi l’ori/Inu Satani ko ni dun l’ori aye mi…/Ọrun o ni k’abamọ p’ohun gbe mi ga…/Imọlẹ mi ko ni wọ l’okunkun.../Emi ri Satani to ṣubụ bi mọnamọna/A ṣegun Dragoni nipa ọrọ ẹri ẹnu wa/Satani ko ni s’ajọyọ p’alagbara ṣubu/Omiran mi o ni d’arara b’Oluwa ti ń bẹ.”

Posthumously, however, it would appear that the very machinations Toluwanisings prayed against have encircled him like the enveloping grips of a boa constrictor. The invisible demons of this world seem to be celebrating his passage, while those who should have protected his memory – including members of his immediate and extended family – have perfected plans to reduce this musical giant into a pygmy in the court of public opinion. On the day Toluwanisings passed, every road led to the imagined blood the prowling cat spilled out of the Swahili monkey. All the monkey’s renowned tree-climbing theatrical skills became effete in an instant. The most knowledgeable became the most foolish, and the most celebrated became the most vulnerable.

Toluwanisings’ death and the social media conceit that followed confirm the age-long wisdom of our forebears: if the well-known acrobatic tree-to-tree escape from its foes meets the monkey on plain, treeless ground, the creature becomes as helpless and vulnerable as any ordinary mammal. Ancient Yoruba wisdom packages this as: “Bi igi o ba sunmọ igi, ọmọ ẹdun a d’ope” – when trees fail to stand close to one another, the young monkey loses its agility and becomes a big-time fool.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Before we even examine Toluwanisings’ tragic post-death drama, we must confront the horrifying circumstances surrounding his final hours. It was a familiar Nigerian tragedy that unfolded: the gospel musician slumped in his home; medical attention was fatally delayed and ultimately denied, and Àwòko flew away with his melodious voice.

For decades, Nigeria has grappled with the twin evils of hospital emergency management – systemic negligence and outright rejection – which have consumed some of the finest minds and sweetest voices of our country. Added to these is the third evil: the notorious refusal by hospitals to treat emergency and gunshot victims without police reports. Added together, they constitute an unfeeling bureaucratic cruelty that continues to send citizens to early graves.

Reports indicate that as Toluwanisings fought for breath upon slumping, he was rushed to approximately seven to eight different hospitals across the city of Ibadan, including the apex federal tertiary institution, the University College Hospital (UCH). Each institution either rejected him outright or presented one administrative excuse after another. They passed the dying artist around in a macabre game of medical hot potato, until the Owner of the leash on the goat’s neck finally pulled it into eternity.

Predictably, social media collapsed under the weight of anger and unfeeling cross-examinations. Àwòko’s sudden, needlessly avoidable silence provoked widespread outrage online, as netizens poured bile on Nigeria’s broken health infrastructure. They then resurrected that haunting, tragic national shibboleth: May Nigeria never happen to us.

Yet, the moment Toluwanisings’ eyes closed to open in eternity, the conversation shifted from the systemic failure that killed him to a toxic, voyeuristic dissection of his personal life. The posthumous uproar and needless media harangue attending Toluwanisings’ passing and burial sound so absurd. They bear a striking resemblance to the dark spectacle that followed the death of Ilerioluwa Oladimeji Aloba, widely known as Mohbad, in 2023.

Mohbad was just 27 years old when he died on September 12 of that year. A talented singer and songwriter too, his death detonated a complex web of controversy, ranging from allegations of Lagos music underworld bullying and assault to disputes over the paternity of his infant son, coroner’s inquests, and disgraceful family squabbles over his estate. For years, that young boy’s corpse remained trapped inside the dark coldness of the morgue, suffering endless postponements while living relatives traded insults on social media.

The Mohbad spectacle reminded me of the decades it took for the secrets of Asipa Oyo, Amuda Olorunosebi, to be covered by Ilẹ Ọgẹrẹ Afọkọyeri – the earth’s crust. Gruesomely murdered on his Oyo Alaafin farm on November 26, 1992, with acid poured on his body by his assailants, he remained unburied for seven years, until November 26, 1999. Ilẹ Ọgẹrẹ Afọkọyeri is not a mere descriptive phrase; it is a sacred metaphysical name the Yoruba gave to the earth and soil. To our ancestors, the earth is not a passive, inanimate natural resource or mere dirt under our feet; it is a living, conscious, spiritual entity possessing an interconnected affinity with the divine. The earth-crust is venerated as the ultimate, considerate concealer of the human creature’s secrets when life is done.

Instead of allowing Ilẹ Ọgẹrẹ to grant Toluwanisings that sacred cover immediately after he breathed his last, his family members from Ikirun began to heap mounds of hot ash on his memory. For weeks, public attempts were made to paint him as an ungrateful child who abandoned his father, lavished his fortune on his wife’s family, and lived a hypocritical life of a wolf in a sheep’s clothing.

In the heat of this online trial, the question of where his body should be interred morphed into a bitter public war. While his widow favours a quiet, dignified burial in a modern cemetery, his father and patriarchal relatives insist on burying him either inside his newly completed Ibadan residence or beside his late mother’s grave in Ikirun – warning that otherwise, Irẹlẹ, Ikirun’s deeply venerated ancestral guardian deity and mythical god, would unleash its mortal strike. There is nil consideration for Toluwanisings’ young wife and two little girls, except their patriarchal ego and inflated manhood. The contestations has become messy, laughable, and – pardon the word – utterly idiotic. A man who spent his life crafting melodies to heal broken hearts became, in death, a piece of bone fought over by dogs.

If we take a step back from our local grief, however, we will realize that this posthumous hubris is not unique to contemporary Nigeria. Throughout music history, the corpses and legacies of legendary artists have passed through remarkably similar, sordid corridors of greed, hypocrisy and family warfare.

Take the case of my revered musical totem, Winston McIntosh, known to the world as Peter Tosh. By the way, I ported from his friend and arch-rival, Bob Marley, to Tosh when I discovered Tosh’s boundless depth, poetry and philosophy were way out of Bob’s. Sorry, I digressed. Peter was the uncompromising co-founder of The Wailers whose posthumous Grammy recognition celebrated his genius. Shot in the head during a violent home robbery on 11 September, 1987, Tosh’s death immediately triggered a chaotic funeral planning process marred by a thick confetti of familial, religious, and political conflicts.

As Tosh’s body was being prepared for interment, two different men suddenly surfaced claiming to be his biological father. One was Alfred McIntosh, backed aggressively by Tosh’s common-law wife, Marlene Brown; the other was James McIntosh, who was eventually confirmed by Tosh’s grieving mother, Alvera Coke, as his father. A fierce feud erupted over his burial site between Marlene Brown and his mother. While Brown insisted on her legal right to manage the funeral, his mother demanded that her only child be brought back to her home parish of Westmoreland. Because the Jamaican state did not legally recognise common-law marriage, the government handed the body to Tosh’s mother.

Tosh’s funeral descended into utter madness. As a devout Rastafarian who spent his life denouncing the hypocrisy of state institutions, the attempt by the Jamaican government to dominate Tosh’s official state funeral sparked protests. How could the same “Babylon” that hunted Tosh to death – whose polais-mon (police) cracked his skull for smoking ganja – be same mourner shedding crocodile tears at his funeral? His Rastafarian brethren thus turned the funeral into a raucous, chaotic demonstration. To compound the surreal drama, a self-proclaimed prophet marched up to the casket, unlidded it in front of the congregation and fruitlessly chanted commands for Tosh to “rise from the dead!”

Similarly, the tragic end of Apala music legend, Ayinla Omowura, in May 1980 saw a battle over the soul and body of the man who prided himself as the nightingale – a bird the Yoruba also call the Olóbùró. Culturally, the Yoruba appellation for this ancient bird is that it has 200 voices (ẹyẹ olóbùró ní ohùn igba), with its famed beautiful, endless repertoire of songs that come in loud, bold vocal variety. Apologies: I digressed again. Stabbed in the head with a heavy beer glass during a barroom brawl in Ago-Ika, Abeokuta, Omowura died of cranium damage. Though born a Muslim, he was notorious for ignoring daily Islamic prayer rituals. His Itoko home was a haven for traditionalists and fiery masquerades, most notably his personal masquerade named Tankurubaku. His open indulgence in cannabis and violence was also legendary.

Upon Omowura’s killing, the conservative Islamic clerics of his Itoko neighbourhood staunchly refused to administer the Salat al-Janazah (Islamic funeral prayer) on his body, declaring his lifestyle un-Islamic. It was only after community elders reminded the clerics of Omowura’s massive, anonymous financial contributions to their local mosque that the religious leaders reluctantly assented to perform the rites.

The Western world offers equally bizarre examples of squabbles over artists’ corpses. Elvis Presley and James Brown followed that trajectory, with their passages shrouded in ruckuses. When Presley, the “King of Rock and Roll,” died of cardiac arrest on August 16, 1977, he was buried in a mausoleum at Forest Hill Cemetery in Memphis. Shortly after, police arrested four men who had broken into the vault attempting to steal his corpse in order to extort millions of dollars in ransom from his estate. His body had to be exhumed and reburied in a heavily guarded, fortified garden at Graceland.

Similarly, when James Brown, the “Godfather of Soul,” died on Christmas Day in 2006, his body remained unburied for months in a temperature-controlled room while his children and his partner, Tomi Rae Hynie, waged a vicious legal battle over the validity of their marriage, control of his multi-million dollar estate, and the choice of his final sepulchre.

Perhaps the most bizarre posthumous spectacle occurred following the 1973 drug overdose death of country rock pioneer Gram Parsons. Prior to his death, Parsons and his road manager, Phil Kaufman, had made a secret pact: whichever of them died first would be cremated by the other in the high desert of Joshua Tree National Park. Thus, when Parsons died, his stepfather, Robert Parsons, attempted to hijack his body for a private burial in Louisiana to secure control over the musician’s estate. Kaufman responded by posing as a mortuary driver at Los Angeles International Airport and stole the coffin from the hangar. He then drove it out to the Joshua Tree desert, poured five gallons of petrol over the corpse, and set it ablaze. Kaufman was later arrested; however, the charge of cadaver theft against him in court couldn’t stand because it wasn’t explicitly classified as a crime under California law at the time. Kaufman was merely fined $300 for the theft of the wooden casket!

What these global cases reveal is a disturbing, universal human impulse: society is deeply, structurally unfair in its posthumous assessment and handling of artists.

When a musician is alive, we consume their talent, exploit their vulnerabilities, and demand that they serve as vessels for our inspiration, our worship, or our entertainment. But the moment breath leaves their lungs, we strip them of their human dignity. The living descend, like vultures, upon their corpses – relatives fight over property, fans trade salacious rumours, religious institutions pass sanctimonious judgments and the public turns their personal tragedy into cheap online entertainment.

Toluwanisings spent his short life crafting songs that offered solace to thousands. He sang of triumphing over mockery, of light piercing through darkness, and of giants refusing to become pygmies. Yet in death, he became temporarily trapped in the very noise, malice, and belittlement he spent his career singing against.

These are my questions for Toluwanisings’ sabre-rattling uncle, who has become the mythological social media dragon breathing out fire and brimstone over the preferred site of his burial: Does he know that, upon cessation of breath from the nostrils, the living body has no more worth than a log of wood? Why prioritize a log of wood’s welfare over that of the living?

Whether Toluwanisings is buried in the finest sepulchre on earth like Michael Jackson (whose crypt burial site at the Great Mausoleum–Holly Terrace in Forest Lawn Memorial Park cost $590,000 for the crypt title alone, out of a total private funeral cost of more than $1 million) or the modest cemetery replica of where President Umaru Yar’Adua was interred, like every man, maggots will feast on the body a few days post-interment.

Why compound the pain of a widowed young woman who would have to daily agonize as she wakes to see a cryptic grave that was once her ebullient husband? If there is a need to sell Toluwanisings’ new house, especially to finance his young kids’ education, does this uncle realize that a home used as a burial site could bring down its value? The obvious reality is that Toluwanisings’ paternal family is locked up in the ancient patriarchal view of a woman as chattel and unworthy of inheritance, especially since it is obvious that she might remarry.

Society must learn to give the departed their peace. The dead cannot defend themselves, nor can they respond to allegations whipped up by living relatives or social media prosecutors. It is time we let Ilẹ Ọgẹrẹ Afọkọyeri do its sacred work of covering the secrets, the flaws, as well as the bones of the departed, in a modest time frame – human foibles which all the online prosecutors also possess. By doing so, we would allow the art of the dead and not their human limitations, echo into eternity.

The Customs Recruitment Fiasco

The story of Nevada Pierre, the sensational three-year-old American soccer prodigy from Florida, is fast becoming an archetype of how qualification can, ironically, disqualify the qualified. If you look closely enough at the Nevada narrative, you will also tease out a sobering commentary on the shrinking boundary of human patience for natural talent and competition.

Nevada set the internet ablaze recently following a youth soccer match organized by i9 Sports in Winter Park, a game that degenerated into a dispute so heated it required police intervention. The toddler’s brilliant ball control, eclectic dribbling and total pitch dominance left the parents of opposing children visibly incensed. Complaining that the boy was “too advanced,” the disgruntled parents summoned the Winter Park Police Department. But their outrage backfired spectacularly. Rather than suppressing the prodigy, the police dispatch catapulted Nevada into global headlines, earning him an invitation to train at Eddie Johnson’s Orlando-based EJE7 Soccer Academy, the admiration of celebrity children’s entertainer, Rachel Griffin-Accurso and a wave of fan-backed GoFundMe support.

Instructive as the Nevada Pierre episode is, what commands my attention most is its central lesson: how man readily manipulates qualification for selfish ends.

A raging issue that underscores this moral deficit right here in Nigeria involves the Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) and its 2024/2025 recruitment exercise, where candidates who officially triumphed are now being punished for their success.

According to media reports, the NCS published the final list of successful candidates of the exercise in July 2026. They then received formal provisional offers on the official recruitment portal, complete with instructions to fulfill specific prerequisites. These included submission of medical certificates of fitness from state hospitals and formally accepting the offers within a stipulated window. Trusting the sanctity of the process, several candidates resigned from their existing jobs.

Yet, when basic training commenced, these successful applicants discovered to their utter shock that their names had been systematically erased. In their place were entirely new names, individuals who allegedly never participated in the initial screening exercise.

While the Comptroller-General of Customs, Adewale Adeniyi, reportedly intervened by ordering a case-by-case review of the aggrieved applicants’ complaints, the Service continues to defend its posture with the defense that inclusion on its published shortlist does not constitute an automatic guarantee of enlistment.

What the NCS must realise is that when administrative discretion becomes a veil for organisational impunity, institutional integrity leaves through the window. Just as the aggrieved parents in Winter Park sought to police away superior talent out of spite, the arbitrary erasure of verified candidates from the Customs recruitment list signals a dangerous culture where merit is treated as a liability rather than an asset. Comptroller-General Adeniyi’s promised review must move beyond mere damage control to full restitution. A nation that off-handedly mourns its brain drain and institutional decay cannot continue to systematically disqualify its most qualified, simply to satisfy the appetite of elite man-know-man.

Festus Adedayo is an Ibadan-based journalist.

World.title: Decoupling Sovereignty Index (5): How decoupling reinforces itself, By Max Amuchie
World.content:
A territory can register alarming scores across multiple indicators and still leave a fundamental question unanswered: are the forces undermining state sovereignty operating independently, or have they begun reinforcing one another to create a self-sustaining alternative order?

This distinction matters. A state may experience economic extraction by armed groups, territorial insecurity and the weakening of public legitimacy simultaneously. Yet the presence of these conditions does not necessarily mean they have combined into a resilient system capable of reproducing itself despite government intervention.

The challenge is to establish not merely whether sovereignty is weakening, but whether the forces responsible for that weakening have begun to reinforce one another.

This is the problem addressed by the Convergence Indicator of the Decoupling Sovereignty Index (DSI).

In the earlier instalments of this series, we introduced the DSI as a quantitative diagnostic instrument developed to assess the gap between a state’s formal sovereignty and the realities of authority, security, territorial control and institutional performance within its territory.

We examined its three diagnostic vectors—Money, Land and Mind—and introduced the 19 universal indicators through which the instrument seeks to make territorial decoupling systematically observable.

The indicators provide the underlying measurements. But measurements alone cannot fully explain the relationships among the conditions they describe.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Two territories might register comparable levels of insecurity yet face fundamentally different challenges. In one, the loss of state authority may be concentrated in a particular sector, leaving other institutions and territorial arrangements relatively resilient. In the other, economic extraction may finance territorial expansion, territorial control may facilitate coercive rule, and that rule may progressively displace the state’s capacity to regulate everyday life.

The second territory presents a more complex problem. Its weaknesses are not merely accumulating; they are becoming mutually reinforcing.

The DSI’s Convergence Indicator is designed to investigate this distinction.

From Separate Weaknesses to a Self-Reinforcing System

Sovereign decoupling does not necessarily follow a straight line. Weakness in one dimension of governance may remain contained, while another dimension continues to function.

A state might struggle to prevent kidnapping while retaining control over agricultural production and local dispute resolution. It might lose effective control over a rural corridor without losing the population’s confidence in its public institutions. Alternatively, it might maintain a visible security presence while failing to prevent the economic exploitation of residents.

These are different configurations of decoupling, and each may require a different policy response.

The danger intensifies when the weaknesses begin feeding into one another.

Consider a territory in which a non-state armed organisation derives revenue from kidnapping, extortion or illegal taxation. The proceeds finance recruitment, weapons, logistics and further territorial expansion. Control over territory then enables the organisation to regulate movement, influence production, restrict access to markets and impose rules on residents.

As the organisation’s practical authority grows, it may become increasingly capable of extracting resources, protecting its economic networks and punishing those who resist its demands.

Some residents may comply because they fear retaliation. Others may depend on arrangements imposed by the organisation because formal institutions cannot provide effective alternatives. Still others may adjust their behaviour simply because the organisation has become a persistent feature of the local political and economic environment.

Such compliance must not automatically be interpreted as voluntary allegiance or legitimacy. Nevertheless, it can contribute to the organisation’s capacity to maintain control.

The resulting relationship is circular.

Economic extraction finances territorial power. Territorial power enables further extraction. Coercive authority regulates behaviour, while the resulting compliance can make the organisation more difficult to displace.

Money reinforces Land, while the resulting arrangements affect the Mind vector through coercion, perceived legitimacy, competing allegiances and the population’s relationship with formal state institutions.

The three vectors begin to interact as parts of a larger system.

This is the central analytical proposition behind the Convergence Indicator: the significance of decoupling depends not only on the severity of individual weaknesses, but also on whether their interaction produces a more resilient alternative order.

Why Convergence Matters

If the underlying indicators are moving in different directions, the resulting pattern may represent uneven or sectoral decoupling.

The state may be losing control over a particular economic activity while retaining the ability to protect the surrounding population. It may face territorial insecurity without having lost the credibility of its institutions. It may also retain opportunities to reverse a particular weakness through a targeted intervention.

Under such circumstances, a policy response can focus on the specific source of the problem while strengthening the institutions that remain functional.

However, where adverse conditions across Money, Land and Mind increasingly reinforce one another, interventions directed at individual symptoms may have limited effects.

A military operation might disrupt an armed organisation without dismantling the economic networks that finance its return. An economic development programme might increase commercial activity without protecting traders from extortion. A public information campaign might seek to rebuild trust while residents remain exposed to coercion.

In each case, the intervention addresses a genuine problem but may leave the relationships sustaining that problem largely intact.

The Convergence Indicator is intended to help analysts distinguish between these situations.

Its purpose is not simply to establish that several indicators have high scores. Rather, it is to assess whether the underlying evidence supports a finding that adverse conditions are interacting across the three vectors in ways that intensify and sustain decoupling.

This requires more than observing simultaneous deterioration. Researchers must identify the relevant relationships, establish the direction of the indicators and apply explicit rules for determining whether the evidence supports a convergence signal.

The distinction is essential to the DSI’s credibility as a quantitative instrument. High scores across multiple indicators may suggest a serious crisis, but the claim that the crisis has become self-reinforcing requires additional analytical justification.

The Event Horizon: When Shadow Authority Becomes Resilient

The DSI uses the term Event Horizon to describe a critical condition in which a Shadow Order has become sufficiently resilient and institutionally embedded that formal state intervention can no longer easily reverse its position. The concept draws attention to a potentially consequential transition.

At an earlier stage, a non-state organisation may exploit a specific weakness in state authority. Its activities may remain geographically limited, economically dependent on particular opportunities or vulnerable to targeted disruption.

As its power expands, however, it may develop a broader system of economic extraction, territorial control and coercive regulation. These capabilities can reinforce one another, enabling the organisation to survive interventions that address only one dimension of its power.

The territory may then become increasingly difficult to recover through isolated security operations or conventional development programmes.

An Event Horizon, in this analytical sense, is not simply a point at which violence reaches a particular level. It describes the possibility that an alternative order has acquired sufficient internal resilience to reproduce the conditions supporting its authority.

The distinction between resilience and legitimacy is important. A Shadow Order may persist without enjoying popular support. Its durability may depend on coercion, economic dependence, the absence of credible alternatives or the population’s inability to resist safely.

Nor does the concept imply that recovery becomes impossible after a particular threshold has been crossed. Rather, it signals the possibility that restoration will require a more comprehensive response than interventions designed to address individual symptoms.

For the DSI to operationalise the Event Horizon concept, the methodology must specify the evidence and decision rules required to distinguish severe but reversible decoupling from a more consolidated alternative order.

The concept provides an analytical proposition to investigate, not a universally established threshold that can be assumed to apply identically across territories.

Three Convergence Signals of Particular Importance

Within the DSI’s current indicator architecture, three designated combinations carry particular analytical significance. They illustrate how relationships among indicators can help identify broader patterns of territorial and institutional breakdown.

1. M6 and L6: Agricultural Sovereignty Collapse

Agriculture is not merely an economic activity. In many vulnerable territories, it sustains household income, food availability, local markets and the productive use of land.

When agricultural livelihoods are undermined by economic pressures and territorial insecurity, the consequences can extend far beyond reduced output.

Farmers may abandon their fields because access is unsafe. Traders may be unable to transport produce. Disrupted production can reduce household income, while displacement can weaken the labour and commercial networks needed to restore agricultural activity.

Declining production may, in turn, increase economic vulnerability and deepen dependence on alternative sources of income or coercive arrangements.

The relationship between M6 and L6 is intended to flag conditions associated with the breakdown of agricultural sovereignty: a situation in which the practical capacity to sustain agricultural production and livelihoods is seriously compromised.

The analytical concern is the interaction between the relevant economic and territorial conditions, not simply the existence of agricultural decline.

2. L7, L3 and MD5: Human Sovereignty Collapse

The second designated combination concerns the conditions under which people can live, move, maintain livelihoods and exercise agency within their communities.

Where territorial insecurity and competing systems of coercion become entrenched, residents may be forced to flee, abandon productive activities or reorganise their lives around the demands of armed actors.

Others may remain physically present but lose meaningful freedom of movement, access to essential resources or the ability to make ordinary decisions without fear.

These conditions affect more than physical security. They can weaken the social and economic foundations of community life and undermine the practical relationship between residents and the institutions expected to protect them.

The designated relationship among L7, L3 and MD5 is intended to signal this broader pattern of human sovereignty collapse.

Here, human sovereignty refers to the practical conditions under which people can exercise agency and sustain ordinary life. It does not replace or negate the legal sovereignty of the state.

The distinction matters because a territory may remain internationally recognised as part of a sovereign state while its residents experience severe constraints on their everyday freedom and security.

3. L5 and MD1: Justice Sovereignty Collapse

The third combination addresses the practical authority of the state in the administration and enforcement of justice.

Where formal institutions cannot reliably protect residents, resolve disputes or enforce legal decisions, alternative arrangements may emerge.

These arrangements can be imposed by armed organisations or maintained by other authorities operating beyond the state’s effective reach. Residents may comply because the alternatives are inaccessible, because they perceive an alternative arrangement as more predictable, or because resistance carries unacceptable risks.

Predictability under these conditions should not be confused with fairness, legitimacy or voluntary acceptance.

The relationship between L5 and MD1 is intended to flag circumstances in which the state’s effective authority over justice is seriously compromised.

The consequences may extend beyond individual disputes. When residents cannot depend on formal institutions for protection or redress, the credibility of those institutions may decline further. That weakening can make it harder for the state to rebuild public confidence and restore its authority.

These three designated combinations demonstrate the intended analytical value of convergence signals: they direct attention to relationships among indicators that may reveal broader patterns of breakdown.

Their exact definitions and operational implications must be documented in the DSI methodology. The presence of a designated combination should not, without supporting evidence, be treated as conclusive proof that a particular form of collapse has occurred.

From Measurement to Strategic Diagnosis

The Convergence Indicator occupies a distinct position within the DSI architecture.

The 19 universal indicators provide the underlying field measurements. The Convergence Indicator synthesises evidence about relationships among those measurements to help determine whether decoupling is sectoral, uneven or potentially self-reinforcing across the three vectors.

It therefore addresses a question that individual indicator scores cannot answer on their own: are the forces undermining state authority developing into a mutually reinforcing system?

This question has direct implications for policy.

Where the evidence points to a relatively contained weakness, targeted interventions may be appropriate. Where the evidence indicates that economic extraction, territorial control and competing authority reinforce one another, interventions may need to address those relationships together.

The practical implications will depend on the circumstances of each territory. The DSI does not presume that all forms of convergence require an identical response, nor that one score can substitute for detailed contextual analysis.

Its contribution lies in providing a structured way to examine the systemic relationships that should inform that analysis.

The instrument’s value will ultimately depend on the transparency of its scoring rules, the quality of its evidence and the results of empirical application. These requirements are particularly important if the Convergence Indicator is to support comparisons across territories or guide decisions with substantial security and development consequences.

The DSI is being developed by Sundiata Post, with its methodological work administered through the Sundiata Post Knowledge Lab (SPKL). The forthcoming DSI Methodology and Indicator Manual will document the technical specifications and operational guidance required to support its application by researchers and policy practitioners across Africa and the Global South.

The Convergence Indicator represents one part of that developing architecture. Its task is to make the relationships sustaining decoupling more visible and to help analysts distinguish a collection of weaknesses from a system capable of reproducing them.

Yet diagnosis alone cannot determine whether a proposed recovery programme is structurally viable.

Even when the sources of decoupling are understood, the state must still confront another question: in what order should it rebuild the conditions required for effective authority?

That is the problem addressed by the DSI’s second higher-order diagnostic.

In the next instalment, we examine the Recovery Sequencing Score and the proposition that sustainable sovereign restoration depends not only on what governments do, but also on whether the conditions necessary for recovery are established in the right order.

From the desk to the world.

Max Nwabueze Amuchie is a scholar-journalist, CEO of Sundiata Post and Lead Researcher at the Sundiata Post Knowledge Lab (SPKL), Abuja. He developed the Insecurity Triad, the Trinity of Sovereignty Decay (TSD), the Decoupling Sovereignty Index (DSI) and the Sundiata Post Model (SPM). He is an Expert Member & Peer Reviewer, Behavioural Sciences at ScienceOpen. Email: [email protected]. X: @MaxAmuchie

World.title: In Makkah, Tinubu prays that Nigeria’s diversity would lead to prosperity
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu has beseeched Almighty Allah to transform Nigeria’s rich diversity into a source of prosperity, unity, peace and sustainable development for the benefit of all Nigerians.

President Tinubu offered the prayer on Sunday in the holy city of Makkah, Saudi Arabia, while hosting members of his delegation for dinner.

The president expressed the hope that Nigeria’s ethnic, religious, and cultural diversity would continue to serve as a source of strength and national advancement rather than division, stressing the need for citizens to embrace mutual understanding, peaceful coexistence and a shared commitment to the country’s progress.

He prayed that Almighty Allah would bless Nigeria with enduring peace, harmony and prosperity, and grant the nation’s leaders the wisdom, courage and foresight to steer the country towards greater development and improved living conditions for its people.

“May Almighty Allah bless Nigeria, convert our diversity into prosperity as a country,” the president said.

President Tinubu also prayed for divine guidance and protection for Nigerians at home and abroad, asking Allah to strengthen the bonds of brotherhood among citizens and inspire a renewed spirit of patriotism, compassion and service to the nation.

The President noted that Nigeria’s abundant human and natural resources, coupled with the talents, creativity and enterprise of its diverse population, provided a strong foundation for building a prosperous and inclusive nation.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The dinner with members of his delegation in Makkah provided an opportunity for fellowship and reflection on Nigerians’ shared aspirations for a peaceful, united and prosperous country.

President Tinubu urged Nigerians of all faiths and backgrounds to keep working together in the national interest, expressing confidence that, with faith in Almighty Allah, unity of purpose, and collective determination, Nigeria would overcome its challenges and realise its full potential.

The Chairman of BUA, Abdulsamad Rabiu, reaffirmed President Tinubu’s commitment to peace, unity and prosperity of Nigeria.

“Today is actually the third dinner we’re having with His Excellency Mr President since we came to Makkah on Thursday night or Friday morning when Mr President arrived.

“So, we discussed, and the discussion was, you know, to always continue to pray for Nigeria, for peace, for unity and for Nigeria’s prosperity. To again, you know, thank His Excellency for his passion, for what he’s doing for Nigeria.

“And also for us, it’s quite important because, as I said, it has given us the opportunity to come and pray not only for ourselves and our families, but also for Nigeria.

“We will continue to support His Excellency in whatever capacity we can and definitely, as you all know, Mr President is very passionate about the country. He’s working very hard, and we’ll continue to support him,” he said.

Kwara State Governor and Chairman of the Nigerian Governors’ Forum, Abdulrahman AbdulRazaq, said the forum is overwhelmed by the president’s passion and commitment to achieving a united and prosperous nation.

“Only Allah can reward you; we will continue to pray for you daily and pray for Nigeria that you lead. May Allah continue to strengthen you in making the right decisions, strengthen your wisdom, your boldness, your audacity, your courage. May Allah lead you to the right path,” he said.

The Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, Lateef Fagbemi, also prayed for Almighty Allah to continue to strengthen the President in his determination to deliver governance and justice to all Nigerians irrespective of their religion or ethnic backgrounds.

The dinner was attended by Yobe State Governor Mala Buni, Kaduna State Governor Uba Sani, Jigawa State Governor Mohammed Namadi, Sokoto State Governor Ahmed Aliyu, Borno State Governor Babagana Zulum, Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare Mohammed Pate, National Security Adviser Nuhu Ribadu, Chief Executive Officer of Oando Plc Wale Tinubu, Special Adviser to the President on Political Matters Ibrahim Masari, and Chief of Staff to the President Femi Gbajabiamila, among others.

Bayo Onanuga

Special Adviser to the President
