In traditional Mexica narratives, the flower’s intense yellow or orange color came directly from the sun. Cempasúchil’s golden-orange glow and unique aroma were said to guide departed souls back to a ceremonial banquet for them, prepared by their living relatives.

Hence, from time immemorial, the Tagetes erecta (the scientific name for the cempasúchil flower) has been used to decorate altars of the dead in different parts of Mexico, mainly during the first two days of November.

Cempasúchil flowers in the Day of the Dead festivities

Today, this plant, native to Mesoamerica, can be found growing wild in various ecosystems in Mexico. It’s also found in Central American countries, including Panama, Honduras and El Salvador. It can grow as tall as 1 meter, and its buds can reach 5 centimeters in diameter. This extremely versatile plant easily adapts to its surroundings, flourishing in temperate oak forests or in a tropical rainforest’s humidity.

Cempasúchil production in Mexico is primarily focused on the flower’s ceremonial purposes. In late October and the first days of November, the country is covered in an orange blanket of cempasúchil as people across Mexico invoke the spirits of their loved ones during Day of the Dead festivities.

Even centuries after the tradition began, cempasúchil flowers still brighten Mexicans’ altars, lighting the way back home for the souls of the departed so that, for just one night a year, we can see our loved ones again.

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: El Jalapeño: Baja man protests three-week CFE outage by hosting open bar in lobby
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

LA PAZ, Baja California Sur — Demonstrating remarkable civic resourcefulness in the face of infrastructure challenges, a local resident whose electricity was cut off for three weeks converted the customer service lobby of the Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) into a temporary open-bar hospitality suite on Tuesday afternoon.

Equipped with a five-speed countertop blender, a sack of limes, coarse salt and bottles of tequila and damiana, the La Paz resident plugged directly into a primary outlet behind the ticket-dispensing kiosk, offering freshly blended margaritas to fellow customers waiting in line for billing dispute resolutions.

“If the federal grid cannot deliver electricity to my freezer, I must bring my ice to the grid,” said the resident, who noted that three weeks of unanswered service tickets and unkept reconnection promises had left his home appliances thoroughly non-functional. “The administrative process takes three hours anyway. It is simply good manners to offer refreshments while we wait for ticket number 47 to be called.”

CFE staff reportedly observed the operation with a mixture of bureaucratic neutrality and procedural deliberation, noting that while utility regulations prohibit unauthorized commercial vending in public facilities, current policy contains no explicit clause regarding the non-commercial distribution of frozen cocktails in waiting areas.

The impromptu tasting station quickly stabilized lobby morale, with several citizens in line offering to supply additional ice and fresh citrus in exchange for priority access to the blender’s frozen treats. One CFE employee estimated that the protest successfully reduced perceived wait times across the branch by about 40%, despite no change in actual ticket processing speed.

Utility representatives later confirmed that while the man’s power status remains under review, official policy guidelines are currently being evaluated to determine whether guest appliance usage in administrative lobbies constitutes a billable service tier.



The not-quite-so-powerless resident, meanwhile, promised to bring the rest of his kitchen appliances the following day if his service still hadn’t been reinstated.

World.title: In Tepoztlán, the dead get one more week to celebrate
World.content:
If you’ve ever seen Disney’s “Coco,” you’ll remember Miguel Rivera had to complete his journey from the Land of the Dead to the world of the living before the afterlife closed for another year. In Mexican culture, that’s usually one day after the veil between the two planes is lifted.

But in Tepoztlán, a Pueblo Mágico with mountains resembling the world of “Avatar,” the farewell to the dead doesn’t end on Nov. 2.

The dead linger for another week — and while they do, the celebration continues.

What is ‘La Octava’?

The term “La Octava” comes from Roman liturgy. It describes an eight-day cycle in which “the believer is turned from one bound to this world into one bound to heaven.”

The Catholic Church continues to celebrate octaves, such as the Octave of Christmas (Dec. 25 to Jan. 1) and the Octave of Easter, from Easter Sunday to Divine Mercy Sunday.

In Tepoztlán, people also commonly observe an octave after a death.

“When somebody dies, we hold a rosary for eight days, until, on the last day, we officially send the dead to the underworld,” says 78-year-old Thomas Muzquiz, a Tepozteco.

Thomas connects this Catholic practice with the celebration of Day of the Dead.

“When Catholicism was introduced to Mexico, it merged with Indigenous tradition,” he explains.

Day of the Dead beautifully fuses pre-Hispanic beliefs with Catholic observance. Food offerings, copal and flower trails coexist alongside processions of saints’ images and crosses.

But when we look behind the copal smoke and past the vivid decorations, we can see that Day of the Dead in Tepoztlán and its octave is more than just a remembrance of those who have passed.

It is about continuing to work on relationships and caring for one another, welcoming the deceased with love and respect: to hang out together, eat their favorite food and have a shot or two of their favorite mezcal, while mariachis set the tone for the night.

La Octava de Tepoztlán and pondering the meaning of death

In Tepoztlán, the first calling of the dead begins at midnight on Oct. 18. Churches across Tepoztlán ring their bells to remind residents that the dead are just around the corner. On Nov. 1 and 2, families welcome their deceased loved ones with offerings and flowers.

“We put cempasúchil out because it is believed to be the only flower the dead can see and smell,” adds Anabel Muzquiz, Thomas’ daughter and a professional tour guide.

But the welcome does not end on Nov. 2. Tepoztlán accommodates its deceased for another week.

On Nov. 8 and 9, one can still experience the spirit of Day of the Dead in Tepoztlán, when residents reunite for La Octava and finally send their deceased home. Nov. 8 is dedicated to children, while Nov. 9 marks the farewell to adults.

On Nov. 9, people gather at the cemetery to clean and decorate the graves of their dead kin. A procession of saints’ images from different barrios in Tepoztlán travels to the main cemetery in the town center for Mass and remembrance.

“There’s rice pudding, fruit or green mole, mezcal and coffee — whatever they liked,” says Elena, Thomas’ wife, describing the altars renewed on Nov. 9. “The children make little skulls out of chilacayotes and ask for sweets. There are mariachis, and there’s food.”

Walking the streets of Tepoztlán, visiting the different churches in the barrios or strolling around the cemeteries on Nov. 9 is a beautiful opportunity to experience the spirit of Day of the Dead apart from the big festivities and locura of the main event.

It invites people to reflect on their extraordinary relationship with the deceased and gives them another week to ponder the meaning of death, while copal smoke and cardboard skeletons fill the surroundings with humor and a sense of playfulness.

What makes Day of the Dead so peculiar in Morelos?

Other parts of Morelos, like Tepoztlán, are known for their elaborate rituals around Day of the Dead. The Indigenous community of Coatetelco, for example, has a tradition of hanging floating altars decorated with corn.

Its observances also begin in September, when the milpa yields its first corn harvest.

In her paper, “La fiesta: recreación de la cultura y la tradición,” anthropologist Dr. María Cristina Saldaña Fernández describes the Mesoamerican worldview underlying traditions of honoring the dead, in which duality — observed in day and night, cold and heat, life and death — played a fundamental role.

She also mentions how pre-Hispanic observances honoring the dead were connected to the agricultural calendar and coincided with the harvest.

This worldview understood life and death as a continuous process, like the germination, growth, death and return of crops, which can still be observed in Coatetelco and their corn-filled altars.



‘It’s becoming diluted, becoming more like Halloween’

However, although the cycle of life and death prevails, Day of the Dead celebrations, whether in Morelos or elsewhere, are subject to change.

“I remember how people used to light bonfires on every street corner to gather around,” says Thomas, remembering Day of the Dead in Santiago Tepetlapa some 70 years ago. “Back then, the chilacayote was the best. Now you see more mass-produced plastic pumpkins and costumes. It’s becoming diluted, becoming more like Halloween. It’s a different version now. Each generation changes things in response to its surroundings.”

According to Saldaña’s paper, politics, literature, media and cinema have also shaped the celebration, adding new elements while discarding others.

But even as La Octava changes, visitors can still respectfully join the festivities and bid farewell to the dead for another year — all while sipping their favorite mezcal, joining old friends and family, and building new relationships with the living and the deceased.

Katy Alivraz is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: From the archive: How Mexico’s Day of the Dead helps us remember the people we’ve lost
World.content:
The goal of our “From the archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in October 2019 — shows us how remembering lost loved ones can be a colorful celebration of life, love and the memories that keep them with us.

Day of the Dead is by far my favorite holiday in Mexico. My first experience with it was in 2002, when I was here as a university student.

The director of my study abroad program here in Xalapa piled a few of us into his pickup truck and we drove to Naolinco, a picturesque mountain town known for its leather products.

I was immediately enchanted. Altars were all over the place — in people’s homes, in public spaces, in restaurants and stores. As we walked along the street, people invited us into their homes for tamales, bread and homemade wine.

There were carolers at the cemetery. Carolers! With guitars! The brightly colored petals and exquisite smell of cempasúchil, “marigolds,” were everywhere.

Since then, Day of the Dead has caught on north of the border as well. Even before the popular movie “Coco” came out, the southern Texas city I return home to was starting to embrace its Mexican heritage in more expansive ways than it ever had before, with altars, decorated skulls and papel picado, “colorful tissue paper with designs,” suddenly appearing alongside Halloween decorations.

Who knew that the dead could bring us together?

Each year in my home we set up our altar with the same enthusiasm with which we decorate the Christmas tree. As the years pass and more people we know and love die, we’ve had to switch to a bigger table, as our collection of dead has grown.

My grandmother is there, as is my mother. Traditionally, the flower petals are to be sprinkled from the altar to the front door so that the dead can find their way back home from the other side to enjoy the offerings laid out for them.

My grandmother, in life, would not have appreciated her place on the altar. Like many Protestants of a certain age, she was suspicious of the “magical” elements mixed in with modern Catholicism.

Day of the Dead is, of course, a mixture of Catholic and Indigenous tradition, one that the Spaniards were only partially successful at co-opting. At least they got to move the dates to the ones they wanted. (I like to think that my grandmother, now on the other side, would be totally cool with it.)

Death is a universal reality, and all cultures have different ways of dealing with it. When I was growing up in central Texas, death was taboo, something no one wanted to talk about; it was sad at best and terrifying at worst.

Halloween was a time not to think about the dead we knew, but to have fun dressing up and getting candy (and subsequent cavities). When I learned later of the history of Halloween from pagan tradition to Catholicism’s version, All Saints’ Day, I felt decidedly more creeped out.

Why should we spend any time at all thinking about death? How uncomfortable!

How to confront death

My attitude since has evolved considerably. Now that I’m an adult, death has moved closer and closer to me in the form of the passing of actual people I’ve known and loved, and in the reality and certainty of my own mortality as the years go by.

I’m hopefully still a long way from it, but none of us really knows, do we? For something that’s such a firm fact of life, we sure do avoid thinking about it a lot.

Mexicans don’t (as much), and I think there’s something to be learned from that. We can accept that we’re going to die. We can paint skulls on our faces to remind all of us that life is for the living — that we won’t be around forever, so we’d better get to it!

What does Day of the Dead do for us? It keeps the memories of our loved ones alive. It keeps this culture alive and reminds us of the people we came from. Feel guilty about not thinking enough of your loved ones that have already passed on? Don’t: remembering to do that is built into an annual holiday here.

I am not religious myself. I don’t pretend to know what happens after death, though as an agnostic I fully expect that we simply cease to exist in the way a flame from a candle goes out. As Richard Dawkins has said, we know that consciousness is wrapped up in the brain, and we know that the brain rots, so I have no illusions.

To me, this news is not too disappointing, as I’m fairly certain that, as a dead person, I would not have the consciousness to care. Disappointing would be getting to that point of not existing and not having done anything worthwhile.

That said, I do believe that there is a way to keep our dead alive, and Day of the Dead helps us to do that. Because while they might not still be around, they live on in us, and this holiday helps us remember that in an active way. The ways they shaped us, influenced us, taught us and loved us live on.

Death is sad. We don’t usually wish for it, but learning to accept it and not fear it (at least not too much) is a worthy exercise. Celebrate, remember and love your dead. Sit and chat with them a while.

Share some hot chocolate, some tamales, some pan de muerto, play their favorite music, decorate your face the way their faces look now.

Welcome them back, at least for a couple of days, and celebrate your own beating heart.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Farewell to Cárdenas, a resignation at the INE and a record-breaking Catrina
World.content:
Listen to this article

The headlines of the week in Mexico began with news of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s reelection in Brazil, which left President Claudia Sheinbaum “very happy” and, in her words, was “a breath of fresh air” for Latin America and the Caribbean.

But at home, Mexico’s governing political movement Morena suffered another setback as the resignation of National Electoral Institute (INE) president Guadalupe Taddei raised fresh doubts about the integrity of figures tied to the government, even as Sheinbaum insisted Morena is not to blame. Meanwhile, the opposition National Action Party (PAN) announced six presumptive gubernatorial candidates for the 2027 elections.

This week also brought the death of Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas, a towering figure of Mexico’s democratic transition. And as the country heads into Day of the Dead (and Formula 1 Grand Prix) weekend, Sheinbaum called on new generations to preserve the holiday’s traditions.

Didn’t have time to catch Mexico’s top stories of the week of Oct. 26? Here’s what you missed.

Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas dies at 92

Cárdenas, a three-time presidential candidate and the son of President Lázaro Cárdenas, died in Mexico City on Wednesday. A member of the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) for more than 30 years, he left the party in 1987 and ran in 1988 as the candidate of a left-wing coalition. He is widely believed to have won that election, but Carlos Salinas de Gortari was declared the winner. Cárdenas went on to co-found the Democratic Revolution Party (PRD), contested the 1994 and 2000 elections, and served as Mexico City’s first elected mayor from 1997 to 1999.

Sheinbaum called him “a man of steadfast principles,” and Thursday’s mañanera centered on a tribute to him. Asked what he leaves the Mexican left, she answered: “Honesty and democracy.” A public tribute with his coffin present was set for Friday at the Palacio de Bellas Artes. His son Lázaro Cárdenas Batel is Sheinbaum’s chief of staff.

INE president resigns; Sheinbaum weighs in

Guadalupe Taddei announced her resignation as INE president on Sunday after media outlets, including Reforma, reported that companies tied to businessman José Alfredo Hernández Casillas, with whom she reportedly has a close personal relationship, won lucrative INE contracts. She is the first head of the INE or its predecessor, the IFE, to resign since 1990. The Federal Auditor’s Office has opened an investigation, and Taddei said: “Each allegation must be examined with evidence.”

On Monday, Sheinbaum called the resignation “good” and said an audit was needed. On Tuesday, she pushed back on journalist Carlos Loret de Mola’s claim that “Taddei is Morena,” noting that the Chamber of Deputies, not the president, chose Taddei, who was picked by lottery in 2023. By Thursday, Sheinbaum went further, saying she believes Taddei “betrayed the trust of the people of Mexico.” She also said her government will propose turning the state-run printer Talleres Gráficos de México into a state-owned company to supply most electoral materials. The INE’s focus remains the June 6, 2027, elections.

IMSS workers promised 8% raise

After weeks of protests, Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) director Zoé Robledo presented a plan of 12 actions in 120 days. It includes an 8% salary increase, permanent positions for almost 11,000 temporary workers, 2,500 new specialist doctors, more than 18,000 additional beds and gurneys, and a push to guarantee medicines and clear the surgical backlog. Whether it satisfies workers, and ends shortages that have outlasted earlier government efforts, remains to be seen.

Dog poisonings rattle Condesa

Poison hidden in sausage left in and around Mexico City’s centrally located Parque España killed at least three dogs Tuesday, prompting an animal cruelty investigation. The toll later reached four. Attorney General Bertha Alcalde Luján said tests found methomyl, a highly toxic insecticide, in capsules placed inside the meat, and authorities recovered 14 suspect pieces.

On Friday, police arrested a 58-year-old man, identified as Salvador “N,” a block from the park after he resembled a person in images circulating on social media. He was detained for resisting arrest, and prosecutors cautioned that they had not yet established whether he was responsible. Residents are avoiding the park, and Cuauhtémoc borough Mayor Alessandra Rojo de la Vega urged pet owners not to let animals eat anything off the ground.

Guadalajara water plan and allegations of torture

On Wednesday, Jalisco Governor Pablo Lemus announced a “historic agreement” with the federal government to invest 25 billion pesos (US $1.33 billion) in Guadalajara’s water infrastructure. The plan centers on two new aqueducts, from Lake Chapala and from the Calderón Reservoir, due by the end of 2028. The federal government will contribute 14.5 billion pesos and Jalisco 10.2 billion, and Lemus promised no new debt, privatization or rate increases. The announcement followed large protests demanding clean tap water.

The Oct. 11 protest in particular remains contentious. Two women, among around 10 people who have filed complaints with the Federal Attorney General’s Office, allege they were tortured by Jalisco state police. At least 39 people were arrested and dozens hurt. Lemus has conceded “serious mistakes” were made, Security Minister Juan Pablo Hernández denied ordering force and Sheinbaum has repeatedly denounced the alleged torture.

Citizen scientists make their mark

In Michoacán, residents who spotted unusual marks in a streambed led researchers to at least 50 dinosaur footprints near Apatzingán. The National Institute of Anthropology and History believes the Late Cretaceous tracks were left by three types of dinosaurs and says further study is needed to pin down species.

In Tabasco, residents of Barra de Santa Ana are working to restore coastal dunes. A 30-member community brigade trained by Eni Mexico and UNESCO will replant vegetation and install sand catchers. Erosion has hit 85% of the 30-kilometer coastline between Boca de Santa Ana and Boca de Panteones, and up to 3.5 meters of shoreline are lost each year.

Sheinbaum moves to keep Mexico’s masterpieces at home

Following the Gelman Collection controversy, Sheinbaum plans to strengthen the Monuments Law to prohibit the permanent export of privately owned works declared artistic or historical monuments. A preliminary draft was published Oct. 15. The change would reconcile the law with 10 presidential decrees protecting works by artists including Diego Rivera, Frida Kahlo and David Alfaro Siqueiros. The timing matters, as the Supreme Court is set to hear a challenge to the 1984 Kahlo decree.

Day of the Dead highlights

Mexico City’s cempasúchil production hit a record 10 million plants, up 53.8% from last year, grown mainly on Xochimilco’s chinampas.

The capital unveiled the world’s tallest Catrina in the Zócalo. At 33.4 meters, the papier-mâché figure tops Puerto Vallarta’s 2023 record holder and is the city’s fifth Guinness record this year. The offering is on display through Nov. 3.

At Friday’s mañanera, held amid marigolds and Catrina figures, Sheinbaum described the Mexican view of “death as part of life” and said the holiday has “recovered” from Halloween’s influence, partly thanks to films like “Coco.”

Economy: Exports surge, growth slows and India talks begin

Mexico’s economy grew 0.9% in the third quarter from the previous quarter, down from 1.4% but above the 0.7% economists expected. Year over year, growth of 3.2% was the largest in 12 quarters, helped by a weak third quarter in 2025.

Exports, meanwhile, reached US $77.79 billion in September, up 37.9% and the third-highest monthly total on record. Over the first nine months, exports rose 30.4% to $627.19 billion, driven by computer and electronic equipment sold to the United States amid an AI data center boom. Mexico posted a $9.25 billion trade surplus, but its oil deficit of $25.68 billion already exceeds the 2025 total.

On the trade front, Mexico and India signed terms of reference on Monday for negotiations on a preferential trade agreement. Merchandise trade between the two totaled $8.74 billion in 2024, and a Mexican business mission to India is under discussion for early 2027.

Charlyn Corral makes history at the Ballon d’Or

Pachuca forward Charlyn Corral, 35, won the Gerd Müller trophy for Best Striker of the Year at Monday’s Ballon d’Or ceremony, becoming the first Mexican woman to earn the distinction. She scored 49 goals in 49 matches for club and country and shared the honor with Harry Kane.

In her acceptance speech, she also asked the audience to recognize compatriot Scarlett Camberos, who was among the 30 nominees for the main award.

Looking ahead

Whether Jalisco’s 25 billion-peso water plan will be enough to keep Guadalajara’s streets calm is an open question. The two aqueducts are not due until the end of 2028, work “could” start next year, and the Oct. 11 allegations of police abuse remain under investigation, so residents may be left with promises rather than clean tap water for some time. On trade, Sheinbaum agreed with Donald Trump that a deal with the United States is “very close”, and on Wednesday she said talks were advancing as both sides weigh whether an interim agreement is possible before U.S. midterm elections next Tuesday, Reuters reported. Mexico is still seeking a “significant reduction” in U.S. tariffs on autos, steel and aluminum, while Washington is pressing concerns over automotive content and Chinese investment.

Even a pre-election deal would leave questions for the next Congress, according to an opinion piece in The Hill by Duncan Wood and Ivan Zapien. They argue that a change in control of Congress would not end U.S. pressure on Mexico over trade, migration and security, but a Democratic House could summon officials, scrutinize the USMCA talks and push for tougher labor and environmental enforcement, while Republicans keep pressing on energy and China. Either way, they write, Mexico should expect to answer to more of Washington, more often, after the U.S. declined in July to extend the USMCA for another 16 years.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Why I’m grateful my son is getting the Halloween-Día de Muertos experience I never had
World.content:
The funny thing about growing up in California with Mexican immigrant parents is that you are perpetually intimate with, and distant from, your Mexican roots. Every holiday season, therefore, becomes a delightfully unique interpretation of both cultures mashed together.

Tamales wrapped in banana leaves and filled with turkey for Thanksgiving? Opening gifts at midnight for Noche Buena, and then again on Christmas morning? Getting your face smashed into a birthday cake?

These are all welcome in my life as a Mexican-American who must constantly toggle between my two identities on both soils.

Sometimes, though, one cultural norm or ideology can overtake the other, leaving one half egregiously overlooked, if not completely erased. For me, that has always been the case with Día de Muertos.

Halloween was the festive U.S. tradition my household embraced in its most suburbanized form: dressing up as Ninja Turtles, trick-or-treating with pumpkin-shaped buckets, and devouring pounds of Jolly Ranchers, fun-sized Snickers and M&Ms for weeks after.

I’ve never been the king of spooky season, but I’ve also never avoided it. As I grew older and met my wife, our family Halloween tradition became dressing up in custom-made outfits that reflected our personalities or the region we lived: two high school teachers dressed as our favorite punctuation marks; two Boston post-grads dressed as the local subway trains. (Spoiler: this year we are dressing up as Chedraui employees.)

And yet, despite traveling to Mexico regularly throughout my life, and having immigrant parents who spoke Spanish and were connected to their roots in Veracruz in different ways, I don’t have any real Día de Muertos memories from my childhood.

Finding the tradition

It wasn’t until the 2010s that I recall the concept entering mainstream culture in California and elsewhere beyond Mexico. For my wife and me — both as a couple, but also in our respective Mexican-American upbringings throughout the 1990s and 2000s — we never experienced our parents or family members building altars in our California homes. Not until maybe around Pixar’s “Coco” (2017), that is.

That tradition has quickly spread. Within the past decade, it has become more commonplace to see altares, ofrendas and Día de Muertos-themed households worldwide. Of course, it existed long before “Coco,” but it wasn’t as ubiquitous as it is today.

When my son was born in 2023, my wife and I had already spent significant time in Mexico, including traveling to Oaxaca for a month during Día de Muertos season and fully immersing ourselves in its wondrous spirit of parades, parties and gravesite visits.

We had learned, while exploring Mexico’s vast regional scenes and lodging with family members in various states across the span of multiple summers, about the importance of Día de Muertos as a form of intimate ancestral remembrance. In contrast to the candy-collecting rampage we’d always known the end of October to be, we’ve been able to incorporate those important elements of Día de Muertos into our lives — and in our son’s understanding of this time of the year.

Now, having fully transplanted our lives to Veracruz, we get to experience the best of both worlds as a young family: the playful, goofy costumery and decorations of Halloween, combined with the artisanal charms and spiritual connectivity of Día de Muertos.

I wouldn’t have it any other way.

Building core memories

Undoubtedly, our son’s autumnal memories will be completely different than ours: Instead of knocking on doors in a cul-de-sac with a group of neighborhood kids, he’s going to a field of cempasúchiles in a mountainous pueblo to get his photo taken on a horse that is whimsically painted like a calavera. Instead of visiting the pumpkin patch and riding a train through cornstalks and bales of hay, his abuela and bisabuelo are coming over to our house to eat pan de muerto and build a collective family altar with photos of family members that he, or even I, will never meet.

Each has their own joys and core-memory-building functions, and I enjoy them both. I hope he does, too.

It’s true that our current community doesn’t offer much traditional Halloween vibes, in the Americanized sense. You may see a decorative witch or black cat dangling from a window, here and there. Earlier this week, I walked past a large inflatable ghost on someone’s balcony, but it was awkwardly angled to avoid the mess of wires that complicate our narrow, colonial streets.

It’s just a different atmosphere in these smaller Mexican cities and towns, and the sidewalks don’t really allow for large groups of children to roam around without parents losing their minds over incessant traffic safety.

Trick-or-treating vs. Día de Muertos parades

In 2024, we flew to Mexico City for Halloween and Día de Muertos. It was noticeably different from our experience in Veracruz. A local group of parents organized families online for a neighborhood walk, with designated homes that had registered in advance, so we knew who would be giving out candy.

Similarly, we went to a mercado in Mexico City that weekend for a “calaverita” — a Mexican version of trick-or-treating, where kids dress up and go stall to stall asking for treats.

In those instances, my son, wife and I got to experience some of that old-school Americana by walking around Mexico City with strangers — some, but not all of them, international — and knocking on doors (or wandering shop aisles) together. That version of Halloween offers a communal, neighborly bonding that isn’t always seen during other holidays, which more often than not take place inside homes with close family members, rather than out in public and in the streets. We certainly could use more of it.

Then, there’s the other side of it all: attending a Día de Muertos parade and being part of a collective throng of spectators, while ceremoniously dressed performers and various forms of alebrijes dance, flutter and chant around you. (It’s worth noting that Día de Muertos parades, like the one in Mexico’s capital, are relatively new traditions in many areas; they weren’t commonplace when I was growing up, but are a part of Día de Muertos’ increasing popularity.)

I’m glad my son will get to be immersed in those cultural experiences in ways my wife and I weren’t for Halloween.

Fusing traditions in an ever-connected world

Having access to those dual experiences is a life hack, really. That’s not to say that Halloween has never existed in Mexico, or that Día de Muertos is nonexistent in California. In each case, the cultural traditions are becoming more fused than ever before, largely thanks to social media, travel access and other global factors.

You no longer have to be in Oaxaca’s Centro to experience Día de Muertos, nor do you have to reside in a U.S. suburb to appreciate Halloween. Depending on where you are, you may not be able to fully replicate the magic of the other — but you learn to salvage whatever aspects you can.

By being in Mexico, we are reminded that we will always have generous access to, and understanding of, both celebratory worlds. That’s ultimately the beauty of being a Mexican-American binational family, no matter the seasonal holiday or time of year.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: What to Do in Nairobi in November 2026: Fashion Week
World.content:
NAIROBI · Culture

Kenya Fashion Week lands on Sunday 22 November and RX Fest rallycross fills Kasarani on 14 and 15 November. Here are the confirmed dates, prices and venues, day by day.

Nairobi city centre at golden hour (file photo). Photo: Rio Times library

NAIROBI — This is your guide to things to do in Nairobi in November 2026, from a rallycross weekend to fashion and club nights. Prices are in Kenyan shillings (KES); at about 129.8 to the dollar (RT, 1 November), KES 1,000 is roughly US$7.70.

The month starts with chess in Kibera and a run of Saturday-night shows on 7 November. It builds to a motorsport weekend on 14 and 15 November and ends with fashion and large club nights.

Every listing below comes from the organiser’s page or its ticket seller, Mookh or Ticketsasa. Times and prices can change, so check the seller’s page before you travel.

5 to 8 November: Fashion, Chess and Nightlife

Thursday 5 November KIGALI Nexus Pt 4 Essence Bar & Grill, Nairobi · from KES 2,199 (about US$17) · Mookh A midweek night out listed on the Mookh ticketing platform. The listing gives no start time, so confirm it with the venue before you go.

Saturday 7 November, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Kibera Chess Tournament Olympic Kibera, off Kibera Drive · KES 200 (about US$1.50) · Mookh The Passion Driven Chess Club runs a one-day community competition for young players from Kibera, one of Nairobi’s largest informal settlements, and beyond. It is the lowest entry price on this list, and the event is tagged kid-friendly.

Saturday 7 November, 5:00 p.m. to 3:00 a.m. The Bar Symphony Alloy Bar and Lounge, Sarit Centre car park, 6th floor, Lower Kabete Road · KES 2,500–4,000 (about US$19–31) · Mookh An orchestral night that reworks music, cocktails and nightlife in one setting. Early-bird tickets are sold out, and the price rises by phase from the Phase One price.

Saturday 7 November, 6:00 p.m. to 4:00 a.m. Funky Town: Camp Mulla Live MASSHOUSE, Ngong Racecourse · from KES 3,000 (about US$23); VIP KES 6,000 (about US$46) · Mookh A live band and DJ night for guests aged 18 and over, featuring the Kenyan group Camp Mulla. Group-of-five tickets are also listed.

Sunday 8 November, from 7:00 a.m. Amac Awards, Season 2 Nairobi · KES 300–2,000 (about US$2.30–15) · Ticketsasa Ticketsasa, a Kenyan ticketing site, sells Regular (KES 700, about US$5.40), VIP (KES 1,500, about US$11.50), VVIP (KES 2,000, about US$15) and Kids (KES 300, about US$2.30) tickets until 6:00 p.m. on the day. The listing carries no programme.

13 to 15 November: Dance, Drifting and Rallycross

Friday 13 November, 7:00 p.m. Ballpoint Afro-Latin Dance Party Village Market, Limuru Road · KES 1,000 (about US$7.70) · Ticketsasa The November edition is hosted by Hameco Limited Events. The advance ticket is redeemable against KES 500 (about US$3.85) of spending.

Saturday 14 November, 7:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. Nairobi Drift Box Nyayo National Stadium · KES 1,200 advance, KES 1,700 at the gate (about US$9 and US$13) · Ticketsasa A day of drifting takes over the stadium. Early-bird tickets closed on 25 October, and advance sales end on Thursday 12 November.

Saturday 14 and Sunday 15 November, from 7:00 a.m. Saturday RX Fest Round 3 Kasarani Safari Rally Ground · KES 500 weekend pass (about US$3.85) · Ticketsasa RX Motorsport Kenya Management Ltd hosts head-to-head rallycross, racing on a closed circuit rather than against the clock. Ticketsasa lists it from 7:00 a.m. on Saturday to 10:00 p.m. on Sunday.

21 to 29 November: Clubs, Catwalks and Concerts

Saturday 21 November, 9:00 p.m. to 6:00 a.m. Good Circle KODA Nairobi, Ring Road Mkungu Close, Kenrail Towers · KES 2,000 advance, KES 2,500 at the gate (about US$15 and US$19) · Mookh Altarra Concepts promotes an all-night mix of Afrotech, gqom, Afro house and 3-step. Early-bird tickets are sold out.

Sunday 22 November, 12:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m. Kenya Fashion Week MASSHOUSE, Ngong Racecourse · Regular KES 3,500 (about US$27); VIP front row KES 10,000 (about US$77) · Mookh Kenya Fashion Week describes itself as a platform for established and emerging Kenyan designers. Tickets are listed for the 7:00 p.m. show, and the early-bird price has closed.

Saturday 28 November, 4:00 p.m. to 3:30 a.m. The House of Kodong: All Hands on Deck A.S.K. Dome, Nairobi showground · KES 5,000 (about US$39) · Mookh Kodong Klan stages a large outdoor night at the A.S.K. Dome, a showground arena. The first advance tier has sold out, and a two-instalment payment plan is offered.

Sunday 29 November, 10:00 a.m. PAWsh Sundays The Carnivore Grounds, Nairobi · KES 1,500 (about US$11.50) · Ticketsasa Zero Four Zero Four Media and Events hosts the Sunday session, and tickets sell until 6:00 p.m. The listing gives no description of the programme.

Planning Your Nairobi November

The busiest dates are Saturday 7 November, with three events, and Saturday 14 November, when drifting and rallycross run on the same day. Book early for the paid tiers, because several early-bird and first advance tickets have already sold out.

Both Mookh and Ticketsasa sell online in Kenyan shillings.Nairobi traffic is heavy around Ngong Racecourse, Kasarani and the city centre on show days.

Use a ride-hailing app for late returns and allow extra time.

Not confirmed: the Kenyan outlet K24 reports that the German house collective Keinemusik plays Uhuru Gardens on Saturday 21 November, but we found no ticket page, so we list no price or time. The organiser’s own website for RX Fest, rxmotorsportkenya.com, shows no readable dates; Ticketsasa gives 14 and 15 November, so confirm with the organiser. We also left out events whose dates or prices we could not match across pages.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is Kenya Fashion Week in Nairobi in November 2026?

The Mookh listing gives Sunday 22 November 2026, 12:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m., at MASSHOUSE, Ngong Racecourse. Regular tickets were KES 3,500 (about US$27) and VIP KES 10,000 (about US$77).

When is RX Fest Round 3 in Nairobi?

Ticketsasa lists Saturday 14 and Sunday 15 November 2026 at the Kasarani Safari Rally Ground. A weekend pass costs KES 500 (about US$3.85).

What is there to do in Nairobi on 7 November 2026?

Three listed options are the Kibera Chess Tournament by day, plus The Bar Symphony and Funky Town in the evening. Prices run from KES 200 (about US$1.50) to KES 6,000 (about US$46).

Where do I buy tickets for Nairobi events?

Most events here sell through Mookh or Ticketsasa, both online in Kenyan shillings. Always check the seller’s page for the current price and start time.

Is there a free event in the guide?

No. Every event listed here has a paid ticket, and the cheapest is the Kibera Chess Tournament at KES 200 (about US$1.50).

World.content:

Taemin plays Lima on Friday 6 November, The Strokes follow on 20 November and Gorillaz close the month on 23 November at a new venue. The month, day by day.

LIMA — This is your guide to things to do in Lima in November 2026, and the month belongs to big touring acts. A K-pop star, an American rock band and a British virtual band all play the Peruvian capital within three weeks.

Prices are in Peruvian soles (S/); at about S/3.47 to the dollar (RT, 1 November), S/100 is roughly US$29.Every date below comes from a ticket seller, an organiser announcement or Peruvian press.

We left out anything we could not confirm, so the list is short but reliable.Dates, venues and prices can change, and some prices were published months ago.

Check the seller’s page before you buy.

Friday 6 November: Taemin Makes His Peru Debut

Friday 6 November Taemin, LiMiNaL World Tour Arena Monumental, Lima · S/240, S/400 and S/560 (about US$69, US$115 and US$162) · Teleticket Taemin, a South Korean solo singer and member of the K-pop group SHINee, gives his first solo concert in Peru. The show is part of his 2026–27 world tour, and the S/240 ticket is the Tribuna (stand) zone. Start time was not in the sources we could open.

Mid to Late November: Rock, Dance Music and Pop Legends

Friday 13 November Hardwell with Mike Williams Multiespacio Costa 21, San Miguel · from S/125 with an Interbank card, S/143 otherwise (about US$36 and US$41) · Teleticket Dutch DJ Hardwell returns to Peru about two years after headlining ULTRA Perú 2024. Dutch producer Mike Williams joins him as a special guest. Customers of the bank Interbank get a 15% discount on Teleticket, subject to the organisers’ terms.

Friday 20 November The Strokes Estadio Universidad San Marcos, Lima · S/218.50 to S/448.50 (about US$63 to US$129) · Ticketmaster Peru The New York rock band plays Lima on its tour for the new album Reality Awaits. Tribuna seats start at S/218.50, and the Cancha 1 standing area costs S/448.50.

Monday 23 November, 9:00 p.m. Gorillaz, The Mountain Tour Lurín Live, km 32 Panamericana Sur · S/342 to S/463 (about US$99 to US$134) · Ticketmaster Gorillaz, the animated band created by Damon Albarn and Jamie Hewlett, play Lima for the first time. The show moved from Arena 1 Park in San Miguel to Lurín Live, a large site south of the city, and earlier tickets remain valid. Parking costs S/40 (about US$12), and a return bus service is listed at S/12 (about US$3).

Planning Your Lima November

The Gorillaz show needs the most planning. Lurín Live is about 32 kilometres south of central Lima on the Panamericana Sur, so allow extra time and book your return trip before you go.

A new batch of Gorillaz tickets went on sale on 22 October. We could not confirm how many remain.

Teleticket and Ticketmaster Peru, the two main Peruvian ticket sellers, are the main ticket sellers for these shows. Buy from the seller named on each card and avoid resale sites, which list the same shows at higher prices.

Not confirmed: Cypress Hill is listed for Tacna on 13 November, not Lima. We also could not confirm a Greeicy date at Arena Monumental, the Lima Latin Pop Fest Vol. 3 on 28 November, or the dates of the 54th Japanese Culture Week and Matsuri AELU. The start time of Taemin’s show and of Hardwell’s show was also not available.

Frequently Asked Questions

When does Taemin play Lima in November 2026?

Friday 6 November 2026 at Arena Monumental, his first solo concert in Peru. Tickets cost S/240 to S/560 (about US$69 to US$162) on Teleticket.

Where is the Gorillaz concert in Lima?

Lurín Live, at kilometre 32 of the Panamericana Sur, on Monday 23 November 2026 at 9:00 p.m. It moved from Arena 1 Park in San Miguel, and earlier tickets remain valid.

Is Cypress Hill playing in Lima in November 2026?

We found Cypress Hill listed for Tacna on 13 November, not for Lima. We could not confirm a Lima date.

How much are tickets for The Strokes in Lima?

Ticketmaster Peru lists Tribuna seats from S/218.50 (about US$63) up to Cancha 1 at S/448.50 (about US$129). The show is on Friday 20 November at Estadio San Marcos.

PLAYA DEL CARMEN — This is your guide to things to do in Playa del Carmen in November 2026, from the last day of Día de Muertos to a triathlon, a beach-resort music festival and a jazz series. Prices are in Mexican pesos (MXN); at about 18.80 to the dollar (RT, 1 November), MXN 1,000 is roughly US$53.

Día de Muertos, the Day of the Dead, falls on 1 and 2 November, so only the final day of the big Xcaret festival is left. The rest of the month is quieter, with a public holiday on Monday 16 November and the two big weekends at Xel-Há (a nature park) and Xpu-Há (a beach area south of town).

Listings come from organiser and resort pages and from the city’s published festival calendar. Times and prices can change, so check the seller’s page before you travel.

Monday 2 November: The Last Day of Día de Muertos

Until Monday 2 November Xcaret Festival of Life and Death Xcaret Park, Riviera Maya, south of Playa del Carmen · Tickets via Grupo Xcaret (price not confirmed) Xcaret, a Riviera Maya theme park run by Grupo Xcaret, stages the 20th edition of its Día de Muertos festival from 30 October to 2 November. Guanajuato is the guest state, and the last day is Monday 2 November.

Mid November: Holiday, Maya Crafts and the Xel-Há Triathlon

Wednesday 11 to Sunday 15 November Peninsular Forum of Maya Handicrafts and Culture Playa del Carmen · Venue to be announced · Price not published The city’s autumn festival calendar lists a five-day forum with artisans from across the Yucatán Peninsula. We found no venue or opening hours yet, and the listing comes from a press report of the municipal calendar rather than an organiser page.

Saturday 14 November, from 06:30 Xel-Há Triathlon: Olympic distance and elite race Xel-Há, Riviera Maya, between Playa del Carmen and Tulum · Entry MXN 3,360 (about US$179) · triatlonxelha.com and asdeporte.com The 16th edition opens with the Olympic course of a 1.5 km swim, 40 km bike ride and 10 km run. Organisers list MXN 100,000 (about US$5,320) for the elite category, and registration was due to close on 31 October or when places sold out, so this is now a day for spectators.

Sunday 15 November, from 06:30 Xel-Há Triathlon: Sprint, relay, youth and first-timer races Xel-Há, Riviera Maya · Sprint entry MXN 3,250 (about US$173) · triatlonxelha.com Sunday brings the shorter Sprint race plus the relay, children’s and first-time women’s categories. Race organisers say all entry fees go to a conservation charity and the Mexican Red Cross.

Saturday 14 to Monday 30 November Mercadito Navideño (Christmas market) Esplanade of the Municipal Palace, Playa del Carmen centre · Admission not published The city calendar lists a market of locally made gifts, food, crafts and seasonal products. Opening hours are not yet published, so check before you go.

Monday 16 November Revolution Day holiday Nationwide · Article 74 of Mexico’s Federal Labour Law Mexico marks the anniversary of the 1910 Revolution on the third Monday of November rather than on 20 November. Banks and public offices close, and many shops and restaurants stay open.

Late November: Festival Weekend, Jazz and Thanksgiving

Friday 20 to Sunday 22 November Ember Shores Barceló Riviera Maya Resort, Xpu-Há, on the coast south of Playa del Carmen · Sold only as resort packages (price on the festival site) US electronic artist ILLENIUM hosts the fifth Ember Shores, a three-day festival held inside the resort. Packages cover the room, food, drinks and transfers from Cancún airport, and there are no stand-alone day passes.

Wednesday 25 November to Saturday 12 December Jazz Fest Playa del Carmen Quinta Avenida (Fifth Avenue) and other city venues · Free or ticket status not announced The city calendar lists performances and street activations along Quinta Avenida, with an emphasis on local musicians. Artists, stages and times had not been announced when we checked.

Thursday 26 November, 18:30 Thanksgiving dinner at La Marea Viceroy Riviera Maya, Xcalacoco, a coastal village north of Playa del Carmen · Price not published · Reservation required Chef Alejandro Salgado leads a four-course menu with roast turkey and live acoustic music by the sea. Reserve through the resort by phone or email, as the page lists no online booking price.

Planning Your Playa del Carmen November

The Xel-Há race weekend (14 and 15 November) and Ember Shores (20 to 22 November) fall close together. Book hotels early for both, as resort rooms near Xel-Há and Xpu-Há fill up.

Xcaret, Xel-Há, Xpu-Há and Xcalacoco all lie outside the city centre, between about 10 and 40 minutes by road. Plan a taxi or private driver for late returns.

Several city events (the craft forum, the Christmas market and Jazz Fest) are listed by the city without hours or prices. Check the municipal calendar for updates in the week before each one.

Not confirmed: we could not verify Día de Muertos events after 2 November beyond Xcaret, nor the Mukbil Pollo food festival or the Jazz on Fifth line-up. We also found no ticket price for Xcaret’s festival day, the Viceroy dinner or the Ember Shores packages.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is on in Playa del Carmen in November 2026?

The Xcaret Festival of Life and Death ends on 2 November. The Xel-Há Triathlon runs on 14 and 15 November, Ember Shores on 20 to 22 November, and Jazz Fest from 25 November to 12 December.

Is there a public holiday in Playa del Carmen in November 2026?

Yes. Revolution Day is observed on Monday 16 November, the third Monday of the month, under Article 74 of the Federal Labour Law. Banks and public offices close.

Can I still enter the Xel-Há Triathlon?

Registration was due to close on 31 October or when places sold out. Check triatlonxelha.com for any remaining spots; otherwise the races are open to watch.

Can I buy a single day pass for Ember Shores?

No. Tickets are sold only as resort packages at the Barceló Riviera Maya, which include the room, food, drinks and airport transfers from Cancún.

Is there a Thanksgiving dinner in Playa del Carmen?

Yes. The Viceroy Riviera Maya serves a four-course Thanksgiving dinner at La Marea on Thursday 26 November from 18:30. Reservations are required.

World.title: What to Do in Johannesburg in November 2026
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG · Culture

Wednesday 4 November is a public holiday for the local elections, and Oskido’s Big Day Out and Piano People fill 28 November. The month, day by day.

Wanderers Stadium in Johannesburg (file photo). Photo: Charles Heiman, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

JOHANNESBURG — This is your guide to things to do in Johannesburg in November 2026, from a family pantomime to the city’s big open-air music days. Prices are in rand (R); at about R16.7 to the US dollar (market-data provider RT, 1 November), R100 is roughly US$6.

The month opens with an unusual midweek break. Wednesday 4 November is a national public holiday so that South Africans can vote in the local government elections, which choose city and town councils.

The big music days then cluster on Saturday 28 November.This guide lists only events we could confirm with an organiser, venue or official page.

Times and prices can change, so check the seller’s page before you travel.

Early November: Pantomime and a Holiday

Until Thursday 24 December Alice in Wonderland pantomime Joburg Theatre, Braamfontein (a central arts and student district) · from R170 (about US$10) · Webtickets, a South African ticket seller Director Janice Honeyman stages the family pantomime, with Desmond Dube, Russel Savadier and Brendan Van Rhyn in the cast and Ashley Scott as Alice.

Wednesday 4 November Election-day public holiday Nationwide · declared by President Cyril Ramaphosa under South Africa’s Public Holidays Act Most workplaces and public services close, so expect a quiet city. Check opening hours with venues you plan to visit.

Saturday 7 November: Tembisa and Linksfield

Saturday 7 November Tembisa Kota Festival Transnet School of Rail, Esselen Park · Computicket, a South African ticket seller A daytime festival built around the kota, the township sandwich of bread stuffed with chips, egg and polony.

Saturday 7 November, 12:00 to 22:00 Kunye Jozi XI Huddle Park, Linksfield (a golf and events venue in the eastern suburbs) · Howler, a South African ticket seller The Afro-house showcase returns to Huddle Park. The event is cashless, so bring a card or phone for payments. We could not confirm the ticket price.

Late November: Soweto, Newtown and the Big Days

Saturday 28 November, 12:00 to 22:00 Oskido’s Big Day Out Huddle Park, Linksfield · R695 general, R1,950 VIP (about US$42 and US$117) · Webtickets only Oskido, a veteran of South African house music, runs two stages this year, with Liquideep, Brothers of Peace and MDU named as the first headliners.

Saturday 28 November Piano People Johannesburg Old Park Station, 140 Carr Street, Newtown · from R500 (about US$30) · Howler The amapiano festival, built on South Africa’s piano-led house sound, is listed for 28 and 29 November on the organiser’s Howler page. Uncle Waffles, a DJ and producer, is named as headliner on a local events listing.

Saturday 28 November, 18:00 The Music Vault: ILali Big Top Arena, Carnival City, Brakpan (a casino and entertainment complex east of Johannesburg) · from R250 (about US$15) Sun International, a casino and resort operator, lists the show on its Carnival City events page.

Saturday 28 November Miss Soweto, 47th edition Soweto Theatre, Jabulani The Soweto beauty pageant crowns its winner at the Soweto Theatre. We could not confirm the start time or ticket price.

Sunday 29 November: Music in the Garden

Sunday 29 November, from 13:00 Sunset Music Series: Sjava Walter Sisulu National Botanical Garden, Roodepoort · from R195 (about US$12), excluding booking fee Sjava, a Zulu-language singer-songwriter, headlines the afternoon concert in the gardens.

Planning Your Johannesburg November

Saturday 28 November is the busiest day of the month: Oskido, Piano People, a concert in Brakpan and the Miss Soweto final all fall on it. Pick one early and book ahead.

Most events sell through Webtickets, Howler, Quicket or Computicket, and foreign cards generally work on them. Huddle Park events are cashless.

Distances are large. Use e-hailing apps instead of driving home after dark, and allow extra time to reach Brakpan, Linksfield or Kempton Park on show days.

Not confirmed: we could not verify several listings that circulate online, including comedy, jazz and silent-disco nights, so they are left out. We also found no November fixtures at FNB Stadium or Ellis Park, Johannesburg’s main football and rugby grounds.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there a public holiday in Johannesburg in November 2026?

Yes. Wednesday 4 November 2026 is a national public holiday, declared by President Cyril Ramaphosa for the local government elections.

What is the biggest music event in Johannesburg in November 2026?

Oskido’s Big Day Out on Saturday 28 November at Huddle Park. General tickets cost R695 (about US$42) on Webtickets.

Where can I take children in Johannesburg this November?

Janice Honeyman’s Alice in Wonderland pantomime runs at Joburg Theatre until 24 December, with tickets from R170 (about US$10) on Webtickets.

Where do I buy tickets for Johannesburg events?

Most listings sell through Webtickets, Howler, Quicket or Computicket. Use the seller named on each event.

World.title: BTS Ends São Paulo Run as Reviews Stay Open
World.content:
Photo: Horcoff / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

BTS, the South Korean pop group, closed its three-night São Paulo run on Saturday and left Brazilian regulators with open questions. Our BTS São Paulo live updates hub follows the run and the reviews that came after it.

Key Facts Who and what: BTS, the South Korean pop group, played its third and last São Paulo show on Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026.

Crowd: São Paulo’s tourism company SPTuris projected 253,374 fans over three nights; no official count has been published.

Reviews: Brazil’s consumer secretariat Senacon suspended five resale sites; São Paulo agency Procon-SP logged 518 complaints against promoter Live Nation.

Still open: Official crowd and incident figures, and whether Senacon’s suspension of the resale sites holds.

Three Sold-Out Nights at One Stadium

BTS played the third and last of its three sold-out São Paulo shows at the MorumBIS football stadium on Saturday, Oct. 31. The concert was due to start at 8 p.m. in São Paulo (Brasília time, UTC−3), which is 7 p.m. Eastern Time.

The nights of Oct. 28, 30 and 31 were the only Brazilian dates of the ARIRANG World Tour, which is scheduled to run to March 2027 across 34 cities. Ticketmaster, the official seller, marked all three dates sold out, and sales closed in under 90 minutes.

The group last played in Brazil in May 2019, with two shows at Allianz Parque, a São Paulo arena. This tour marks its return to group activity after solo projects and military service in South Korea.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Brazil ranks 1st of 14 with 75.0 points. Strongest pillar: military means (100); weakest: state capacity & security (56). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Neymar, the Brazilian footballer, attended the Oct. 30 show with family. He joined a crowd that SPTuris projected at about 84,000 fans a night.

File photo: the MorumBIS stadium in São Paulo, May 2023. Photo: Mtvdanilo / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How Big Was the Crowd, and How Did Fans Get In?

SPTuris, the city tourism company, projected 253,374 spectators across the three shows, with a capacity of 84,458 per show. Press estimates run from more than 80,000 to about 90,000 fans a night, and none is an official count.

The São Paulo state Military Police has run a security operation named BRAvO around the stadium since Oct. 27. CET, the city traffic engineering company, deployed 82 traffic agents on Saturday.

On the opening night, Oct. 28, fans reported long queues, trouble validating tickets and a gate that stayed closed for about an hour. A storm also blocked roads to the stadium before that show, and fans demanded that the gates open.

These accounts come from spectators and press reports. No official figure for the number of people affected has been published.

Why Regulators Are Still Looking

Senacon, the national consumer secretariat under Brazil’s Justice Ministry, suspended five resale platforms as a precaution on Oct. 28. It cited a risk of collective damage of difficult reparation and opened sanction proceedings against four of the five, not Viagogo International.

The five platforms are BuyTicket, FunBuyNet, StubHub, TicketSwap Brasil and Viagogo International. BuyTicket said it was still operating and had received no formal notification.

Procon-SP, the São Paulo state consumer protection agency, recorded 518 complaints against Live Nation Brasil, 460 of them about the show structure, as of Oct. 21. Live Nation confirmed four screens, all on a central tower, while other legs of the tour had 12 LED panels in a 360-degree layout.

The São Paulo state prosecutor’s office gave Ticketmaster 15 days to explain how it calculates its service fee, after a complaint from a state legislator. The start date of that period was not found, so the deadline cannot be fixed.

What It Means for US Readers

The Brazilian reviews target ticket resale and the show’s staging, not the band. They draw a US audience because Live Nation promotes the tour and owns Ticketmaster, its ticket-selling arm.

The tour’s North American leg opened in Tampa, Florida, on April 25. It ended in early September at SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles.

What Is Not Known

No official attendance figure or incident balance for the Oct. 31 show has been found, and no Military Police, city or SPTrans (the city transit authority) numbers were available. Claims of overcrowding on the opening night remain allegations by spectators.

It is not known whether Senacon’s suspension was upheld or challenged. The outcome of Procon-SP’s notification of Live Nation is also unknown.

We found no poll by a named institute on this story. We also found no prediction-market odds.

Sources

Published Sunday, Nov. 1, 5:30 p.m. ET. Source: Senacon, Procon-SP, the São Paulo state prosecutor’s office, SPTuris, CET, the São Paulo state Military Police, statements by Live Nation Brasil, and The Rio Times reporting.

When was BTS’s last São Paulo show?

Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026, at the MorumBIS stadium, scheduled for 8 p.m. in São Paulo (7 p.m. ET). It followed shows on Oct. 28 and 30.

Which authorities are reviewing the shows?

Senacon, the national consumer secretariat, suspended five resale platforms, and Procon-SP logged 518 complaints against Live Nation Brasil. The state prosecutor’s office gave Ticketmaster 15 days to explain its service fee.

World.title: Raft Capsizes on Chile’s Maipo River, 3 Dead
World.content:
Three women died when a raft capsized on the Maipo River, a popular rafting river near Santiago, Chile, on Sunday.

Key Facts Who. Three women died; reports differ on how many others were aboard.

What. A raft capsized on the Maipo River in a popular rafting canyon.

Where. San Alfonso sector, San José de Maipo, a mountain municipality southeast of Santiago.

When. Sunday 1 November 2026, at about 14:30 Chile time.

As of 1 November 2026, 21:00 GMT. Figures were still changing.

A raft capsized on the Maipo River in Chile on Sunday 1 November 2026, and three women died. It happened at about 14:30 local time in the San Alfonso sector of San José de Maipo, a mountain municipality southeast of Santiago.

The Cajón del Maipo is a river canyon near the capital that is known for whitewater rafting and adventure tourism. Visitors from abroad can book such trips from Santiago, so the questions raised here are practical ones.

What We Know

The alert came through the emergency number 133. Police, firefighters, emergency medical staff and municipal safety teams went to the river.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Chile ranks 3rd of 14 with 63.6 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (86); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (38). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Three women died, and their names and ages have not been released. Their bodies were found in several sectors of the river valley, including San Alfonso, El Melocotón and Cascada de las Ánimas.

Roberto Pérez, the mayor of San José de Maipo, confirmed the three deaths. The municipality promised further updates as information is confirmed.

Reports differ on how many people were on the raft. Early accounts gave figures from at least seven to 12 people, and a later report said 13.

Early afternoon reports said two people were missing and that search teams were working near the Las Vertientes bridge in strong currents. A later report said ten people had been rescued, and eight of them were taken to the hospital in San José de Maipo.

The Asociación de Empresas de Rafting del Cajón del Maipo, the local rafting companies' association, said the boat was not operated by any of its member companies, but by private individuals. It said registered member firms were helping with the rescue and described river conditions as “normal and safe”.

No cause has been confirmed. Police, including Chile's investigative police (PDI), are looking into the capsizing.

File photo: the Andes above Santiago. It does not show the accident site.

What Is Not Known

The exact number of people aboard, rescued and missing is not settled. Counts shifted through the afternoon and may change again.

The names, ages and nationalities of the three women have not been released. Published accounts do not say whether any foreign visitors were involved.

The cause has not been confirmed by investigators. Early reports offered no official explanation.

It is unclear who owned the raft and what safety equipment was on board. Those details have not been made public.

No one has been publicly named as responsible. Until investigators report, the cause and any responsibility stay open.

What It Means for Travelers and US Readers

The rafting association says the boat was run by private individuals and not by one of its member companies. That is the association's account, and the owners have not been identified.

What follows is general advice and not a finding about this accident. Before booking a river trip, check that the operator is a registered company and that its guides are trained.

Ask whether every passenger gets a life jacket and a helmet. Ask too whether a safety briefing is given before launch and how many people the raft is meant to carry.

Trained guides and proper equipment matter on every river trip. A calm start does not remove the need for them.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened on the Maipo River?

A raft capsized on Sunday 1 November 2026 in the San Alfonso sector of San José de Maipo, southeast of Santiago, Chile. Three women died, and officials were still confirming how many others were aboard and rescued.

Why did the raft capsize?

The cause is not confirmed. Police are looking into the capsizing, and no official explanation has been published.

Was a registered rafting company involved?

The local rafting companies' association says the boat was not operated by any member company but by private individuals.

Have the victims been identified?

Not publicly. The names, ages and nationalities of the three women have not been released.

World.title: Mexico’s Buen Fin Sale Starts Nov. 13
World.content:
Perisur shopping centre in Mexico City at dusk, in a file photo from 2025. Liverpool opened a new zone there on 10 September. Photo: Ehécatl Cabrera / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

Key Facts

When: Friday, Nov. 13, to Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. El Buen Fin (“the good weekend”) is Mexico’s yearly discount event.

Friday, Nov. 13, to Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. El Buen Fin (“the good weekend”) is Mexico’s yearly discount event. Forecast: Business chamber Concanaco Servytur expects 235 billion pesos (US$12.5 billion) in sales spillover, about 7% above 2025.

Business chamber Concanaco Servytur expects 235 billion pesos (US$12.5 billion) in sales spillover, about 7% above 2025. Lottery: The tax agency’s 500 million peso (US$26.6 million) draw is set for Friday, Dec. 4, noon Mexico City (1 p.m. Eastern Time).

The tax agency’s 500 million peso (US$26.6 million) draw is set for Friday, Dec. 4, noon Mexico City (1 p.m. Eastern Time). Next deadline: Businesses must register by 11:59 p.m. Mexico City time on Thursday, Nov. 12.

Mexico’s biggest shopping event starts in less than two weeks, and its sponsors expect the slowest growth in years. Our El Buen Fin updates hub follows every step, and this guide sets out the dates, the forecast and the lottery for US readers.

Five Days Starting Friday

El Buen Fin, Mexico’s annual discount programme coordinated by the Economy Ministry with the private sector, runs for its 16th edition from Friday, Nov. 13, to Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. Last year’s edition ran Thursday to Monday, also five days, so this year the window moves to Friday through Tuesday.

Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The window takes in Revolution Day, the holiday that marks the start of Mexico’s 1910 revolution. Under Mexico’s Federal Labor Law it is observed on Monday, Nov. 16 this year. Schools are also closed that day, which creates a long weekend.

The programme covers physical shops, websites and other sales channels nationwide, so it has no single venue. Participating sectors include restaurants, department stores, electronics, tourism and education.

File photo: shoppers on Calle Madero, a pedestrian shopping street in Mexico City’s historic centre.

Download the PDF checklist

Business Chamber Projects Slower Growth

Concanaco Servytur, the national confederation of chambers of commerce, services and tourism, forecasts an economic spillover of 235 billion pesos (US$12.5 billion). That is about 7% above the 219.2 billion pesos (US$11.7 billion) it reports for 2025, which itself was 26.1% above 2024’s 173.8 billion pesos (US$9.3 billion). We convert all pesos at 18.7856 per US dollar, the rate on the day of writing.

Octavio de la Torre, the confederation’s president, said about 49 billion pesos (US$2.6 billion), or 21%, would come from online sales. Around 186 billion pesos (US$9.9 billion), or 79%, is expected to stay in physical stores, with more than 200,000 businesses taking part.

Fashion is expected to lead shoppers’ intentions at 38%, followed by electronics at 30%, personal care at 27%, appliances at 24% and cell phones at 21%. These shares come from the Concanaco forecast.

Tax Agency Lottery and Price Checks

The SAT, Servicio de Administración Tributaria, Mexico’s federal tax authority, runs a lottery with a 500 million peso (US$26.6 million) pool to encourage electronic payments. Of that sum, 400 million pesos (US$21.3 million) is for consumers and 100 million pesos (US$5.3 million) for registered businesses.

Card purchases of at least 250 pesos (about US$13) at registered businesses between Nov. 13 and Nov. 17 enter automatically, and shoppers need not register. The consumer top prize is up to 250,000 pesos (US$13,300), and 321,260 smaller prizes range from 500 to 20,000 pesos (US$27 to US$1,065).

Profeco, the federal consumer protection agency, offers a Quién es Quién en los Precios tool at elbuenfin.profeco.gob.mx. It covers eight product categories (audio, cameras, kitchen, computing and mobile devices, home appliances, large appliances, TV and video, and ventilation), and it shows minimum, maximum and average prices and each product’s price history.

Dates to Watch

Business registration closes on Thursday, Nov. 12, and the list of participating registrations is due Nov. 27. Shoppers can check by card number from Friday, Nov. 27 whether a purchase qualifies for the lottery.

The draw is reported for Friday, Dec. 4, at noon in Mexico City, with a live broadcast. A winners list is due Dec. 7, and prizes are to be paid by early January 2027.

What It Means for US Readers

Official information is published at elbuenfin.org for participating businesses and at elbuenfin.profeco.gob.mx for price checks. Most of it is in Spanish, so US visitors should check prices in pesos before they compare.

Mexico City is one hour behind Eastern Time in December, so the Dec. 4 draw would start at 1 p.m. ET.

What Is Not Known

We have not found an official start hour for Nov. 13, and we have not opened the organiser, SAT or Profeco pages directly. The dates here come from press reports of official announcements.

Press reports give the draw as Dec. 4 at noon, but we have not seen the tax agency’s own rules for the 2026 draw.

We found no development dated Oct. 31 or Nov. 1, no named poll and no prediction-market odds on this topic. The Concanaco forecast is the only industry projection we have seen, and others, such as online-sales bodies, may publish different numbers.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is El Buen Fin 2026?

It runs from Friday, Nov. 13, to Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, across Mexico. We have not found an official start hour.

How big is the sales forecast?

Concanaco Servytur projects 235 billion pesos (US$12.5 billion) in economic spillover. That is about 7% above 2025, a slower rate than the 26.1% growth the year before.

World.title: Grenada Votes Thursday With 46 Candidates
World.content:
St George's, Grenada's capital and main port, looking out to sea (file photo, June 2025). (Photo: Cuban Boy, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Key Facts

Vote: Thursday, November 5, 2026. Polls are open 5 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern Time (6 a.m. to 5 p.m. in Grenada).

Thursday, November 5, 2026. Polls are open 5 a.m. to 4 p.m. Eastern Time (6 a.m. to 5 p.m. in Grenada). Prize: All 15 seats in the House of Representatives, the elected lower chamber. Eight seats make a majority.

All 15 seats in the House of Representatives, the elected lower chamber. Eight seats make a majority. Field: 46 candidates. The governing and opposition parties contest every seat, and a new party contests nine.

46 candidates. The governing and opposition parties contest every seat, and a new party contests nine. Next date: Monday, November 2, special voting for police officers, ahead of polling day.

Grenada, a Caribbean island nation, heads to the polls on Thursday, and the week begins with a vote by the police. Our Grenada election updates hub tracks every step, and this guide sets out the calendar, the stakes and the clock for readers in the United States.

The ballot matters beyond the island because Grenada is a small, English-speaking democracy close to Venezuela. A change of government would be watched in Washington, in London and in the wider Caribbean.

The Calendar for the Week

Voting day is Thursday, November 5, 2026, with polls open from 6 a.m. to 5 p.m. local time. That is 5 a.m. to 4 p.m. on the US East Coast, because Grenada keeps the same clock all year and US clocks went back an hour on Sunday, November 1.

The next fixed date is Monday, November 2, when police officers vote early. The dates and hours here come from press reports, because we could not open the official notice from the Supervisor of Elections, the official who runs the poll.

File photo: Hillsborough Bay on Carriacou, one of the islands that make up Grenada.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What Is at Stake

Voters choose all 15 members of the House of Representatives, each in a single-member constituency. The candidate with the most votes in a seat wins it, which is known as first past the post, and a party needs eight seats to form a government.

Prime Minister Dickon Mitchell leads the National Democratic Congress (NDC), which won nine seats in the last election, held on June 23, 2022. The opposition New National Party (NNP) won the other six.

The NNP is the only party in Grenada’s history to have won all 15 seats, and it has done so three times. That record shows how quickly one side can sweep a small chamber when the national mood turns.

The Contenders

Emmalin Pierre leads the NNP and is the leader of the opposition. She took over from the party’s founder, Keith Mitchell, a former prime minister who led the NNP until December 2024.

A third force, the Democratic People’s Movement (DPM), was launched on November 16, 2025, by Peter David, a former foreign minister. Reports say the DPM is fielding candidates in nine of the 15 seats, while the NDC and the NNP are contesting all of them.

The three leaders met on Wednesday, October 28, at 7 p.m. ET for a debate at the Grenada Trade Centre in St George’s. It gave undecided voters their last long look at the main contenders before polling day.

What It Means for US Readers

Polls close at 4 p.m. ET on Thursday, so the first results could arrive during the American evening. Check back with our hub for the count, because a result is not final until the electoral authorities declare it.

Observer missions, including one from the Organization of American States, a regional body of 35 countries, are expected. Their preliminary statements usually follow within days of the vote.

For travellers and investors, a clear result matters more than the winner, since a close finish in a 15-seat chamber can leave the government in doubt. A third party also adds a new variable, because it may split the vote in the seats where it stands.

What Is Not Known

We found no news dated October 31 or November 1 that changes the schedule, and no representative poll from a named institute. We also found no prediction-market price on the race, although our search cannot rule out that one exists.

It is not known whether the DPM will take votes mainly from the governing party or from the opposition. The current party standings in the chamber, after defections since 2022, are also not confirmed here.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the Grenada election and when do polls open?

Grenada votes on Thursday, November 5, 2026. Polls are open from 5 a.m. to 4 p.m. ET, which is 6 a.m. to 5 p.m. local time.

How many seats does a party need to win?

All 15 House seats are contested, each decided by first past the post. A party needs eight seats for a majority.

World.title: Costa Rica Dollar Supply Hits Record 20 Years After Colón Devaluations Ended
World.content:
Costa Rica is marking 20 years since it abandoned the system of controlled devaluations that let the Central Bank weaken the colón against the U.S. dollar in small, predictable steps. The anniversary arrives as the foreign exchange market posts record dollar supply, keeping the exchange rate near its lowest level in two decades.

Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) President Róger Madrigal revisited the 2006 reform on Friday, Oct. 30, during the presentation of the institution’s October Monetary Policy Report. The weighted average exchange rate in the Foreign Currency Market (Monex) closed that day at ₡452.08 per dollar, about 35% below the record ₡696.76 set on June 21, 2022.

The BCCR board approved the change on Oct. 13, 2006, and it took effect four days later, ending the crawling peg the country had used since 1984. Under that system, the bank adjusted the rate in small daily increments, so the colón lost value against the dollar at a steady, predictable pace.

The 2006 reform replaced the peg with an exchange rate band. The dollar could move between a ceiling and a floor, and the Central Bank intervened when the rate reached either limit.

Costa Rica moved to the current managed float in February 2015. The rate is now set mainly by supply and demand, although the Central Bank can step in to prevent sharp swings. The shift also cleared the way for the inflation-targeting framework the bank formally adopted in 2018.

According to the October report, average daily dollar supply in the exchange market so far this year reached about $152.9 million, up from $134.9 million in the same period of 2025. Average daily demand rose from $108.1 million to $122.3 million, leaving a daily surplus of about $30.6 million.
