In 1884, local residents raised funds to erect a cast-iron cross. Nearby, at the edge of the woods, they built a simple hut.

One half became an improvised folk museum called Tarasova Svitlytsia (“Taras’s Chamber”); the other served as the home of a caretaker. The exhibits included a copy of Kobzar, an oil portrait of the poet with a halo above his head, brushes belonging to an unknown artist, a kobza, a traditional Ukrainian stringed instrument, and an old visitors’ book lying on a table.

Embroidered Ukrainian towels, known as rushnyky, hung on the walls, including some bearing Shevchenko’s image. Many of those who brought them could neither read nor write, yet knew his poems by heart.

Secret reports from the Kaniv gendarmerie on visitors to the site have survived in the State Archives of the Kyiv Region. People came to Chernecha Hill not only from neighboring villages but from far away. Surveillance intensified ahead of major anniversaries.

The authorities refused to permit either accommodation for pilgrims or the establishment of an association to maintain and protect the grave. A document dated April 8, 1910, from the Kyiv provincial authority responsible for public associations explained why. Such an association, it warned, “would provide a convenient means of bringing together activists and adherents of the Ukrainophile party, allowing them to gather in an isolated place, difficult for the administration to observe and monitor.”

The association’s activities, officials cautioned, “would be directed toward strengthening propaganda for the cultural and political autonomy of Little Russia.” They even found evidence of suspicious intentions in the application’s failure to specify the language to be used for official business. The implication was clear: the language in question might not be Russian.

The Moscow art theatre at Shevchenko’s grave

The warnings from the gendarmerie and the authorities’ fears of “advocates of autonomy” did not deter prominent figures in Russia’s artistic and intellectual circles.

Zinaida Tarakhan-Bereza, the oldest living staff member of the Shevchenko National Reserve, cites historical accounts in her scholarly chronicle The Shrine (Kyiv, 1998). In May 1912, a steamer decorated with Shevchenko’s portrait, embroidered towels and flowers arrived at the Kaniv landing.

“No speeches, politically charged songs or other demonstrative performances!” the “tourists” were reminded once again as they came ashore.

Only two wreaths were permitted at the poet’s grave.

One came from the Ukrainian Club, a national and cultural association headed by the composer Mykola Lysenko. The other was an elaborate wrought-metal wreath decorated with oak leaves, symbolizing eternity, a laurel branch and a bronze plaque bearing the inscription: “A bow to the ground before the genius Shevchenko from the Moscow Art Theatre.”

The Moscow Art Theatre was touring Kyiv at the time. From then on, its actors spent every summer living communally at a nearby hamlet beside Taras Hill, drawing inspiration from the place. Among them were Ivan Moskvin, Yevgeny Vakhtangov and Mikhail Chekhov.

The Ukrainian Club was shut down in 1912.

I examined the leaves from the theatre’s wreath in a museum display case. They have survived two world wars and are now enduring Russia’s invasion.

The Museum in a bomb shelter

Few original exhibits remain on display at the museum. The most valuable surviving objects have been moved to a secure location to protect them from bombing.

“Kaniv, and particularly the Kaniv Hydroelectric Power Plant, has come under fire more than once. But our academic council collectively decided not to evacuate anything outside the country,” says Hanna Manzhara, the museum’s senior collections curator.

She is 80 and cannot imagine her life apart from the museum.

“We resumed work in July 2022 because the number of visitors kept growing. That was such an incentive! We moved the exhibition to the basement, which had been converted into a bomb shelter. At the beginning of this year, we returned to the surface, to the galleries.”

Unlike monuments in Kyiv, Shevchenko’s memorial in Kaniv has not been covered with sandbags. It is not simply a sculpture but a burial mound with a crypt inside, a place where people come to pay their respects.

Yet Russian forces have also struck cemeteries: in Cherkasy in July 2025, in Odesa in October 2024 and in Kramatorsk in April 2023.

Hanna Ivanivna Manzhara, senior collections curator. Photograph: Olga Musafirova

Ukrainian Culture Days in Moscow

The conversation naturally turns to Russia. The Moscow and St. Petersburg periods of Shevchenko’s life and work cannot simply be erased from his story.

Hanna Manzhara recalls taking part in Ukrainian Culture Days in Moscow in 2003, together with Vita Dzyma, a senior researcher.

“The Ukrainian Center on Arbat Street asked us to take part.

“We brought an exhibition featuring lifetime editions of individual poems, as well as publications from 1911 and 1914, marking the 50th anniversaries of his birth and death. We added woven Ukrainian folk towels made by Marуsia Vasylashchuk, a traditional craftswoman. The response was fantastic! Teachers from Moscow came, along with members of the Ukrainian diaspora. Our fellow museum professionals were particularly remarkable in the attention they gave us.”

“And, of course, there were collectors,” Dzyma continues. “I won’t name them; we lost contact a long time ago. But copies of Moscow newspapers reporting on Taras Shevchenko’s funeral found their way to Kaniv through antique shops on Arbat Street.

“The museum was preparing for reconstruction, and we were trying to build up our collection.”

Manzhara adds: “You see, the life and work of the Kobzar are far broader than anything we ourselves could convey to an audience.”

Dzyma has a similar story. In the family of the St. Petersburg literary scholar Ieremiya Aizenshtok, a self-portrait of 16-year-old Taras was discovered, dating from the time he served as Engelhardt’s personal attendant, or kazachok. Research and evidence suggested it was the earliest portrait of the Kobzar.

“But Aizenshtok’s relatives asked for a very high price. The Kaniv museum simply couldn’t afford it. What happened to the portrait, and who owns it now, is unknown.”

At that moment, the author’s phone begins to vibrate: an air-raid alert has been issued in Kyiv.

On social media, Russian military personnel who have spent nearly five years launching missiles, including at Ukrainian museums, are sarcastically dubbed “Pushkinists.” Among the institutions hit have been the Hryhorii Skovoroda Museum in Skovorodynivka, the Kupiansk Museum of Local History and the Odesa Fine Arts Museum.

A Shrine to an Icon: The Museum Under Soviet Rule

“Now the working people of Ukraine and the Soviet Union will be able to become more familiar with the great legacy of the poet-revolutionary, a fighter against the social and national oppression that weighed so heavily on the peoples of the former tsarist Russia,” the republican newspaper Kommunist wrote in 1936.

The newspaper recalled that in 1923, a temporary monument had been erected over Shevchenko’s grave “in place of the cross so hated by the poet and all working people,” and that a temporary exhibition had been set up nearby in 1934. At the same time, construction of a museum was underway on Taras Hill.

Visitors often ask why the Soviet authorities invested so heavily in the project during the Holodomor, the famine that devastated Ukraine. It was the first building in Ukraine designed specifically to house a museum. Until then, museums had generally occupied historic aristocratic or manor houses.

Vita Dzyma offers an explanation:

“Look around: every home had a portrait of Shevchenko – embroidered, painted, burned into wood or assembled from straw. Kobzar lay beside the Bible, or took its place when the campaign against religion began.

“The villages at the foot of Taras Hill were being starved to death. People hired themselves out to work on the construction site for a piece of bread. They carried stones by hand, as in ancient Egypt. Yet they were proud of their work. The Shevchenko Museum was no less than a temple.

“Arguing with Ukrainians about this is a losing battle. Taras is both a father and a prophet!”

Vita Dzyma, senior researcher at the museum. Photograph: Olga Musafirova

A sculptural composition of Lenin and Stalin was installed in the entrance hall, while Shevchenko’s bust was moved to the second floor so that it would not compete with them. According to Dzyma, whose account is supported by research, Soviet propagandists in the 1930s seriously pursued the idea of finding a physical resemblance between Lenin and Shevchenko.

The burial mound was given an upgrade, too. Behind a granite balustrade at the base of the monument, a platform was built resembling the speaker’s tribune at Lenin’s Mausoleum, intended for members of the Ukrainian Communist Party’s Politburo.

In 1939, marking the 125th anniversary of the Kobzar’s birth, Nikita Khrushchev, the first secretary of the Communist Party of Ukraine, spoke at the opening of the museum and the unveiling of the new monument.

“The tradition of placing microphones beside Shevchenko and addressing the community as if speaking on his behalf, from his elevated position, has survived to this day,” Hanna Manzhara explains.

The museum under nazi occupation: Director Dmytro Lebedko

In mid-August 1941, the last train carrying mobilized troops left Kaniv across the bridge over the Dnipro. The bridge was bombed, and its ruins can still be seen from Taras Hill.

There was no time to evacuate the museum before the Nazi occupation. Its staff scattered. The women I spoke to avoid going into detail about what happened next. “It would be disrespectful to the local residents,” they say.

Dmytro Lebedko, a former librarian at the reserve who had been mobilized into the Red Army and survived the bombing of his train, found himself in two roles at once: collaborator, having agreed to work with the occupying forces, and preserver of the museum’s collection.

The Nazis did not close the museum. Instead, they ordered it to be put in order and kept open. Visitors, mostly German soldiers, were brought through in formation. For the first time, not a single entry appeared in the visitors’ book.

The local population was afraid to visit Taras Hill, even though in the nearby district center of Horodyshche, the Nazis had toppled a statue of Karl Marx and replaced it with one of Shevchenko.

Archival documents preserve Lebedko’s testimony: “In 1941, I managed to recover from the village of Pekari 15 chairs, about 2,000 books, two carpets embroidered with portraits of Shevchenko, six silk curtains and a number of other valuables.”

After becoming director, he carried out a full inventory of the museum’s collection, cataloguing 4,000 items. He was not afraid to compile a list of paintings and drawings that the local Nazi district commissioner had supposedly taken for “temporary use.” He also recorded every vase and carpet appropriated by yet another official with an interest in “Slavic exoticism.” Then he took a risk that could have cost him his life: he moved the most valuable objects into a hiding place, sealed it behind a wall and went into hiding himself.

After Soviet troops arrived, Lebedko still managed to help restore the museum, which the Nazis had ransacked shortly before retreating. He voluntarily admitted in court to having been involved in a “Ukrainian nationalist Bandera organization.”

The authorities demanded that he strengthen his self-incriminating statement. “I thought Soviet rule would no longer exist in Ukraine and that Ukraine would become independent. I now understand the serious political error in my views,” he was made to say.

He was convicted of treason and sentenced to the maximum term. Three years later, he died in the Norilsk labor camps from a perforated stomach ulcer.

Dmytro Lebedko was 47, the same age as Taras Shevchenko. His name was erased from the history of the reserve for decades. Museum staff emphasize that only 10 exhibits from the prewar collection have survived to this day.

Yanukovych’s makeover

Toward the end of Leonid Kuchma’s presidency, plans emerged for a major restoration project in Kaniv. A nationwide fund was established specifically to restore historical and architectural heritage sites, and UkrNDIproektrestavratsiya, a Ukrainian research and design institute specializing in restoration, was selected to develop the project. Its specialists proposed returning the building to its original appearance, based on the drawings of architect Vasyl Krychevsky.

In the 1930s, Krychevsky had been unable to realize his full vision. His design was deemed “too Ukrainian,” and both he and his closest student, Petro Kostyrko, were removed from the project. The construction was completed by more compliant hands. As a result, museum staff, whose building had received no major restoration since World War II, were afraid even to express their hopes aloud.

The project stalled, then resumed under President Viktor Yanukovych. According to those involved, the massive, even pompous building made a strong impression on him. If the museum was to host the annual Shevchenko National Prize ceremony, Ukraine’s highest state award for achievements in culture and the arts, it had to meet the president’s aesthetic standards.

Few understood Yanukovych’s tastes better than Hanna Herman, one of his closest allies, a member of parliament from the Party of Regions and head of its humanitarian policy team, and her protégé, architect Larysa Skoryk.

“History repeated itself,” Vita Dzyma says. “At the final stage, UkrNDIproektrestavratsiya was removed from the project, and the national character of the design was discarded. ‘No painted decoration on the exterior – this isn’t some village hut!’ they said. But the preparatory work for the majolica facade had already been completed. The same was true of the alfresco work – the decorative painting in relief.

“The Ministry of Culture’s scientific and methodological council convened and decided: whitewash it!”

Hanna Manzhara adds: “Even the surviving fragments of Krychevsky’s original work, which had miraculously survived the previous war and were rediscovered during the restoration, were covered up again.”

Skoryk developed a stripped-down design concept. The polychrome landscape inspired by the poem Haidamaky was replaced with a monochrome version.

The original coffered ceiling was concealed behind a stretch ceiling. Red lines of Shevchenko’s poetry ran across the gray fabric like information scrolling through a subway station. Glass replaced the wooden mosaic partitions in the entrance hall, while granite slabs took the place of parquet flooring.

“We wanted at least to restore the unique botanical and floral patterns on the columns.

“Both museum staff and Krychevsky’s relatives wrote to Yanukovych. It made no difference. What we got was a gray-and-white renovation,” Dzyma concludes.

She asks whether the author noticed the granite boulder at the entrance, in the center of the lobby. The author is puzzled. Surely this is not a geological museum.

▇ “Shevchenko is the cornerstone of the national idea. It’s a metaphor!”

Photographs From 1944 and a Forced-Labor Camp in the Museum

The author’s attention was drawn to two framed photographs on the wall, dated the last day of January 1944. Yakov Davidzon, a frontline correspondent, arrived at Taras Hill immediately after Kaniv was liberated. He found the museum surrounded by barbed wire, with burned books, torn paintings and shattered sculptures. Sixteen shrapnel wounds had been counted on the pedestal of Shevchenko’s monument.

“We learned only in 1981 that a forced-labor camp had operated inside the museum during the final months of the occupation,” says Valentyna Avramenko, head of the Tarasova Svitlytsia section.

She recalls a visitor from Moscow who wandered through the galleries as if he knew every corner of the building. It turned out that he was a native of the area who, as a teenager, had been caught in a roundup.

Young people were deported to the Reich for forced labor, while children as young as 13 or 14 were made to dig trenches and build fortifications. Several hundred schoolchildren were held inside the building, half-starved, sleeping on damp, rotting straw alongside horses. A toilet had been hacked directly into the parquet floor. Armed guards marched the children to the banks of the Dnipro with shovels and forced them to work under gunpoint. If one escaped, the others were beaten almost to death.

Staff at the reserve began tracking down the former child prisoners and recording their testimonies. Those who had survived long enough were later helped to submit applications for compensation from Germany. Why had no one spoken about the camp sooner?

The author found the answer herself in an archival leaflet issued by the Taras Shevchenko partisan unit, which operated in the forests of the Cherkasy region:

“We will find and kill everyone who helps the Germans build defensive lines along the Dnipro!”

Makohon’s bust: From Kaniv to Volodarka

In Davidzon’s second photograph, Shevchenko’s bust has a bullet hole in its forehead. The resemblance to the monument in Borodianka, shot up by Russian forces in 2022, is chilling.

The author was told that Ivan Makohon, a prominent Soviet Ukrainian sculptor, had created the plaster bust in 1937 specifically for the opening of the museum in Kaniv. But the work’s fate after World War II remains unknown. It is held neither in the museum’s exhibition nor in the collection of Ukraine’s National Art Museum.

The sculptor’s son, Ihor Makohon, himself a painter, sculptor and graphic artist, is now 90 and lives in Italy. He was surprised to hear the story of the wounded, missing Kobzar.

“There must be some misunderstanding! I visited Kaniv in the mid-1950s and took photographs. The bust was on the second-floor balcony, completely undamaged.

“In 1961, my father decided to modify the composition slightly, adding shoulders. The new version was more monumental. Two plaster casts were made in the workshop at the Kyiv Art Institute, where Professor Makohon taught, and the mold was preserved.”

More than 60 years passed. In 2024, Ihor Makohon received a request from Volodarka, a district center in the Kyiv region. Local residents wanted to install a “historic” Shevchenko monument by Makohon and asked for his permission.

Ihor Ivanovych not only found the original mold but also arranged for the bust to be produced.

“We cast the bust in concrete with the lads and took it to Volodarka. There was enormous interest, and a lot of people gathered,” he recalls.

The unveiling took place on the Feast of the Intercession of the Holy Mother of God, which Ukraine also celebrates as the Day of Defenders and Defendresses. The project fulfilled an idea conceived by Oleksandr Ushynskyi, a local resident, environmentalist, researcher of the Holodomor, Maidan protester and war veteran.

In 2014, Ushynskyi volunteered for the front, defended Donetsk airport and later established a community museum dedicated to the Russian-Ukrainian war in his hometown. The monument in Volodarka became the 1,385th monument to Shevchenko in Ukraine and around the world.

The nazis, the communists and Russian propaganda

“Both the Nazis during World War II and the Soviets used Shevchenko to manipulate Ukrainians’ minds for propaganda purposes,” says Ihor Solovey, head of the Center for Strategic Communications and Information Security under Ukraine’s Ministry of Culture.

“The Nazis tried to exploit our national sentiments under the guise of ‘friendship.’

“They took passages from Kobzar and amplified them to turn people against Soviet rule. The message was supposedly about resistance to Russian oppression, mixed with all sorts of vile nonsense about ‘Jewish Bolshevism.’ They even put Taras’s words on posters – the familiar line: ‘Muscovites are strangers; they bring you harm.’

“To present themselves as benefactors, the Nazis deliberately published his poetry and prose during the occupation and ran articles about Shevchenko that served their purposes. They wanted people to believe that Ukrainian culture was free and flourishing under the Reich.”

“The Communists did exactly the same thing. They just dressed it up differently to persuade Ukrainians to fight the Germans. Think of the famous rallying cry: ‘Drench freedom in the enemy’s blood!’” Solovey continues.

Eighty years have passed. In June 2026, Ukraine’s Security Service announced that a 57-year-old woman from Kaniv had been formally notified of suspicion over the dissemination of “materials justifying and denying the Russian Federation’s armed aggression against Ukraine.”

The woman reportedly referred to the invasion as a “special military operation,” urged support for the Russian army and openly promoted pro-Kremlin narratives among acquaintances and colleagues. According to investigators, she was one of the deputy heads of the Shevchenko National Reserve.

Modern Russian propaganda reproduces methods first used under the Russian Empire and later adopted by the Soviet Union. One is to present Shevchenko primarily as part of Russian culture, pointing to the fact that he wrote his diaries and prose in Russian.

Another is to portray him as a “pan-Russian poet,” downplaying the importance of his work in shaping Ukrainian national identity.

But those carrying out Russia’s full-scale war on Ukrainian soil increasingly see Shevchenko, his monuments and his museums not as shared cultural heritage, but as an adversary and a source of resistance.

World.title: Mayor and entrepreneur: Transparency International calls for dismissal of Georgian officials over business ties
World.content:
TI identifies 24 officials heading private companies

Transparency International Georgia (TI) has identified 24 serving public officials who simultaneously hold directorships at 30 private companies, in violation of anti-corruption legislation.

The officials include mayors, deputy mayors, heads of municipal councils and representatives of state agencies.

Georgian law prohibits public officials from simultaneously engaging in business activities. TI says officials whose violations are confirmed must be dismissed.

Under the law, newly appointed officials have 10 days to relinquish their positions as directors of commercial organisations. Failure to comply requires them to leave public service.

According to the list published by Transparency International Georgia, the officials named include:

Merab Bekaia – deputy head of Tbilisi’s Isani district administration and director of private company Hydraulic Service +.

– deputy head of Tbilisi’s Isani district administration and director of private company Hydraulic Service +. Nino Vashakidze – deputy head of Tbilisi City Hall’s Property Management Agency and director of two private companies, Bidara and Il Gudauri.

– deputy head of Tbilisi City Hall’s Property Management Agency and director of two private companies, Bidara and Il Gudauri. Guram Sagaradze – head of the Foreign Ministry’s International Economic Relations Department and director of private company Kospot.

What the law says

Article 13 of Georgia’s Law on Combating Corruption restricts public officials from engaging in business activities and managing private companies. The aim is to separate public and private economic interests and reduce the risk of conflicts of interest.

At the same time, the law allows public officials to own shares in commercial enterprises, which gives them a different legal status from that of a company director.

Transparency International Georgia argues that simultaneously holding public office and managing a private company creates corruption risks. The organisation calls on the government to take action in accordance with the law.

World.title: Light industry lifts Turkmen exchange quotations value
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 2. The total value of external quotations published for the October 23 trading session on SCRMET has increased by 0.4%.

The figure is calculated by Trend based on official data published by SCRMET (The State Commodity and Raw Materials Exchange of Turkmenistan) on its website.

According to the calculations, the total value of external quotations published for the October 23 trading session has increased to $99.97 million from $99.6 million a day earlier.

The growth was driven by the light industry sector, where the total value of external quotations has grown up to $3 million from $2.6 million on the session a day earlier. Trend’s calculations show that the figure has increased by 14.6%.

According to Trend’s calculations, the values in the remaining three categories remained unchanged:

- Petrochemicals - $69.7 million;

- Agriculture - $25.8 million;

- Mechanical engineering - $1.4 million.

As in the previous session, no quotations were registered for the construction materials sector.

The State Commodity and Raw Materials Exchange of Turkmenistan (SCRMET), established in 1994, is the country’s main organized marketplace for trading commodities and one of the key institutions through which Turkmenistan conducts and facilitates foreign trade. The exchange brings together domestic producers, exporters, and foreign buyers through regular trading sessions, where a range of export-oriented goods are offered and transactions are concluded. Its trading portfolio covers petrochemicals, polymers, textiles, cotton products, construction materials, machinery, and chemical goods, among other commodities.

SCRMET also plays an administrative and information role in Turkmenistan’s trade system. In addition to organizing trading sessions and registering export-import contracts, the exchange publishes official quotations based on transactions conducted on the platform. These quotations provide information on the commodities traded, their values, and the markets involved, making SCRMET data a useful indicator of the composition and direction of exchange-based trade.

Through these quotations, SCRMET provides a snapshot of the value and sectoral composition of goods offered to international buyers during each trading session, reflecting shifts in the country’s export offering and highlighting which industries dominate Turkmenistan’s exchange-based trade.

Chronicle of the 37th day of the Second Karabakh War:

- The Ministry of Defense of Azerbaijan has disseminated a video of the destruction of enemy personnel.

World.title: First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva watched "Thikra: Night of Remembering” dance production (PHOTO)
World.content:
Photo: Press Service of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 1. On November 1, the dance production "Thikra: Night of Remembering" was performed at the Azerbaijan State Academic National Drama Theater as part of the Baku International Arts Festival (BIAF-2026).

First Vice-President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Mehriban Aliyeva, along with her family members, watched the performance.

"Thikra: Night of Remembering", the latest work by acclaimed director and choreographer Akram Khan, was commissioned by Wadi AlFann, a global destination for contemporary art based in Al-Ula, Saudi Arabia.

Created in collaboration with award-winning visual artist Manal Al-Dowayan, Akram Khan Company’s final touring production draws on the ancient landscapes, mythology and cultural heritage of Al-Ula.

Through sacred rituals and shared recollections, an all-female ensemble transcend the boundaries of time, bridging past and present to invoke an act of spiritual renewal.

The production features an original score by Indian-American singer and composer Aditya Prakash.

The visual aesthetics of the play were created by "Wadi AlFann" artist Manal Al-Dowayan, renowned for her large-scale multimedia installation featured at the Saudi Arabian pavilion during the 60th Venice Biennale.

In the Thikra project, the artist blends traditional craftsmanship with contemporary forms. Natural dyes mirror the color palette of the desert, while geometric motifs rooted in Al-Ula’s heritage highlight the symbolic role and significance of each character.

The production draws on the ancient landscapes, mythology and cultural heritage of Al-Ula. The site-specific world premiere of the play was presented in January 2025.

World.title: Five people rescued in Kiribati after three months at sea
World.content:
Five people, including two children, have been found alive after drifting an estimated 5,400 kilometres to a remote island in Kiribati, about three months after their boat went missing in Micronesia.

They were part of a group of nine who set off on July 30 on what was meant to be a routine one-hour crossing between the islands of Murilo and Ruo, in the Federated States of Micronesia, when they were caught in a storm.

The US Coast Guard in Micronesia suspended its search on August 9 after 10 days, covering 25,000 nautical miles with the help of US Navy and Air Force aircraft.

On Sunday, villagers on Fanning Island in Kiribati spotted the drifting boat and rescued the five people on board.

The member of parliament for the area, Kaotitaake Rakoroa, said they were taken in and cared for by the pastor of the local Uniting Church.

He said police on Kiritimati Island, the closest urban centre to Fanning Island, relayed news of the rescue to him in the capital, Tarawa.

"The group has already been treated by our medical officials on the island," he said.

Lost fisherman rescued off Kiribati Luka Rahan set off on a fishing trip with his cousin, but experienced issues with the boat's motor and, with no anchor on board, started to drift.

He recommended they take the earliest flight to Kiritimati Island for further medical treatment.

Photos and videos of the five were posted online on Sunday, shortly after they were brought ashore.

The members of the group are yet to speak publicly about their ordeal and have asked for their privacy to be respected. Family members in the Federated States of Micronesia told the ABC they have been in contact with some of the group.

Chuuk State Governor Alexander Narruhn issued a statement on Sunday evening thanking God for their survival.

"There were nine people aboard the boat that went missing. Thanks be to God for his love and mercy that five of the nine people have been found.

"We continue to pray for their four companions."

Details of what happened to the other four people have not been revealed.

The governor said he had asked the Federated States of Micronesia's president to begin diplomatic talks with the Kiribati government to bring the survivors home.

The rescue is the latest of several in Kiribati waters.

Last week, 18-year-old Luka Rahan from Bougainville in Papua New Guinea was rescued between the islands of Tarawa and Maiana after drifting for 41 days. His cousin died during the ordeal.

The pair had set out on a fishing trip in northern Bougainville in September, but had engine trouble and drifted more than 2,000km to Kiribati.

Last month, three other Bougainvilleans returned home after drifting at sea for about 70 days. They were found near Kiritimati Island.

World.title: Indigenous women connect to culture through traditional crafts
World.content:
Wadja Wadja woman Vivianne-Lee Watson was working at her local community's women's shelter when she was asked to attend a weaving workshop.

And the rest — as the saying goes — is history.

"My only aim was to transport the ladies out that day, and one of the facilitators came and asked me, 'Do you want to learn how to weave?'" Ms Watson reflected.

"I had in my head, 'No, I don't have an artistic bone in me.'"

She started with a bracelet and, within 24 hours, she had made a basket.

Vivianne-Lee Watson has created a safe space in her community for yarning and creating. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

That was six-and-a-half years ago, and it quickly became more than a hobby.

Earlier this year, Ms Watson resigned from her stable full-time job to take her side hustle further.

"I found that it [my job] wasn't filling my cup as much as I thought it would, which is why I chose to resign … [and] step into my business full time," she said.

"I'm just shocked by the many doors that have opened for me."

Vivianne-Lee Watson showing others how to use the needle and raffia for weaving. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

Over the past few months, she has held workshops, which are free for anyone to join, in her hometown of Woorabinda, an Indigenous community 170 kilometres south-west of Rockhampton in central Queensland.

"It's been very rewarding for myself, but also for the women, seeing the ladies come out … having my elders here and teaching them something, when they've been the one that has been teaching me," she said.

It's also created a safe space for locals.

"It's a good time out for us ladies to be together, a good yarning circle," Woorabinda resident and Mayi-Yapi woman Annie Asse said.

"If someone doesn't want to do something, they can simply just sit here and have a yarn.

"We don't judge nobody, we're all here for each other, and it's good for our mindset."

For Bwgcolman woman Veronica Johnson, who is from Palm Island and moved to Woorabinda this year, it has been a way to make friends.

Bwgcolman woman Veronica Johnson was new to Woorabinda and came along to the workshops as a way to make friends. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

"It's brought me out of my shell … it's very lovely," she said.

"It's given me that inspiration, consideration with the women, how to connect within ourselves."

Sharing crafts, traditions and culture is an important part of ensuring ancient Indigenous ways don't get lost in a modern society.

"It keeps people grounded for who they are, where they come from, why they matter in life, basically," Woorabinda resident and Wadja Wadja woman Patricia Rankin said.

"We want them all here just to learn something, and any little problems they may have, they might connect with someone."

The attendees at the workshop do all sorts of crafts from beading, making jewellery, painting, weaving and other crafts. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

Indigenous weaving practices date back tens of thousands of years, with ancestors crafting baskets, dilly bags, nets and fish traps from natural resources like reeds, bark and plants.

"Something I'm very passionate about is to help people reconnect to their roots, because that was something that I struggled with for so long, wanting to know who I was and where I came from," Ms Watson said.

It has been a way for her to connect with her family heritage, not just the Woorabinda Wadja Wadja mob she grew up around, but the Mayi-Yapi in the Gulf country.

"I'm not just an Aboriginal woman, but I'm a Torres Strait Islander woman too, and weaving is a part of that side of my family as well," Ms Watson said.

Vivianne-Lee Watson's daughter Kaeleigh Watson-Brown making a pair of earrings. (Supplied: Vivianne-Lee Watson)

Kaeleigh with Eden, who bought her earrings. (Supplied: Vivianne-Lee Watson)

While she has taught people of all ages, being able to pass her skills onto her two daughters, aged seven and 10, has been extra special.

Her eldest was recently commissioned by a local health service worker to weave a pair of earrings.

"The smile that she had on her face … and she got paid for it, so she thought that she was deadly with it," Ms Watson said.

World.title: Serial rapist to be released despite 'high risk' to WA community
World.content:
A high-risk sexual offender who has spent most of his life behind bars for raping multiple women and a five-year-old girl in Western Australia's far north is set to be released from prison.

Warning: This story contains details of sexual assault.

Adrian Pindan was convicted of five sexual offences from 1989 to 2007 and received a 10-year prison sentence in 1997 for the rape of a five-year-old girl.

In 2012, a WA Justice imposed an indefinite detention order on Pindan, who is now aged 59 and has been in custody since 2007.

However, last week a Supreme Court Justice agreed to Pindan's release, despite accepting he remains a high-risk serious offender.

Adrian Pindan attacked women across Derby (pictured), Broome and Fitzroy Crossing in WA's Kimberley. (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

Justice Bruno Fiannaca said the risk to the community could be mitigated by suitable accommodation, "significant" NDIS funding and 24-hour supervision, in his judgment handed down on October 23.

The 52 conditions of his release include electronic monitoring, a curfew, avoiding contact with female community members, and not consuming alcohol.

Justice Fiannaca granted a suppression order to prevent the publication of the suburb of Pindan's future accommodation to avoid community members targeting him.

A WA Supreme Court Justice last week decided the high-risk sex offender would be released under strict supervision. (ABC News: Jack Stevenson)

'Indiscriminate' offending

Pindan's ongoing detention order has been reviewed and subsequently extended six previous times between 2014 and 2021.

The court heard his offending occurred in the Kimberley towns of Fitzroy Crossing, Derby and Broome over an 18-year period.

Pindan raped three women and the five-year-old child, with the offences being labelled as "indiscriminate".

He also broke into an elderly woman's home in Broome in 1988 and tried to assault her while she was in bed with her husband.

The court heard that while in prison, Pindan displayed "predatory" behaviour towards female staff, but Justice Fiannaca accepted this behaviour had reduced in recent years.

Pindan was transferred from the West Kimberley Regional Prison to Perth's Acacia Prison in August 2023 after being assaulted by a fellow inmate, after allegedly saying "he was going to rape someone".

Cognitive impairment and lack of services

Pindan has a cognitive impairment, preventing his participation in any rehabilitation program or taking any step to address the causes of his offending.

When issuing the ongoing detention order in 2012, Justice Lindy Jenkins said "determined efforts" needed to be made to avoid him spending the rest of his life in prison.

However, when granting Pindan's release, Justice Fiannaca said these conditions were now in place.

"I am satisfied the respondent's circumstances have changed, both in terms of some changes in his behaviour and in the measures now available to manage his risk in the community," he said.

Pindan is set to be released into the community on December 2, with a supervision order put in place for seven years.

World.title: Irish 1,500m champion remembered as inspiration after death at 34
World.content:
Ciara Mageean, who won gold in the 1,500 metres at the 2024 European championships, has died. She was 34.

A statement posted on her Instagram page said she died of cancer on Sunday morning.

"At 6:30am this morning, Ciara lost her battle with cancer surrounded by her loved ones," the statement read.

"A beloved daughter, sister, wife, friend and inspiration to so many, she will be deeply missed."

Mageean won European gold in Rome two years ago, having clinched silver in the 1,500m in Munich in 2022.

She placed fourth at the 2023 world championships and represented Ireland in two Olympics.

"Athletics Ireland is deeply saddened to learn of the passing of Ciara Mageean," a statement from Athletics Ireland read.

"Ciara was a much-loved and inspirational figure who touched the lives of so many. Her courage, warmth and spirit will leave a lasting legacy."

World Athletics said it was "deeply saddened" by the news, calling her "an inspiration to many, on and off the track".

Australian middle-distance runner Jessica Hull also posted a tribute.

"There are no words. Just the most beautiful person in every way imaginable," she wrote on Instagram.

"Lucky to have shared some miles with you but even more special to have celebrated milestones at the finish line together, I'm so grateful for every moment, rest easy Ciara."

World Athletics president Sebastian Coe joined those paying tribute.

"It is with great sadness that we learned of Ciara's passing this morning at such a young age," Coe said.

"A European champion and inspiration to many, it is a sad day for our sport — her loss will be felt across the athletics community."

AP

World.title: Matt Canavan enters Capricornia race to set up One Nation showdown
World.content:
Nationals leader Matt Canavan has said he wants to run for the seat of Capricornia at the next election, potentially setting up a high-profile showdown with One Nation.

The senator confirmed today he will seek pre-selection for the Central Queensland seat that will be vacated by outgoing Nationals' chief whip Michelle Landry.

Senator Canavan's bid for the lower house was widely anticipated after the ABC revealed last week Ms Landry's intention to retire ahead of the next election, expected in 2028.

James Ashby, One Nation's party director and close political ally to Pauline Hanson as her former chief of staff, is also publicly considering putting his hat in the ring.

"There's going to be a real fight on for the next election," Senator Canavan told ABC Radio Capricornia today.

Senator Canavan said he needed to "step up" and take a risk by running for the House of Representatives during a "volatile" climate.

"It falls to me," he said after Ms Landry's resignation, adding he "desperately wanted" a change of government.

"I'm happy to sacrifice potentially my own political future to do that," he said.

"I want to be on the front lines with my troops as well. I'm the leader of the Nationals.

"I just have to be there in the trenches with them."

James Ashby is weighing up a possible run in the Central Queensland seat. (ABC News: Jacob Kagi)

Senator Hanson has said she will not run in Capricornia, and when asked about Mr Ashby's intentions, she said she wouldn't make any decisions this far out from the election.

Nationals deputy Bridget McKenzie was asked on ABC Radio National Breakfast if the move was a risk for her Senate colleague.

"In this current political environment there is always a risk running for lower house seats," she said.

"I think Matt's got a great proposition. He has delivered for that community alongside Michelle Landry for a long period of time."

She said One Nation "has made a big song and dance … of wanting to get the PM out of the lodge" and she urged the party to target Labor seats instead of Coalition-held electorates.

Decision months in the making

Senator Canavan, who lives in Yeppoon in the electorate, became leader of the Nationals in March this year, replacing David Littleproud, who stepped down.

He currently holds the number two spot on the Liberal National Party of Queensland (LNP) Senate ticket, behind Liberal James McGrath.

A successful move from the Senate to the lower house would shore up the likelihood of Senator Canavan becoming deputy prime minister in a Coalition government, and assure those in the Nationals who hold the view that their leader should sit in the House of Representatives with the other major party leaders.

Senator Canavan said he had been mulling the decision for a while after Ms Landry approached him a few months ago to signal she was considering leaving politics.

He stressed he was nominating for preselection in the seat and was not yet the candidate.

"We're a grassroots party, and whether I'm leader or whatever, I've got to go and present before the Capricornia branch of the LNP and seek their support," he said.

He said the next election would be a "referendum on Net Zero" and that government needed to "unleash our nation's energy resources again", including coal, oil, gas and uranium.

"We should be building nuclear power stations," he said.

"The way to get cost of living down is to do everything, to build everything, to increase the supply of electricity."

Last year, the Nationals went ahead of their Coalition partners in abandoning their commitment to reach net zero emissions by 2050, with the Liberals under then-leader Sussan Ley following.

World.title: Australia's first Indigenous-owned water testing lab opens in regional Qld
World.content:
Australia's first Indigenous-owned water testing lab has opened, empowering more traditional owners to work on sea country and land management.

Nyamgim Gung means "looking at water" in the Gurang language and is the namesake of the new laboratory that sits next to the Burnett River at the Bundaberg Port, 400 kilometres north of Brisbane.

Nyamgim Gung means "looking at water" in the region's Gurang language. (ABC Wide Bay: Nikki Sorbello)

The lab was built by the Gidarjil Development Corporation overseeing projects in Gladstone and Bundaberg on behalf of traditional owner groups Bailai, Gurang, Gooreng Gooreng and Taribelang Bunda.

Environmental scientist and lab manager Nirali Vadgama has been working to establish the lab since 2022, achieving national and international accreditation through the National Association of Testing Authorities in September.

Environmental scientist and lab manager Nirali Vadgama says the lab shows science can thrive in regional areas. (ABC Wide Bay: Nikki Sorbello)

"That means science can thrive right here in regional areas," Ms Vadgama said.

Built with sophisticated technology and automation, Ms Vadgama said they were able to test a wide range of parameters including nutrients, trace elements, hardness and alkalinity.

"We are specialised in seawater, but we are not just limited to that. We can also do all kinds of water, that is river water, fresh water, brackish water," she said.

The lab will test water samples collected by Gidarjil's Indigenous rangers, that help them manage water quality, and provide another income stream for the not-for-profit by offering water testing services to other organisations.

Building self-determination

Gidarjil CEO Margaret Blackman described the decision to set up the testing laboratory as "out of the box" thinking.

"We want to empower other Aboriginal organisations up and down the coast to manage their country, to manage their sea country and to build self-determination for their people.

"And that's the vision of what Gidarjil was set up for, to empower our local traditional owners, but not only that, help other traditional owner groups learn how to manage their sea country and work towards establishing something like this."

Margaret Blackman hopes the lab will empower other Aboriginal organisations to learn how to manager their country. (ABC Wide Bay: Nikki Sorbello)

Previously, water samples collected on country were sent to Brisbane for analysis.

Nyamgim Gung will test the group's own water samples, as well as testing for other organisations. (ABC Wide Bay: Nikki Sorbello)

Ms Blackman said having the regional lab meant faster answers for its own water quality projects and greater independence and scientific authority in caring for its waterways.

"It means our people can test our own water, on our own country, to a standard the whole world recognises," she said.

Ms Blackman said they were working with on-site training organisation Yalga Binbi Institute to teach young Indigenous leaders about on-country management.

"Then hopefully they might go on to be a scientist and then they can run this lab, then it'll be an all-Indigenous-powered water lab," she said.

Biara Baron Wellington, Kelly Simpson, Tabitha Simpson and Shontelle Simpson are part of Gidarjil's first female-only ranger group. (ABC Wide Bay: Nikki Sorbello)

In conjunction with the lab's accreditation, the organisation launched its first all-female ranger program Dulba Muni, meaning "strong women" in Gurang language.

Biara Baron Wellington has been helping in the water lab, logging data and collecting and preparing samples.

"It's really cool to be part of it from the start, collecting the water at the sites and then actually being able to see the data and see the health of the water and actually get to know the results firsthand," Ms Wellington said.

"It's a very culturally significant thing to do. It's what our ancestors have been doing for tens of thousands of years, so for us to carry that on and care for country to this day is really special."

World.title: Matildas star continues remarkable WSL goalscoring run in huge win
World.content:
Ellie Carpenter continues to thrive in her new, more attacking role at Chelsea, scoring her fifth goal of the season as the Blues powered to a 6-0 win at Charlton to stay top of the Women's Super League table.

But champions Manchester City remain level on points with Chelsea after Carpenter's fellow Australian international Mary Fowler delivered the crucial assist to eke out a late 2-1 win at London City Lionesses on Sunday (Monday AEDT).

Carpenter is still nominally a full-back, but her ever-increasing influence higher up the park has turned her into a regular goalscoring threat from right wing-back as coach Sonia Bompastor adopts more attacking tactics.

With Chelsea already two up after 10 minutes at The Valley through Nathalie Bjorn and Melvine Malard, Australian football's player of the year Carpenter popped up in the box just three minutes later to slot home the rebound after a Lauren James pot shot was parried into her path by Charlton keeper Anna Koivunen.

Finishing decisively, Carpenter could celebrate her fifth goal in 13 games in all competitions this season, including four in the league, compared with the three she amassed in all 29 games last season.

With Chelsea dominating and Malard scoring her second before the break, Charlton took off its experienced Matilda Emily Van Egmond at the break in a tactical bid to halt the slaughter.

It worked, partially, in that the Blues scored only twice more through Aggie Beever-Jones and Giulia Dragoni, but were frustrated not to double their tally despite their dominance.

At London City's humble Bromley ground, the Ballon d'Or trophy won in midweek by Spanish superstar Alexia Putellas was on view, and the celebratory mood continued when home striker Jana Fernandez equalised in the 72nd minute following Khadija Shaw's league-leading ninth goal of the season for City.

But Fowler, who made an impact during the half-hour she spent on the pitch after coming off the subs' bench, quickly made a decisive intervention a couple of minutes after the equaliser, putting in a pinpoint cross from the right that Lauren Hemp headed home.

The win left unbeaten City on 22 points, only behind Chelsea on goal difference, with the Lionesses third on 16.

Kyra Cooney-Cross and her teammates were frustrated as Arsenal drew with Aston Villa. (Alex Burstow/Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

Arsenal's troubles continued, though, with its three Matildas Caitlin Foord, Kyra Cooney-Cross and Steph Catley all starting in a frustrating 1-1 draw at home to Aston Villa.

Only an 85th-minute equaliser from Alessia Russo prevented another embarrassing defeat after Chasity Grant had put Villa ahead against the run of play in the 25th minute.

Remarkably, Arsenal chalked up 28 attempts on goal — including a combined seven from the Australian trio — compared to Villa's lone successful effort.

Tottenham Hotspur thumped Birmingham City 4-1 away to move up to fourth while West Ham United beat Liverpool with the same scoreline.

AAP

World.title: Nine die as business jet crashes on Florida roadside
World.content:
US officials say a small private jet has crashed into a southern Florida neighbourhood killing all nine people aboard.

The Learjet 60 erupted into a giant fireball when it crashed near a busy road at 12:50pm on Sunday, local time.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement on X: "Today's plane crash in Palm Beach County, is a horrific tragedy."

The crash left a flaming crater in the ground. (Supplied: Eduin Cruz/via Reuters)

The aircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was heading to the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.

Authorities did not immediately say what caused the crash or who was on board.

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said the crash left a crater in the ground.

There were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground injured or killed, he said.

"It was a cataclysmic plane crash," Mr DeSantis told reporters at the scene.

"It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road."

The plane was heading east at 35,000 feet (about 11 kilometres) when pilots reported turbulence, icing and precipitation and requested to climb 2,000 feet (about 610 metres).

Moments later, the plane entered a steep dive, first 10,000 feet per minute, then 20,000 feet per minute and up to 30,000 feet per minute, speeding the plane beyond its design limits, according to air traffic control recordings and flight tracking data.

A pilot declared an emergency and issued distress calls. The plane banked sharply to the right before it crashed steeply into the ground.

Minutes before the crash, the pilot reported ice accumulating on the jet and turbulence that was jolting it by as much as 700 feet, according to air traffic control recordings captured by LiveATC.net.

"We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence," the pilot told controllers.

But the situation rapidly deteriorated.

After encountering precipitation and requesting to climb, the pilot declared an emergency as the aircraft began losing altitude at an alarming rate.

The circumstances of the crash remain under investigation. (AP: Mark Elias)

"We're descending 8,000 — mayday, mayday — we're descending 10,000 feet per minute," the pilot radioed.

"We are in an over-speed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute," the pilot radioed.

"We're going to crash into the ground."

Video from cars captured the moment the aircraft plunged from the sky before striking near the road and exploding.

Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site.

Palm Beach County authorities are evacuating about 600 people from a nearby mobile home community while federal officials investigate the crash.

One Nation’s party director James Ashby, Hanson’s closest and most influential aide, is based within the electorate in the coastal town of Yeppoon.

World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX slides lower, banks jump Stan Choe Updated November 2, 2026 — 10:31am ,first published 5:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The Australian sharemarket has started the week in negative territory but financial stocks are stronger ahead of the Reserve Bank’s interest rates call on Tuesday. The S&P/ASX 200 was down 12.2 points, or 0.1 per cent, to 8895.9 in early trade. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.29¢. Westpac said it expects interest rates to remain “elevated” into 2027 and house prices to have fallen by nearly 11 per cent by March as it reported a $6.8 billion full-year profit. Westpac’s profit in the year to September was down 1 per cent from the previous year. The bank’s net interest margin – a key measure of profitability – fell by 3 percentage points to 1.86 per cent for the second half of 2026 as lending competition remained strong and more customer accounts qualified for savings bonus rates. Its shares are up 1 per cent in early trade while its big four peers are also stronger, with Commonwealth Bank rising 1.1 per cent, National Australia Bank up 0.8 per cent and ANZ 0.8 per cent higher. On Friday, a selloff for tech stocks got even worse on worries that Wall Street’s frenzy around artificial-intelligence technology sent prices too high. The S&P 500 tumbled 1.8 per cent for its worst day since June, and it closed out a third straight losing week. The weakness for technology stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 2.9 per cent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 572 points, or 1.1 per cent.



Wall Street suffered more weakness in AI stocks on Friday. AP The US stock market remains only 3.1 per cent below its all-time high, which has boosted the value of workers’ retirement accounts, but it’s become increasingly shaky as Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States approach. Worries about AI in general have already become a concern for voters across political parties, and President Donald Trump has historically used the stock market’s performance as a measure of his own success. Intel’s stock led the way lower and plunged 28.6 per cent for its worst drop since 1974. The chipmaker gave a forecast for profit in the final three months of this year that fell short of analysts’ expectations, as CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the personal-computer industry continues to feel pressure. The drop came even though Intel reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Related Article Analysis

Bonds The $315b debt binge that’s driving up the cost of borrowing Amazon fell 1.4 per cent after reporting a weaker profit for the summer than analysts expected. Potentially more concerning for investors was Amazon’s reporting that it burned through $US42.4 billion ($60.3 billion) of cash over the prior 12 months, according to a measure called free cash flow. It spent $US94.8 billion on property and equipment, primarily through investments in artificial-intelligence technology.



A day earlier, Alphabet’s stock dropped more than 12 per cent to its worst day on record and dragged the S&P 500 down after telling investors it burned through more cash during the summer than the spring. The company behind Google and YouTube cited similar, mammoth investments in AI. Worries are rising about whether all the hundreds of billions of dollars will produce enough profit and productivity to make the investment worth it. At the same time, stocks of computer chip companies and other winners from the frenzy to build AI data centres have come under pressure on concerns that high interest rates may slow the further build out of data centres. “We’re moving out of the hopes and dreams phase of the AI trade and into the ‘show me’ phase,” said Joe Tigay, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, in a note to investors. A drop of 4.2 per cent for Nvidia, the chip company that became the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward, outweighing even Intel. In the cryptocurrency industry, meanwhile, stocks tumbled following a hack on the world’s biggest crypto exchange. The price of bitcoin fell below $US77,000 from more than $US86,000 earlier this month, and a US-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean unit was likely behind the attack that impacted more than $US6 billion worth of crypto at Binance.



Coinbase Global fell 10.6 per cent even though it reported stronger results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Strategy, which says it owns about 4 per cent of the total supply of bitcoin, fell 7.8 per cent. It also reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, while saying its chief financial officer will resign next week for personal reasons. Binance customers pulled $US3.64 billion, or 2.1 per cent of its assets, as the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange went back online on Sunday after the hack. Binance said withdrawals were stabilising after an initial spike and deposit volumes had remained “substantial”. The exchange said it had now covered 95 per cent of the $US6.3 billion of stolen assets. Outside of tech, stocks were more resilient as many rallied after reporting stronger profits for the summer than analysts expected. Nearly as many stocks rose within the S&P 500 index as fell. ExxonMobil climbed 2.2 per cent, and Chevron added 1.8 per cent after the oil giants reported stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected. Mondelez International rose 3.9 per cent after the company behind Oreo cookies and Ritz crackers reported stronger-than-expected growth.



Colgate-Palmolive climbed 2.3 per cent after higher prices for its products around much of the world helped it deliver better revenue and profit than analysts expected. Expectations are high for US companies’ ability to make bigger profits, even though people around the world are feeling discouraged about high inflation and high fuel prices. Such expectations are what drove the S&P 500 to its record earlier this month. All told, the S&P 500 fell 140.32 points to 7,580.07. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 572.25 to 51,770.31, and the Nasdaq composite sank 747.73 to 25,437.00. In the bond market, Treasury yields eased in a signal that investors were buying US government bonds in search of something safer to own. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93 per cent from 4.98 per cent late Thursday and from more than 5.30 per cent earlier in the month. Related Article Superannuation Super funds slammed for ‘blaming customers for complaints’



Treasury yields fell even though oil prices bounced higher, something that usually drives yields upward because it worsens inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.4 per cent to $US113.43. It’s near the high end of its range since the war with Iran sent oil prices and inflation higher. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe following sharper swings in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi dropped 3.5 per cent as worries about AI hit its tech-heavy market, while the Hang Seng in Hong Kong climbed 1.5 per cent. Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 2.1 per cent after the Bank of Japan decided to keep interest rates steady, echoing moves made earlier in the week by the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank. Nearly all appointments for the first month of the gun buyback scheme in NSW have been filled by 340 gun owners, with over 2400 firearms expected to be handed over, police in the state say.

Speaking as the buyback begins today, NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon asked for patience as the number of participating police stations increases over the coming months.

NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon (left) and Police Minister Yasmin Catley (right) Audrey Richardson

“I want to make sure that this operates smoothly and safely, so we want to scale it up, make sure that those consumers that are actually surrendering their firearms have a good experience,” Lanyon said.

Lanyon said police would continue to target criminals with illegal firearms, but said there was “no doubt” that reducing the number of guns generally in the community would improve safety.

Police Minister Yasmin Catley said the scheme would reduce the number of firearms able to be stolen and used for violent crime.

World.title: Martha Stewart responds to Halloween costume uproar after dressing as homeless person
World.content:
CultureCelebrityCelebrity life Martha Stewart responds to Halloween costume uproar after dressing as homeless person Chris Hook November 2, 2026 — 10:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Lifestyle mogul and TV presenter Martha Stewart has responded to the furore after an image of her dressed as a homeless person for Halloween was posted to her Instagram account, then quickly deleted. The image showed Stewart with a smudged face, dressed in ripped jeans and a ragged cardigan, holding a sign with the message, “I am hungry help me!!” and was among several images in a carousel promoting her range of candles, sold via US shopping network QVC. Martha Stewart has addressed criticism of her Halloween costume. Instagram “My QVC candles are perfect for Halloween!!!” the images were captioned. The image of her costume was screenshotted by social media users and widely circulated, prompting a backlash, to which she responded early Monday morning (AEDT).



Related Article Homelessness Homelessness crisis hits breaking point as services turn away desperate Australians However, in her statement to the New York Post’s Page Six column, the 85-year-old stopped short of apologising. “I am distressed that my Halloween costume yesterday, which was intended to bring more awareness to the very serious subject of homelessness, has offended people, which was never my intention,” she said in the statement on Monday morning (AEDT). “Homelessness continues to remain one of America’s greatest challenges and ongoing crises, something that I care deeply about and I have spent a significant amount of time and effort supporting charities that combat this ongoing social epidemic. I am committed to continuing to make a difference,” she said. Stewart has amassed a reported $570 million fortune through her lifestyle and homewares empire.



Celebs embrace Halloween spirit Also getting buzz for her Halloween costume was supermodel Heidi Klum, who dressed as a giant severed hand for her annual Halloween party in New York on Saturday (US time), 25 years after she began hosting the much-anticipated event. Heidi Klum dressed as her own severed hand. getty Klum was unrecognisable, with only her eyes and mouth showing, blood dripping from her mouth as she stuck her tongue out. The top of the hand ended in a gory assortment of dangling ligaments and tendons. She had an ensemble of helpers in blood-stained hazmat suits. The idea came to her last year to be a giant hand — specifically her own left hand, with long red nails, a thumb ring, and her engagement ring and wedding band.



“I looked at my hand and I thought, ‘Hey, I think I could fit my body in this somehow,’” Klum said. It’s not the first time she has gone viral with a wild Halloween costume. Neil Patrick Harris and husband David Burtka arrive at the party. AP Photo/Evan Agostini The supermodel-turned-TV personality went viral in 2022 when she arrived at the party on the end of a fishing line, encased in a slithering worm costume. In past years, Klum has come dressed as the Greek myth Medusa, a peacock, a 2.4-metre-tall Transformer, a werewolf from Michael Jackson’s Thriller music video, a clone accompanied by several Klum lookalikes, and Kali, the multi-armed Hindu goddess of death and destruction.



Jade Thirlwall as an angel statue. AP Photo/Evan Agostini Klum said it took about five to six hours to get into her hand costume this year, but making it took a lot longer. She posted hints on her Instagram earlier in the day as bloodied prosthetics were applied to her face. “Hands down, the hardest thing is carrying it,” Klum said. “It’s quite heavy.” Her husband, musician Tom Kaulitz, did not attend this year because he was on tour. But the details on her costume include a tattoo of his name on her ring finger, along with her palm lines and veins. “A little bit of Tom is with me,” she said.



Her guests also made a splash with their costumes. Neil Patrick Harris and husband David Burtka arrived as ghoulish twins from The Shining, while UK singer Jade Thirwall seemed to have dressed as an angel statue that had clearly seen better times. with AP Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. Westpac expects interest rates to remain “elevated” into 2027 and house prices to fall by nearly 11 per cent by March as it reported a $6.8 billion profit. On Monday, the country’s oldest bank said the Australian economy was holding up “relatively well” on the back of strong business investment, but that price growth remained above the Reserve Bank’s target. Westpac has posted a $6.8 billion profit. Eamon Gallagher “This is presenting challenges for many households and businesses, although impacts are uneven across the economy,” it said in an announcement to the ASX ahead of the next Reserve Bank interest rate decision on Tuesday where the RBA is widely tipped to raise interest rates for the fifth time this year. Westpac also said it expected house prices to fall by 10.9 per cent from March 2026 to March 2027. In September, house prices nationally were 5.2 per cent below the peak reached in March.



Westpac’s $6.8 billion profit in the year to September was down 1 per cent from the previous year. The bank’s net interest margin – a key measure of profitability – fell by 3 percentage points to 1.86 per cent for the second half of 2026 as lending competition remained strong and more customer accounts qualified for savings bonus rates. This was partly offset by stronger business and institutional lending, which grew 12 per ent and 18 per cent, respectively. Despite cost of living pressures, the bank said the share of mortgage balances in hardship “remained low” at 0.6 per cent. Westpac provided more than 42,000 tailored financial hardship assistance and disaster relief packages over the year, but said more than 60 per cent of assisted customers required less than three months of hardship support. The bank said credit quality metrics “continue to reflect customer resilience” despite cost of living pressures and higher interest rates.



The share of accounts held by customers ahead on their mortgage repayments – including offset account balances – remained steady at 86 per cent. Nearly four in ten customers are more than two years ahead on their repayments, about one in ten are on-time and only 1 per cent are behind on their repayments. However, Westpac’s credit impairment provisions – money set aside for potential losses when borrowers fail to repay loans – increased to $5.2 billion with the bank citing “economic and geopolitical uncertainty” affecting energy-intensive sectors and discretionary spending. The bank will pay a final dividend of 77 cents a share, taking the full-year dividend to $1.54, up 1 per cent from the previous year. World.title: Democrats turn on each other in Michigan ahead of midterm elections
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaUS midterms Democrats turn on each other in Michigan ahead of midterm elections Joey Cappeleti , Corey Williams and Mike Householder November 2, 2026 — 10:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Detroit — Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the US Senate primary, Haley Stevens, has stunned party officials by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers as Democratic tensions boiled over days before the election that could determine the balance of power on Capitol Hill. Stevens endorsed Rogers after attending a Detroit church service with him. The remarkable show of support for the President Donald Trump-backed candidate in the tightly contested race comes after she was uninvited to a joint event the same day with El-Sayed, who defeated the congresswoman by a slim margin in the August primary. Haley Stevens speaks alongside Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers. AP “Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away,” Stevens said in a video announcing the endorsement, which led her top aide to quit. “And he’s right. And that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today.” El-Sayed dismissed the endorsement when asked about it by reporters later on Sunday, saying he’s focused on issues voters care about, such as the high cost of living.



“At the end of the day I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” he said, adding later: “None of this matters.” Michigan Democratic leaders were left shocked. With just less than 48 hours to go before Election Day, a party that had spent months trying to unite behind its Senate nominee was suddenly grappling with an extraordinary defection in one of this year’s most important races. Democratic nominee for the Senate Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters during a campaign rally in Detroit, Michigan. AP Tensions between the two Democrats have festered since the primary. Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed is a fierce critic of the US ally. He has also been criticised by some in the community for past remarks regarding a Michigan synagogue attack and for appearances with controversial streamer Hasan Piker. El-Sayed, a former Michigan public health official, is facing Rogers, an ex-congressman, for the seat held by the retiring Democrat, Gary Peters. Keeping Michigan in Democratic hands is vital to the party’s effort to win a majority for the final two years of Trump’s second term.



Stevens and El-Sayed were originally scheduled to attend church together, along with other Michigan and national Democrats, including South Carolina representative Jim Clyburn. Democrats hoped it would be a show of unity as they worked to boost turnout in the Detroit area, where concerns have lingered about enthusiasm among Black and Jewish voters in key Democratic strongholds. Haley Stevens, a Democrat from Michigan Bloomberg Related Article US midterms Trump revives final midterm rallies after erupting over idea he was ‘sick’ Instead, Stevens swayed to gospel music alongside Rogers in the pews at Perfecting Church, while El-Sayed was a few miles away at a different house of worship campaigning alongside prominent Democrats, including Clyburn. The Associated Press attended both services as the dramatic split-screen unfolded. After the church service north of Detroit, where Stevens and her fiancé Jason Turkish worshipped with Rogers and his wife, Kristi, the congresswoman told reporters, “I’m not turning my back on Democrats. It is this one vote.”

A source with knowledge of internal decisions told this masthead Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is eager for Mawson to run once again, but she is yet to reveal her intention for the next election. World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX slides lower, banks jump Stan Choe Updated November 2, 2026 — 10:31am ,first published 5:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
