The Australian sharemarket has started the week in negative territory but financial stocks are stronger ahead of the Reserve Bank’s interest rates call on Tuesday. The S&P/ASX 200 was down 12.2 points, or 0.1 per cent, to 8895.9 in early trade. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.29¢. Westpac said it expects interest rates to remain “elevated” into 2027 and house prices to have fallen by nearly 11 per cent by March as it reported a $6.8 billion full-year profit. Westpac’s profit in the year to September was down 1 per cent from the previous year. The bank’s net interest margin – a key measure of profitability – fell by 3 percentage points to 1.86 per cent for the second half of 2026 as lending competition remained strong and more customer accounts qualified for savings bonus rates. Its shares are up 1 per cent in early trade while its big four peers are also stronger, with Commonwealth Bank rising 1.1 per cent, National Australia Bank up 0.8 per cent and ANZ 0.8 per cent higher. On Friday, a selloff for tech stocks got even worse on worries that Wall Street’s frenzy around artificial-intelligence technology sent prices too high. The S&P 500 tumbled 1.8 per cent for its worst day since June, and it closed out a third straight losing week. The weakness for technology stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 2.9 per cent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 572 points, or 1.1 per cent.



Wall Street suffered more weakness in AI stocks on Friday. AP The US stock market remains only 3.1 per cent below its all-time high, which has boosted the value of workers’ retirement accounts, but it’s become increasingly shaky as Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States approach. Worries about AI in general have already become a concern for voters across political parties, and President Donald Trump has historically used the stock market’s performance as a measure of his own success. Intel’s stock led the way lower and plunged 28.6 per cent for its worst drop since 1974. The chipmaker gave a forecast for profit in the final three months of this year that fell short of analysts’ expectations, as CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the personal-computer industry continues to feel pressure. The drop came even though Intel reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Related Article Analysis

Bonds The $315b debt binge that’s driving up the cost of borrowing Amazon fell 1.4 per cent after reporting a weaker profit for the summer than analysts expected. Potentially more concerning for investors was Amazon’s reporting that it burned through $US42.4 billion ($60.3 billion) of cash over the prior 12 months, according to a measure called free cash flow. It spent $US94.8 billion on property and equipment, primarily through investments in artificial-intelligence technology.



A day earlier, Alphabet’s stock dropped more than 12 per cent to its worst day on record and dragged the S&P 500 down after telling investors it burned through more cash during the summer than the spring. The company behind Google and YouTube cited similar, mammoth investments in AI. Worries are rising about whether all the hundreds of billions of dollars will produce enough profit and productivity to make the investment worth it. At the same time, stocks of computer chip companies and other winners from the frenzy to build AI data centres have come under pressure on concerns that high interest rates may slow the further build out of data centres. “We’re moving out of the hopes and dreams phase of the AI trade and into the ‘show me’ phase,” said Joe Tigay, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, in a note to investors. A drop of 4.2 per cent for Nvidia, the chip company that became the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward, outweighing even Intel. In the cryptocurrency industry, meanwhile, stocks tumbled following a hack on the world’s biggest crypto exchange. The price of bitcoin fell below $US77,000 from more than $US86,000 earlier this month, and a US-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean unit was likely behind the attack that impacted more than $US6 billion worth of crypto at Binance.



Coinbase Global fell 10.6 per cent even though it reported stronger results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Strategy, which says it owns about 4 per cent of the total supply of bitcoin, fell 7.8 per cent. It also reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, while saying its chief financial officer will resign next week for personal reasons. Binance customers pulled $US3.64 billion, or 2.1 per cent of its assets, as the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange went back online on Sunday after the hack. Binance said withdrawals were stabilising after an initial spike and deposit volumes had remained “substantial”. The exchange said it had now covered 95 per cent of the $US6.3 billion of stolen assets. Outside of tech, stocks were more resilient as many rallied after reporting stronger profits for the summer than analysts expected. Nearly as many stocks rose within the S&P 500 index as fell. ExxonMobil climbed 2.2 per cent, and Chevron added 1.8 per cent after the oil giants reported stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected. Mondelez International rose 3.9 per cent after the company behind Oreo cookies and Ritz crackers reported stronger-than-expected growth.



Colgate-Palmolive climbed 2.3 per cent after higher prices for its products around much of the world helped it deliver better revenue and profit than analysts expected. Expectations are high for US companies’ ability to make bigger profits, even though people around the world are feeling discouraged about high inflation and high fuel prices. Such expectations are what drove the S&P 500 to its record earlier this month. All told, the S&P 500 fell 140.32 points to 7,580.07. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 572.25 to 51,770.31, and the Nasdaq composite sank 747.73 to 25,437.00. In the bond market, Treasury yields eased in a signal that investors were buying US government bonds in search of something safer to own. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93 per cent from 4.98 per cent late Thursday and from more than 5.30 per cent earlier in the month. Related Article Superannuation Super funds slammed for ‘blaming customers for complaints’



Treasury yields fell even though oil prices bounced higher, something that usually drives yields upward because it worsens inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.4 per cent to $US113.43. It’s near the high end of its range since the war with Iran sent oil prices and inflation higher. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe following sharper swings in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi dropped 3.5 per cent as worries about AI hit its tech-heavy market, while the Hang Seng in Hong Kong climbed 1.5 per cent. Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 2.1 per cent after the Bank of Japan decided to keep interest rates steady, echoing moves made earlier in the week by the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

KPMG Australia is preparing to axe hundreds more staff within weeks as the fallout from its whistleblower scandal, and government work ban, continues to hit its business.

More KPMG employees will pay the price as the whistleblower scandal hits its business. Thomas Wielecki

Nearly all appointments for the first month of the gun buyback scheme in NSW have been filled by 340 gun owners, with over 2400 firearms expected to be handed over, police in the state say.

Speaking as the buyback begins today, NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon asked for patience as the number of participating police stations increases over the coming months.

NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon (left) and Police Minister Yasmin Catley (right) Audrey Richardson

“I want to make sure that this operates smoothly and safely, so we want to scale it up, make sure that those consumers that are actually surrendering their firearms have a good experience,” Lanyon said.

Lanyon said police would continue to target criminals with illegal firearms, but said there was “no doubt” that reducing the number of guns generally in the community would improve safety.

Police Minister Yasmin Catley said the scheme would reduce the number of firearms able to be stolen and used for violent crime.

World.title: Martha Stewart responds to Halloween costume uproar after dressing as homeless person
World.content:
CultureCelebrityCelebrity life Martha Stewart responds to Halloween costume uproar after dressing as homeless person Chris Hook November 2, 2026 — 10:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Lifestyle mogul and TV presenter Martha Stewart has responded to the furore after an image of her dressed as a homeless person for Halloween was posted to her Instagram account, then quickly deleted. The image showed Stewart with a smudged face, dressed in ripped jeans and a ragged cardigan, holding a sign with the message, “I am hungry help me!!” and was among several images in a carousel promoting her range of candles, sold via US shopping network QVC. Martha Stewart has addressed criticism of her Halloween costume. Instagram “My QVC candles are perfect for Halloween!!!” the images were captioned. The image of her costume was screenshotted by social media users and widely circulated, prompting a backlash, to which she responded early Monday morning (AEDT).



Related Article Homelessness Homelessness crisis hits breaking point as services turn away desperate Australians However, in her statement to the New York Post’s Page Six column, the 85-year-old stopped short of apologising. “I am distressed that my Halloween costume yesterday, which was intended to bring more awareness to the very serious subject of homelessness, has offended people, which was never my intention,” she said in the statement on Monday morning (AEDT). “Homelessness continues to remain one of America’s greatest challenges and ongoing crises, something that I care deeply about and I have spent a significant amount of time and effort supporting charities that combat this ongoing social epidemic. I am committed to continuing to make a difference,” she said. Stewart has amassed a reported $570 million fortune through her lifestyle and homewares empire.



Celebs embrace Halloween spirit Also getting buzz for her Halloween costume was supermodel Heidi Klum, who dressed as a giant severed hand for her annual Halloween party in New York on Saturday (US time), 25 years after she began hosting the much-anticipated event. Heidi Klum dressed as her own severed hand. getty Klum was unrecognisable, with only her eyes and mouth showing, blood dripping from her mouth as she stuck her tongue out. The top of the hand ended in a gory assortment of dangling ligaments and tendons. She had an ensemble of helpers in blood-stained hazmat suits. The idea came to her last year to be a giant hand — specifically her own left hand, with long red nails, a thumb ring, and her engagement ring and wedding band.



“I looked at my hand and I thought, ‘Hey, I think I could fit my body in this somehow,’” Klum said. It’s not the first time she has gone viral with a wild Halloween costume. Neil Patrick Harris and husband David Burtka arrive at the party. AP Photo/Evan Agostini The supermodel-turned-TV personality went viral in 2022 when she arrived at the party on the end of a fishing line, encased in a slithering worm costume. In past years, Klum has come dressed as the Greek myth Medusa, a peacock, a 2.4-metre-tall Transformer, a werewolf from Michael Jackson’s Thriller music video, a clone accompanied by several Klum lookalikes, and Kali, the multi-armed Hindu goddess of death and destruction.



Jade Thirlwall as an angel statue. AP Photo/Evan Agostini Klum said it took about five to six hours to get into her hand costume this year, but making it took a lot longer. She posted hints on her Instagram earlier in the day as bloodied prosthetics were applied to her face. “Hands down, the hardest thing is carrying it,” Klum said. “It’s quite heavy.” Her husband, musician Tom Kaulitz, did not attend this year because he was on tour. But the details on her costume include a tattoo of his name on her ring finger, along with her palm lines and veins. “A little bit of Tom is with me,” she said.



Her guests also made a splash with their costumes. Neil Patrick Harris and husband David Burtka arrived as ghoulish twins from The Shining, while UK singer Jade Thirwall seemed to have dressed as an angel statue that had clearly seen better times. with AP Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. BusinessBanking & financeBig four Westpac expects 11 per cent house price fall, posts $6.8 billion profit Millie Muroi Updated November 2, 2026 — 10:06am ,first published 8:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Westpac expects interest rates to remain “elevated” into 2027 and house prices to fall by nearly 11 per cent by March as it reported a $6.8 billion profit. On Monday, the country’s oldest bank said the Australian economy was holding up “relatively well” on the back of strong business investment, but that price growth remained above the Reserve Bank’s target. Westpac has posted a $6.8 billion profit. Eamon Gallagher “This is presenting challenges for many households and businesses, although impacts are uneven across the economy,” it said in an announcement to the ASX ahead of the next Reserve Bank interest rate decision on Tuesday where the RBA is widely tipped to raise interest rates for the fifth time this year. Westpac also said it expected house prices to fall by 10.9 per cent from March 2026 to March 2027. In September, house prices nationally were 5.2 per cent below the peak reached in March.



Westpac’s $6.8 billion profit in the year to September was down 1 per cent from the previous year. The bank’s net interest margin – a key measure of profitability – fell by 3 percentage points to 1.86 per cent for the second half of 2026 as lending competition remained strong and more customer accounts qualified for savings bonus rates. This was partly offset by stronger business and institutional lending, which grew 12 per ent and 18 per cent, respectively. Despite cost of living pressures, the bank said the share of mortgage balances in hardship “remained low” at 0.6 per cent. Westpac provided more than 42,000 tailored financial hardship assistance and disaster relief packages over the year, but said more than 60 per cent of assisted customers required less than three months of hardship support. The bank said credit quality metrics “continue to reflect customer resilience” despite cost of living pressures and higher interest rates.



The share of accounts held by customers ahead on their mortgage repayments – including offset account balances – remained steady at 86 per cent. Nearly four in ten customers are more than two years ahead on their repayments, about one in ten are on-time and only 1 per cent are behind on their repayments. However, Westpac’s credit impairment provisions – money set aside for potential losses when borrowers fail to repay loans – increased to $5.2 billion with the bank citing “economic and geopolitical uncertainty” affecting energy-intensive sectors and discretionary spending. The bank will pay a final dividend of 77 cents a share, taking the full-year dividend to $1.54, up 1 per cent from the previous year. World.title: Democrats turn on each other in Michigan ahead of midterm elections
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaUS midterms Democrats turn on each other in Michigan ahead of midterm elections Joey Cappeleti , Corey Williams and Mike Householder November 2, 2026 — 10:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Detroit — Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the US Senate primary, Haley Stevens, has stunned party officials by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers as Democratic tensions boiled over days before the election that could determine the balance of power on Capitol Hill. Stevens endorsed Rogers after attending a Detroit church service with him. The remarkable show of support for the President Donald Trump-backed candidate in the tightly contested race comes after she was uninvited to a joint event the same day with El-Sayed, who defeated the congresswoman by a slim margin in the August primary. Haley Stevens speaks alongside Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers. AP “Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away,” Stevens said in a video announcing the endorsement, which led her top aide to quit. “And he’s right. And that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today.” El-Sayed dismissed the endorsement when asked about it by reporters later on Sunday, saying he’s focused on issues voters care about, such as the high cost of living.



“At the end of the day I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” he said, adding later: “None of this matters.” Michigan Democratic leaders were left shocked. With just less than 48 hours to go before Election Day, a party that had spent months trying to unite behind its Senate nominee was suddenly grappling with an extraordinary defection in one of this year’s most important races. Democratic nominee for the Senate Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters during a campaign rally in Detroit, Michigan. AP Tensions between the two Democrats have festered since the primary. Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed is a fierce critic of the US ally. He has also been criticised by some in the community for past remarks regarding a Michigan synagogue attack and for appearances with controversial streamer Hasan Piker. El-Sayed, a former Michigan public health official, is facing Rogers, an ex-congressman, for the seat held by the retiring Democrat, Gary Peters. Keeping Michigan in Democratic hands is vital to the party’s effort to win a majority for the final two years of Trump’s second term.



Stevens and El-Sayed were originally scheduled to attend church together, along with other Michigan and national Democrats, including South Carolina representative Jim Clyburn. Democrats hoped it would be a show of unity as they worked to boost turnout in the Detroit area, where concerns have lingered about enthusiasm among Black and Jewish voters in key Democratic strongholds. Haley Stevens, a Democrat from Michigan Bloomberg Related Article US midterms Trump revives final midterm rallies after erupting over idea he was ‘sick’ Instead, Stevens swayed to gospel music alongside Rogers in the pews at Perfecting Church, while El-Sayed was a few miles away at a different house of worship campaigning alongside prominent Democrats, including Clyburn. The Associated Press attended both services as the dramatic split-screen unfolded. After the church service north of Detroit, where Stevens and her fiancé Jason Turkish worshipped with Rogers and his wife, Kristi, the congresswoman told reporters, “I’m not turning my back on Democrats. It is this one vote.”

World.title: 'If not alive... repatriate my body': Family fears for woman stranded in Cook Islands
World.content:
The family of a Sri Lankan woman who has been stuck in the Cook Islands for three years because Australia and New Zealand refuse to let her transit warns that her "mental state is not good".

Ruchira Ranasingha, 50, fled Sri Lanka hoping to settle in Aotearoa but has been left stuck in limbo after "a disastrous decision" to leave the country for a short stay in the Cook Islands after making a work visa application while on an asylum seeker "open work visa", the BBC reports.

Ranasingha's plight was first reported by Cook Islands News in early October. The newspaper reported that she had arrived in the Cook Islands in November 2023 and had been unable to leave since then.

Immigration New Zealand said it would not comment on her case, citing privacy concerns. However, it noted concerns about her intentions.

Ruchira Ranasingha, 50, fled Sri Lanka hoping to settle in Aotearoa. 123RF

Both New Zealand and Australian immigration authorities have rejected her transit visa applications multiple times.

Ranasingha told the BBC that her only son is getting married this month, and "I really want to be there for his wedding."

"My mother is so worried about what has happened to me that she is constantly in and out of hospital," she was quoted as saying by the BBC.

She told the BBC that she was "scared something is going to happen to me".

According to her brother, who spoke to BBC Sinhala, Ranasingha left Sri Lanka in 2018 after coming under "immense financial pressure" and unable to "repay loans" after being forced to close her small T-shirt factory.

He added that her husband, who was a drug addict, had died about seven years ago.

"One of the times we spoke [with Ranasingha], she told me that if they were not willing to get her back home alive, they might at least repatriate her body," he told the BBC.

Ranasingha has told the Cook Islands News that she was willing to be detained if it satisfied authorities that she had no intention other than to return to Sri Lanka.

She described living without seeing her family for three years as "torture".

But she told the BBC that she was "luckier than others in her position" because the hotel at which she is staying at in Rarotonga was letting her stay free of charge in its staff accommodation and locals providing her with food and clothing.

She said that one of the hotel directors had even provided her a sewing machine to allow her to make a small income.

According to the BBC, Sri Lanka's foreign ministry said it was "taking all necessary steps to facilitate her return to Sri Lanka from the Cook Islands".

"Officials of the Sri Lankan High Commission in Wellington, New Zealand, as well as the relevant New Zealand authorities, are working closely with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on this matter," it said.

Immigration & Secretarial Services, the agency Ranasingha claims got her in this situation, did not respond to the BBC.

Last week, a Wellington-based charity told RNZ Pacific it had offered to escort Ranasingha back home.

World.title: Pahīatua Medical Centre, which suffered staff exodus sold to iwi
World.content:
Tararua Health Group has reached an agreement to sell Pahīatua Medical Centre to Ngāti Kahungunu ki Tāmaki-nui-a-Rua Trust, with the change of ownership taking effect immediately, Omni Health says in a statement.

The decision followed months of turmoil at the medical centre with staff leaving the operation that served almost 5000 patients in the Tararua district. Many said they had left over safety concerns.

Health New Zealand had a review under way of the clinics owned by the Tararua Health Group, which is in turn owned by Omni Health - a network of about 17 practices around the country.

The decision to sell Pahīatua Medical Centre was made in the best interests of patients and the wider local community, with the primary objective of ensuring the continuity of safe, accessible and high-quality healthcare services, Omni Health founder and chief executive officer Mark Wills said in a statement on Monday.

Pahīatua Medical Centre would no longer form part of Tararua Health Group, and would transition to Ngāti Kahungunu ki Tāmaki-nui-a-Rua Trust over the coming weeks.

The medical centre suffered an exodus of staff on one day in October with seven staff, including a doctor and nurses leaving, having resigned in September, and saying they would not return if Omni Health continued to run the centre.

Wills said on Monday he recognised that the past few months had been challenging for many staff, particularly given the uncertainty and public attention surrounding some services.

"Throughout this period, our teams have continued to demonstrate professionalism, resilience and a genuine commitment to the communities we serve. I want to sincerely acknowledge and thank you for that," Wills said.

Staff at the medical centre will transition to roles under the new ownership, and many of the practice's current systems and support services will remain in place during the transition, a statement from the iwi said.

Hayden Hape, Chairman of Ngāti Kahungunu ki Tāmaki-nui-a-Rua, said the acquisition reflects the iwi's commitment to the health and wellbeing of the local community.

"Ngāti Kahungunu ki Tāmaki-nui-a-Rua is pleased to have worked closely with Tararua Health Group to bring Pahiatua Medical Centre into iwi ownership.

"Following what has been a challenging time for staff and the wider community, we look forward to welcoming these dedicated healthcare professionals into our whānau and creating a workplace where they feel valued, respected and proud of the work they do.

"For us, this is about more than taking over a medical practice. It's about giving good people, who have dedicated their lives to caring for others, the opportunity to fall in love with their profession again.

"We believe that when we genuinely care for those who care for our communities, everyone benefits. That is the culture we want to build, and that is our commitment to the people of Pahiatua and the wider Tararua district.

World.title: NZX-listed Locate Technologies sells Bitcoin assets
World.content:
NZX-listed Locate Technologies has sold its Bitcoin assets following a global sell-off of what is increasingly seen as a high risk investment.

The AI powered delivery and logistics company said the sale was completed on Friday 30 October following the stunning theft of cryptocurrencies at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.

Binance said it would cover customer losses of at least US$6.34 billion (NZ$11.26b), as it moved to steady the market, following what was considered to be the biggest financial robbery in history.

"It's pretty horrific. But based on what I've seen, it definitely comes down to the fault from Binance," Crypto Consulting NZ founder Nicolas Turnbull, who is also a director of industry organisation Cryptocurrency NZ.

Turnbull noted Bitcoin had lost just 5 percent of its value as news of the heist broke late last week, led by Binance customers who cashed out $3.64b.

Binance told Reuters the breach was "a complex attack" involving a compromised laptop and malicious software.

However Turnbull said the breach was basically a break and enter of the security Binance used to keep customers' assets, rather like a digital version of a bank safety deposit box, which also displayed what was inside.

"They have a target on their back. . . especially with crypto. Anyone can see the balance, so it's not like they can hide the balance," Turnbull said.

"Everyone can see what's essentially in the safe deposit box, so it creates that appeal . . . you become a target, and essentially they became the target, and they got executed."

In a statement to the market, Locate founder and chief executive Steve Orenstein said its board saw long-term merit in Bitcoin, but sold because of the increase risk to cryptographic assets.

Still, Locate's board decided to liquidate its entire holding of 12.3m Bitcoin on Friday, which generated proceeds of about NZ$1,718,200.

Orenstein said the concern was driven by the rapid progress of AI and by uncertainty over how Bitcoin will become quantum resistant.

However, Turnbull said most retail investors in Bitcoin were in it for the long-haul and wouldn't be spooked by the latest attack on a network operator.

World.title: Fijian PM Rabuka under pressure ahead of crucial vote on constitutional reform
World.content:
Fiji's Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka's coalition government is falling apart ahead of the crucial third reading of a major bill to change the country's 2013 Constitution.

This comes after two of its minor partners, whose support was key to his forming a government in December 2022, have instructed their members of parliament to vote against the Constitution (Amendment) Bill 2026 later this week.

Rabuka needs a two-thirds majority - at least 36 votes - to pass the bill through a 53-seat parliament following the passing of two MPs form the original 55-member parliament.

Rabuka has promised to press on with tabling the bill when parliament resumes on Monday for a vote from lawmakers to get it over the line for a proposed national referendum on 9 December.

Last month, Rabuka had downplayed coalition tensions after prematurely announcing Fiji's first-ever referendum date.

However, things have moved quickly over the weekend after the National Federation Party (NFP) withdrew from the special parliamentary committee led by Rabuka, and declared that the party would not be voting in favour of the bill.

It comes just days after the Social Democratic Liberal Party (Sodelpa) told its three MPs in the coalition - all of whom are Cabinet ministers - to vote against the bill.

"The National Federation Party's exit from the review process leaves the administration facing a high-stakes political showdown ahead of this week's decisive reading of the draft legislation," according to The Fiji Times.

The NFP believes the process is being rushed, while Sodelpa wants a total replacement of the 2013 Constitution - not just amendments to it - as well as the removal of immunity clauses protecting previous coup leaders.

During a consultation on the bill with Lau Province leaders on Friday, Rabuka said it was important to have the numbers for the third reading of the bill.

"Because that determines whether we keep going or [the constitution reform process] ends there."

The prime minister has faced criticism from the opposition, rights groups and community advocates and leaders for rushing the process as Fiji is scheduled to hold an election on or before 6 February 2027 at the latest.

Last week, Mahendra Chaudhry, Fiji's first and only prime minister of Indian descent, warned that the island nation was "worse off today than we were at independence" and that its political leadership had its priorities wrong.

World.title: Senior police staffer calls system for at-risk victims 'outdated'
World.content:
A senior Police staffer involved in the multi-agency response to family violence has publicly criticised the system used by agencies to respond to at-risk victims describing it as "outdated" and "no longer fit for purpose".

On Saturday, RNZ reported that the Government had shelved a system that would have supported "timely multi-agency responses" to family violence and alerted staff to "high-risk situations".

Documents released under the Official Information Act (OIA) obtained by RNZ said the proposed integrated case management project, which had already had $2 million spent on it, was paused last year "as there was no practicable or sustainable way to fund, host and operate the proposed platform".

Officials said agencies would continue with the status quo in the interim, which had several risks, including agencies lacking a shared view of information needed for "effective triage and risk assessment" and "vulnerabilities with regard to data security and information sharing".

Following the article, Police's Waikato District Director for the Integrated Safety Response (ISR) Rachael Douglas posted on LinkedIn with a link to the article.

"We cannot expect better outcomes for whānau while asking our people to work around systems that are no longer fit for purpose," she said.

Douglas said the article raised "an important issue, and one I see firsthand in my role leading Integrated Safety Response (ISR) in Waikato".

"Our current system is outdated. It does not easily support the very things that make an integrated response effective: genuine multi-agency collaboration, coordinated case management, timely information sharing, or ensuring whānau voice is central to decision-making.

"The amount of mahi that goes into making the system work for us, rather than the system work for us, is significant."

Douglas said there was a "real consequence".

"Time spent navigating system limitations is time that could be spent on supporting whānau. In a family violence response, delays matter.

"In Waikato, we have taken an evidence-based approach to improving our practice. We have transformed how we assess risk and threat, challenging longstanding ways of working and strengthening our ability to identify and respond to serious harm."

She said the current system did not adequately support the improvements.

"So our people find workarounds. They adapt, develop additional processes and put in the extra mahi to make good practice possible.

"I am incredibly proud of that commitment. But we should not have to rely on the determination of our people to compensate for systems that have not kept pace with the work."

Douglas said the systems used should not "create additional barriers".

"We need to stop expecting people to work harder around broken processes and start giving them the tools to work better together.

"Ultimately, this isn't about technology. It's about ensuring whānau receive the right support, from the right people, at the right time.

"And that should always be our starting point."

Police have been approached for comment.

Minister for the Prevention of Family Violence and Sexual Violence Karen Chhour earlier said while the technology component of the project was on pause, she had been assured non-technical elements of the "best practice operating model" for multi-agency responses continued to progress.

This included the high-risk protocol and information sharing guidance.

"The decision to pause Project Whetū has not resulted in any reduction to frontline services. This decision will be reviewed in the future and, if practical or sustainable way to host and operate the proposed platform can be found, the technology component of Project Whetū could be resumed.

"This is also subject to any directives from the Government Chief Digital Officer."

Labour's police spokesperson Ginny Andersen said the decision was "an absolute shocker".

"The Government is scrapping a project designed to help agencies identify people at risk of family violence - despite officials warning that without it, vital information cannot easily be shared.

World.title: Review finds no evidence of anti-forestry bias at Gisborne District Council
World.content:
An independent review into Gisborne District Council's regulatory approach to the forestry industry has found it has "acted diligently and in good faith".

The review, released Monday, was commissioned by the council three months ago amidst criticism from industry players and central government that it was being too tough on forestry companies.

It was undertaken by a three-person panel, led by former National MP Chris Finlayson, KC.

Of particular concern was the council's use of enforcement orders - a tool under the Resource Management Act that regulatory bodies can apply to the Environment Court to use to instruct a respondent to carry out certain actions.

Listen to Checkpoint to hear Chris Finlayson's interview after 4pm.

Foresty Minister Todd McClay raised concerns about the orders, and previously said the industry had come to him saying it faced decisions it considered "unworkable and costly" and were considering whether to remain in the region.

However the review found the council was following proper legal process, and the use of enforcement orders had improved forestry practises. The 80-page report provided a thorough analysis of the council's processes, framed by the panel's remit to examine whether these were fit-for-pourpose, reasonable and proportionate to the scale of risk faced by the region.

'GDC is anti-foresty... empty rhetoric'

At the outset, the panel addressed what it stated were "extravagant statements" made to it during its inquiry.

These statements included "GDC [Gisborne District Council] is anti-forestry"; "Forestry does not have a future in Tairāwhiti"; "Forestry companies don't concern themselves with environmental matters".

The panel unpacked these statements as examples of empty rhetoric or hyperbole.

For example, it pointed out that all companies it had spoken to for its inquiry had an appreciation of the environment and the need for their practises to address environmental concerns.

In total, the panel spoke with 12 representatives from six forestry companies. It also spoke to five industry bodies, as well as contractors and logging operators, and owners of Māori land forestry blocks and companies. These made up more than 100 interviews conducted for the review, with technical experts, and representatives from local councils as well as central government agencies included.

In regard to the council's relationship with the forestry industry, the panel stated that at no time had it discerned an "anti-forestry bias".

It stated that it was clear that the council and the forestry industry recognised the importance of commercial forestry to Tairāwhiti, and that the council had specific responsibilities to manage the impacts of that on the environment and community through a competent and transparent regulatory system.

Consenting process on-track

The panel found, overall, the council's consenting process was "generally very sound".

It highlighted two instances which raised concerns over its internal processes. The first was a job  for a compliance officer who "could stand up" to the forestry. The  was published on the council's website earlier this year. The second was the inclusion of enforcement orders as a KPI in the council's revised forestry strategy.

In the first instance, the job  was taken down promptly and was found not to have been properly advertised. The panel said it was important the council avoided "this kind of misstep which conveys the wrong impression".

In the second instance, the panel made a similar observation, cautioning against the kind the wrong impression of impression that could result from a KPI around enforcement orders.

It also looked at the quality of communication throughout the consent process, and time frames for consent applications - which had been highlighted by some forestry companies as cumbersome.

The panel did not find major problems with the timeframes in Gisborne District Council's consenting process, and noted delays were often due to applicants and the need for more information.

It went on to say that "a number of submitters" complained about the amount of requests for further information from the council, however "those requests could be lessened if applicants took more care to address fundamental matters and presented their applications in a coherent and logical manner".

It also noted the problem appeared to be more widespread than in Tairāwhiti, with other councils indicating they struggled with the "low standard of many forestry consent applications".

Despite that, the panel also found Gisborne District Council wasn't without fault. It stated it needed to be "clear, concise and consistent" in its communications with applicants, however "some emails we read dealing with these issues are hardly models of clarity and GDC needs to lift its game".

Enforcement orders "costly" but shown to work

The inquiry also delved into the council's use of enforcement orders.

In the past three years, seven enforcement orders have been issued by the Environment Court directing companies to clean up forestry blocks in Tairāwhiti. Just last week, Summit Forests NZ was officially ordered to clean up a forestry block on the East Cape described by experts as "one of the worst" ever seen.

The panel found enforcement orders had "been more effective at shifting behaviour than previous approaches" when it came to improving forestry practices. However, they were a costly and time-consuming process for the council, which was already struggling to manage demand on its resources and staff.

The panel also stated that naming company directors in enforcement orders had been a top concern when it met with forestry company representatives.

On this, it acknowledged the seriousness of naming individuals and that it was step "which should not be taken lightly". It also found that the council had had "experienced considerable improvement in compliance" since it had begun doing so.

It also noted the council did not have a blanket approach to automatically naming company directors.

Government criticism of Gisborne council 'unfair'

Overall, the panel found the council's approach to the forestry industry had been justified and was proportionate to the risks associated with the geological characteristics of the region, such as the susceptibility of land to erosion.

It also highlighted that forestry practises had improved, though more work needed to be done.

Alongside this, it examined the role of central government in forestry in Tairāwhiti, and its decisions to weigh in on the council's approach to the industry.

Notably, the same week the council announced it had commissioned its independent review into consenting and compliance practises in August, the government appointed "a facilitator" to advise it directly on what was happening with the forestry sector in the region. Minister for Regulation David Seymour also contacted the council in May warning it's approach was potentally risking [investment by forestry companies.

On this point, the panel was clear central government had behaved improperly.

"It is unfair for the Crown to criticise GDC [Gisborne District Council] as it has in recent times," it said.

It also called on central government to address shortfalls in regulatory settings and legislation like the Resource Management Act that was adding to gaps and confusion around the consent process.

In regard to the management of slash, it stated "any uncertainty could be overcome by a conseting process which clearly covers slash discharge".

The Crown must come to the table

Chairperson Chris Finlayson directly addressed the importance of support and engagement from the Crown for the future of forestry and land sustainability in Tairāwhiti following the release of the report. This was particularly important as forests planted in the wake of 1988's Cyclone Bola were due to be harvested within the next five years.

"The Crown has known about the land-use challenges facing Tairāwhiti for decades and played a significant role in establishing the forestry landscape we see today," Finlayson said.

"It cannot now expect council, the forestry industry and local communities to resolve these complex and longstanding issues on their own. The scale of the challenge demands national leadership, appropriate investment and a coordinated approach to land-use transition.

"Central government must take responsibility for the policy settings, resources and solutions that sit within its control," he said.

Gisborne Mayor Rehette Stoltz said the panel findings confirmed the council's approach to forestry had been justified, but acknowedged it could also make improvements in areas like communication with consent applicants.

"The findings provide assurance that the fundamentals of our regulatory approach are sound," she said.

World.title: Which parts of NZ have shrinking population?
World.content:
Audio player for " When does my property become relationship property? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/2292030%2Fwhich-parts-of-nz-have-shrinking-population

Most of New Zealand is growing its population, but some of the bigger cities have been losing people and Wellington is back to a level last seen in 2017.

New Stats NZ data shows two-thirds of the country's territorial authority and Auckland local board areas experienced population growth in the year to June.

About half grew faster than they did in 2025, but the 10 fastest-growing areas were all in the South Island or Auckland.

Selwyn was top, with growth of 2.9 percent. Other fast-growing areas were Mangere-Otahuhu, Papakura, Otara-Papatoetoe and Henderson-Massey.

NZ population growth by district, June 2026. Supplied/Shamubeel Eaqub

Stats NZ said much of Selwyn's growth came from people moving within New Zealand.

Six cities had falls in population. Wellington had the largest, down 0.6 percent, followed by Dunedin, down 0.5 percent, Nelson, Palmerston North, and Napier, all down 0.2 percent, and Porirua, down 0.1 percent.

Stats NZ said, outside Auckland, Christchurch was the largest city with 422,400 people, compared to Auckland's 1.84 million.

Infometrics principal economist Nick Brunsdon said Selwyn and Queenstown had experienced strong population growth for the past couple of decades.

Audio player for " What shrinking populations mean for house prices and rents " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/business/2292030%2Fwhich-parts-of-nz-have-shrinking-population

What shrinking populations mean for house prices and rents Morning Report Download MP3 2m

"No surprises there, that's pretty standard."

He said, where people had previously talked about a "golden triangle" of Auckland, Waikato and Bay of Plenty, that was becoming a "golden baton".

"It's Auckland and Waikato, the corridor just right through to Hamilton and Cambridge, but not so much the Bay of Plenty."

He said tourism was helping grow parts of the South Island.

"We've seen Hurunui, Hanmer Springs, Mackenzie, Tekapo, Southland, Fiordland and Te Anau, as well as Central Otago and Queenstown Lakes... they're all in the top 10 for population growth, which reflects that, with more tourists, you need more staff to look after them.

"You're bringing in more migration to grow the population to get the workers to do the work for the tourists that are also coming in."

Auckland's population growth was relatively unusual while the economy was weak, he said.

"For most of the other areas that have had strong population growth, we can line it up with what's happening employment-wise and say strong job growth, strong employment, strong population, it all matches up.

"Auckland still has a pretty weak economy - it's probably lagging the economic recovery nationally - and yet it has had some quite strong population growth, which is interesting."

Wellington was a standout for loss of population.

"Wellington's population is back to where it was in 2017," he said. "They've had several years in a row of population decline, a large part of that is what's happening in employment.

Net internal migration by district, June 2026. Supplied/Shamubeel Eaqub

"The number of jobs has fallen 6000 over the past three years and a lot of people who've lost their jobs have just left. They're also not attracting people in from overseas, like they would normally."

Smaller provincial centres tended to lose their population through natural decrease.

"They already have more deaths than births, so if they're not getting a lot of migration on top of that, it means they're going backwards. The likes of Timaru, Dunedin, Gore, Stratford, those sorts of areas."

Brunsdon said internal migration did not seem to happen as in the past.

"What seems to be going on is, if people have a change in circumstances, they get itchy feet or they're not happy with how they're getting ahead in life, and they want to shake things up and see if they can get ahead financially somewhere else, right at the moment, people are more likely to say, 'It's time to go overseas to Australia' or whatever it would be, rather than 'it's time to move down to Palmerston North' or something like that."

That had been the case for Northland.

"All of the Northland territories, all the districts in Northland had very slim, practically no population growth," he said. "Normally, what would happen is you'd have a group of people in Auckland that say, 'Oh well, I'm maybe not quite happy with Auckland, it's time to move somewhere else in New Zealand'.

"You normally have quite a nice flow of people from Auckland into Northland, but that's not happening at the moment."

He said areas that lost population could struggle to find workers, when their economies improved.

"That's going to create a bit more of a pull factor that starts pulling people back out of those places like, let's say Christchurch, down to Timaru, or from Auckland into Thames Coromandel.

"I think naturally that economic recovery over the next three years will start to balance that distribution back to normal a little bit."

Retiring baby boomers would also create employment in some areas, he said.

Thames-Coromandel had historically done well pulling people out of Auckland, but had experienced a population decline over the past year.

Net international migration by district, June 2026. Supplied/Shamubeel Eaqub

"There's no shortage of people that want to retire and no shortage of people that want to retire to Thames Coromandel," he said.

"What I wonder is if the Auckland housing market is holding it back, because you may be thinking about or maybe you always had a dream of retiring to the Coromandel, if you're looking at an awful price for selling your house, maybe you're more likely to just sit on your hands, stay in your house and wait for the market to recover, until you can get a better price that will enable you to make that move."

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said places like Auckland and Christchurch had a younger population, which meant they were more likely to grow, due to more babies being born.

He said people moving into New Zealand were increasingly going to places outside Auckland, where there were more job opportunities.

"Kiwis are leaving from those places, the locals are leaving, so those skills shortages bite more in the provinces.

"Think about places like Whakatane, some of the East Cape. Regional migration is all negative there, but international migration is by and large positive.

"Nurses, doctors, people working in horticulture... the labour shortages are really binding."

He said housing supply was keeping up in places like Christchurch, but in other parts of the country that were not expecting the same population growth, houses were only built after people arrived, which created tensions.

Eaqub said the country was likely to rely increasingly on international migration for future population growth, but it was becoming a tricky political issue.

"I think, right around the world, we're seeing this kind of this pushback against high rates of immigration, because there are concerns about jobs for locals, and all those other bits and pieces.

"It's the kind of this twin pressure we've got really big issues with, young people not getting access to jobs and those kinds of things, particularly right now.

"Most of the small towns of New Zealand have massive infrastructure pressures coming down the pipe and if they don't have population growth, they won't be able to afford it."

World.title: '50 cameras': Arsenal's drought-breaking win marred by VAR drama
World.content:
Arsenal has returned to the top of the English Premier League after ending a 14-year drought at Anfield with a 1-0 win over Liverpool in a match involving another VAR drama.

Arsenal striker Kai Havertz tapped in from Declan Rice's low cross in the 16th minute after the hosts were caught trying to play the ball out of their defence.

Liverpool responded strongly as half-time approached and were denied a penalty when Jurrien Timber held Alexander Isak while Isak attempted a header from a cross.

Despite replays showing a clear tug on Isak's jersey, the VAR deemed the incident to not be a foul, much to the dismay of Liverpool captain Virgil van Dijk.

"I think it was also clear penalty. I've seen it back," he said after the game.

Isak did not appeal for a penalty and van Dijk hit back when asked whether his teammate should have made more of the jersey tug in order for the VAR to notice it.

"Doesn't notice it? We have 50 cameras, if there is not even more. Why do you have to complain when there's so many cameras?" he said.

"It is spotted, isn't it? Because everyone's seen it. But yeah, in the end, obviously, it wasn't given, and we lose the game, unfortunately."

There were more gilt-edged chances for Liverpool before the half-time interval as Florian Wirtz curled a free kick against the crossbar while Alexis Mac Allister missed a wide-open header while completely unmarked inside the penalty box.

But Arsenal weathered the storm and defended superbly to keep Liverpool largely at arm's length after the break and seal their first Premier League win at Anfield for 14 years.

Kai Havertz's first-half strike proved to be the difference as Arsenal climbed back to the top of the Premier League table. (David Price/Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

Mikel Arteta's side replaced Manchester City at the top with 24 points from nine games, with City on 21 after losing at home to Brighton and Hove Albion on Saturday, their second successive league defeat after winning their first seven.

Liverpool's second league defeat of the season left them nine points behind Arsenal in fifth place.

For all Liverpool's huff and puff they failed to register an effort on target as Arsenal smothered their hosts with the kind of gritty away display that has become Arteta's blueprint.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: 'Annoying' Alcaraz denies de Minaur Vienna Open title in final
World.content:
Alex de Minaur served up some brilliant tennis, but it still wasn't enough for him to break his dispiriting duck against his "annoying" and virtuoso nemesis Carlos Alcaraz in the Vienna Open final.

In their seventh meeting, Australia's No.1 did his utmost to earn a first-ever win over the great young Spaniard in Sunday's championship match, but despite dragging him into some breathtaking rallies, he invariably came off worse as Alcaraz scorched to a 6-1, 6-4 victory.

"It's great to have you back on tour," de Minaur told the Spaniard afterwards in the Wiener Stadthalle, but couldn't resist adding with a smile: "I will say one thing though: it is very annoying to play against you!"

"But you're one of the good ones, one of the great guys on tour … As for myself, it's been a great week too."

Indeed, de Minaur could find plenty of consolation after a tournament in which he knocked out the new world No.1 Alexander Zverev in the semis, earning his first victory over the German in an individual rather than team tournament, and played perhaps his best tennis of the season.

Now he will fly straight off to Paris for the Masters tournament there, the crucial last qualifying event for the ATP Finals, also knowing he's in the eighth and final spot to be part of the Turin end-of-season men's championship.

"I'm proud to be standing up here and still fighting," said de Minaur, who'll move back to No.8 in the world from No.10 after reaching his third final of the year.

Carlos Alcaraz (pictured) had too much class for Alex de Minaur in the final of the Vienna Open. (Getty Images: Jakub Porzycki/Anadolu)

"So I'm excited for what's left for this year, and hopefully I can continue pushing and have a longer year."

Still, though, de Minaur couldn't cope with the brilliance of 23-year-old Alcaraz, who lifted his fourth title of the season and the 28th of his ‌career, sweeping to victory without dropping a set all week.

After the wrist trouble that ripped a hole in his season, he really is looking back to something like the world-beater who lifted the Australian Open crown at the start of 2026.

Alcaraz, who has dropped only two sets to de Minaur in their seven contests, never looked back again after a scintillating start when he caught the Aussie cold by breaking in the first game, before uncorking a champagne cross-court backhand winner to earn a second break en route to a 4-0 lead.

Happy just to eke out a single game in the opener, de Minaur was stubbornly competitive in the second, producing three sensational points when at break point and 3-4 down just to stay in the fight.

But serving to stay in the match at 4-5, the seven-time grand slam champ went into overdrive, and after applying the pressure to grab match point, played a fittingly wonderful final rally, delivering a drop shot, a lob and then a killing forehand, his 14th of the match, which clipped the baseline to seal the deal.

"He's really fast, you have to earn every point. You might have a winner against everybody — except him," said Alcaraz, acknowledging his opponent's excellence.

AAP

World.title: Antonelli crowned F1 champ after horror crash stops race in Mexico
World.content:
Kimi Antonelli has been crowned Formula 1 drivers' champion at 20, becoming the youngest ever, as Max Verstappen won a chaotic Mexico City Grand Prix on Monday (AEDT).

In a race marred by a horror crash involving Cadillac's Valtteri Bottas after his left-front wheel ripped off while on the straight, Antonelli avoided the chaos, finishing third to seal his maiden world title with four rounds left in the season.

Antonelli just needed to finish ninth to secure the championship in Mexico, and drove a professional race to stay out of trouble and finish third, behind race winner Verstappen and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton.

The Italian became the youngest-ever world champion at 20 years and 68 days, beating Sebastian Vettel's record by three years.

He was overcome with emotion as he crossed the line, breaking down in tears over the team radio before embracing his family and team after the race.

Kimi Antonelli celebrates with his family after claiming the Formula 1 drivers' championship. (Getty Images: Mark Thompson)

"It's a day I will remember forever. Thank you so much to my team, my family, my friends, and all of you guys that support me and the sport," he said after the podium presentation.

"I'm just so grateful. I am going to enjoy every bit."

Antonelli started fourth and kept out of trouble, knowing that he just needed to keep his Mercedes on track to become champion.

Despite staying out of trouble, Antonelli showed everyone why he is world champion with a brilliant lunge up the inside of Ferrari's Charles Leclerc to take third.

Verstappen claims sixth win in Mexico as Hamilton fumes over teammate

Verstappen had never won from fifth on the grid, but changed that on Monday to claim his third win of the season, and sixth in Mexico.

Max Verstappen (left) drove a great race to win in Mexico. (Getty Images: Formula 1/Bryn Lennon)

Ferrari's pole sitter Lewis Hamilton and teammate Charles Leclerc battled for the lead on the opening lap, with Leclerc going around the outside of Hamilton at the turn 4 left-hander.

Both drivers went off track, but Leclerc carried on cutting the corner to hold the lead, while Hamilton fell behind Verstappen.

Leclerc was handed a five-second penalty, much to the bemusement of Hamilton and Verstappen, who felt the punishment was not severe enough for a driver who was able to hold onto the lead and drive in clean air.

"The stewards are basically handing Charles this win," a furious Hamilton said over the radio.

Leclerc and Verstappen both pitted at the end of lap 27 of 71, with Verstappen coming out ahead after Leclerc's penalty was served.

The grand prix was stopped after a horror crash involving Bottas on lap 44 of 71, who had his left-front wheel ripped off under braking and was sent flying into the wall.

From the standing restart, Verstappen got a beautiful launch and held the lead, while Leclerc struggled and then locked his tyres as Hamilton took second.

Hamilton fought Verstappen all the way to the chequered flag, but could not find a way past the Red Bull star.

"It was very hectic out there today," Verstappen said.

"The first start made the race for me [jumping from fifth to second].

"After that, we had a bit of a different strategy. I think we lacked a little bit of pace, but we hung in there and made the right calls at the right time.

"I was sweating a little at the end to keep Lewis [Hamilton] behind."

Antonelli made a brilliant move on Leclerc for this place, with the Ferrari driver struggling with vibration from his tyres after the massive lock-up from the restart.

Leclerc had just enough to hold off McLaren's Lando Norris for fourth, with Mercedes driver George Russell sixth.

Oscar Piastri finished seventh, after starting 12th following a poor qualifying session the day before. The Australian spent the final laps of the race driving with a damaged car after he and Racing Bulls driver Arvid Lindblad collided in a battle for seventh.

Lindblad squeezed Piastri, and the contact between their cars sent the Racing Bulls driver into the wall.

Franco Colapinto (Alpine), Liam Lawson (Racing Bulls) and Pierre Gasly (Alpine) rounded out the top 10.

Relive all the action of the Formula 1 Mexico City Grand Prix on the blog below.

World.title: When Bart Cummings broke his Melbourne Cup rule for Saintly
World.content:
Legendary racing trainer and "Cups King" Bart Cummings rarely showed emotion after big wins or defeats, and he always told people not to get too attached to racehorses.

But even Cummings had exceptions to the rule, and one was the "horse from heaven", Saintly.

The big-striding chestnut gelding with an army of fans gave Cummings a landmark triumph 30 years ago this week in the Melbourne Cup at Flemington.

Going into the big race, Cummings had already won a record nine Cups (his nearest rival at the time was French trainer Etienne de Mestre back in the 1800s), and his campaign to win a 10th proved to be an absolute masterclass.

In his biography, My Life, Cummings told readers there was no particular secret to winning Melbourne Cups.

"There's no magic," he wrote. "There's relentless work, discipline, adherence to your methods and plans, taking a genuine interest in the horse's welfare and above all else, plain commonsense."

Do all this, Cummings believed, and "you make your own luck".

Bart Cummings's normal plan for the Melbourne Cup included the Mackinnon Stakes on Derby Day, like Rogan Josh (right) in 1999. (Getty Images: ALLSPORT/Robert Cianflone)

There may not have been any magic, but there was a plan. A 10,000-metre prep plan, to be precise.

Cummings believed horses that ran in the cup should have completed a series of lead-up runs, and have a total of 10,000m or race distance in their legs before Melbourne Cup day.

A run on Derby Day in the Mackinnon Stakes (2,000m) or the Archer Stakes (2,500m) was usually the cherry on top, training-wise, before the Melbourne Cup three days later.

One person who saw this plan in action up close was Joe Agresta, who was trackwork rider for Cummings for 34 years. When he first saw Saintly for the first time, he wasn't overly impressed.

Joe Agresta rode trackwork for Bart Cummings for 34 years, working five of his Melbourne Cup winners including Rogan Josh (pictured). (Getty Images: ALLSPORT/Julian Herbert)

"He was a nice horse but he was a gangly type of three-year-old," Agresta says.

"Then he came out and he just blitzed them in the Carbine Club Stakes [at Flemington].

"He went back [to Sydney], and [Bart] built him up, then he came back and won the Australian Cup."

Cummings had a beautiful property near the Nepean River in Western Sydney called Princes Farm. The great trainer unofficially referred to it as "horse heaven".

Saintly was bred at Princes Farm and was born there in 1992, the year after Cummings's ninth Cup win with Let's Elope.

When Cummings nearly went bankrupt with the collapse of the Cups King syndicate in the late 1980s, Malaysian businessman Dato Tan Chin Nam was among those who helped support him to keep him afloat.

Chin Nam had owned Think Big, which had won back-to-back Melbourne Cups for Cummings in 1974 and 1975.

When Saintly was born, Cummings gave the businessman a half-share in gratitude for his help.

Saintly's three-year-old season included the Carbine Club Stakes win, and then the Australian Cup win in March 1996 marked another win at Flemington, where his long stride had plenty of room to move.

A few more runs in Sydney followed before Cummings gave Saintly a decent spell. He wouldn't return to the track for nearly five months.

Cummings's lesson learned

For his most important campaign, Saintly was running every couple of weeks in Sydney. After three runs, it was clear Cummings had expectations, but what would come next?

By this time, the permanent jockey had long been Darren Beadman, a top operator who had ridden Cummings's eighth Melbourne Cup winner on Kingston Rule in 1990.

It was early October when Saintly had his fourth and fifth runs, over the space of a weekend at Randwick in Sydney.

The chestnut ran second in the Craven Plate on the Saturday and third in the Metropolitan on Monday, although in the latter race Saintly hit the front but was flat at the end, out-finished by Hula Flight and Nothin Leica Dane.

"Bart rang me and said, 'I'm sending Saintly down [to Melbourne]. I want you to freshen up the horse, I've learned something about him,'" Agresta says.

Saintly was quickly jumping out of his skin, but Cummings didn't want to run him in the Caulfield Cup in mid-October. Instead he aimed him at the Cox Plate.

The two most famous races in Australia are the Cox Plate and the Melbourne Cup.

The Cox Plate (run over 2,040m) is known as the weight-for-age championship of Australasia, where the race does what it says on the box. Horses are given a certain weight depending on their age, with female horses (fillies and mares) given a discount because they are racing against males (colts, horses and geldings).

Then there is the Melbourne Cup, which is a handicap run over 3,200m. This kind of race sees horses given a weight (or handicap), decided by a range of factors including age and past performances. Generally it sees more weight for better horses and less weight for less experienced runners.

At least until earlier this century, the point of the exercise was to produce a hypothetical result where every runner finished together.

The reality is usually far different, but that's the aim of the game.

Up to 1996, only three horses (Nightmarch in 1929, Phar Lap in 1930 and Rising Fast in 1954) had won both the Cox Plate and the Melbourne Cup in the same year.

That year, before it was commonplace, Cummings opted for the Cox Plate as the lead-up for the Melbourne Cup, not the grand final.

The Cox Plate

Moonee Valley's narrow circuit and short finishing straight were not expected to suit Saintly in the 1996 Cox Plate. (Getty Images: Vince Caligiuri)

Some thought the Moonee Valley circuit would be too tight for Saintly. Cummings wanted a solid run in the legs of his star horse of the spring.

When the race began, Beadman kept Saintly quiet back in about sixth place near the fence.

How the Diva did the impossible, 20 years on From quiet beginnings, an unknown English filly came Down Under and changed Australia's racing history by achieving the impossible. This is how Makybe Diva won a historic third Melbourne Cup 20 years ago.

The field began to stretch out. At halfway, he was 10 lengths behind the leaders. Saintly was still sixth 700m out when Beadman began to urge his mount forward.

By the 500, Saintly was making ground going five-wide. Rounding the corner, Filante was leading on the fence narrowly from Juggler then All Our Mob. Saintly went four, five then six-wide as he briefly was on the wrong lead leg.

Watching from the stands, Agresta thought that might be the end of his chances, but once Beadman balanced Saintly up, he moved in. As the crowd roared, the gaps narrowed further, and all four horses were in it. It was Filante leading and Saintly closing.

Saintly rattled down the outside, and they called for a photo as the crowd buzzed about the frantic finish. "From where I was I thought he just got beat, but they said he won," Agresta recalls.

The lesson Cummings had learned was that Saintly didn't back up, so instead of running on Derby Day, the trainer had Agresta gallop him at Flemington.

"The clocker was a guy called Des Spain, and he said to Bart afterwards, 'You know that horse ran a quicker time than [the sprinters] go down the straight [for 1,200],'" Agresta says.

"Bart said something silly like his watch must be broken, but that's when he knew Saintly had a great chance in the Cup."

The Bart Cummings-trained Saintly carried joint-owner Dato Tan Chin Nam's famous chessboard colours with gold sleeves. (Supplied: State Library of Victoria/VRC)

Chin Nam was fascinated with the game of chess, and so his horses ran in eye-catching colours. The black and white checks were like a chessboard, while the sleeves were gold or yellow to represent the sun.

Would the sun rise on another Cummings Cup win?

The Cup itself

Only three years on from Vintage Crop's famous Flemington win, another Irish-trained horse was favourite for the Cup.

Oscar Schindler had won the Irish St Leger, and come third in the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe, so he was seen as the class horse in the race. But would he handle Australian conditions?

Saintly was not a frontrunner, but he drew barrier three for the Cup. This was a simple set-up for Cummings's horse.

"Bart never gave any instructions, but Darren knew he had to bury him [Saintly] away," Agresta says, meaning a spot on the inside.

Cummings didn't want his horse too close to the lead.

Beadman quickly had Saintly out of the ruck and into position on the fence, and by the time the field thundered past the post the first time, the gelding was neatly placed in sixth, right on the fence.

Grey Shot led from Few Are Chosen, Court of Honour and Centico. Not much changed for much of the race.

At halfway Saintly was perfectly placed, still sixth on the fence. The big chestnut had not spent a penny, until about the 800m, when Beadman shifted him off the fence and in a few strides he was into the clear.

"We were up in the stands watching it, and when Darren Beadman pulled out at the 800, he pulled out three-deep, I said, 'This is home,' because there was no way he'd pull that horse out three-deep if he didn't think it was travelling well," Agresta says.

Grey Shot still led at the turn with Nothin Leica Dane coming, but Saintly was in clear air, and he loved the long Flemington straight.

He hit the front at the 300, and soon after moved clear, as nothing could go with him.

"When Beadman let him down, he just sprinted away. It was a great effort by [Beadman and] the horse, and it was probably Bart's greatest training feat. With this horse, everything he did seemed to work," Agresta says.

Flemington erupted, as Beadman rode Saintly past the post, clear of Count Chivas and Skybeau, to clinch Cummings's 10th Cup. Oscar Schindler finished 15th.

Late challenges from Count Chivas and Skybeau could not stop Saintly from winning an incredible 10th Melbourne Cup for Bart Cummings. (Supplied: VRC)

It was a sign of Cummings's experience, that even 31 years after his first Cup win, he was willing to go away from his tried-and-trusted plan because of his understanding of Saintly.

"When I first started working for him, we won a couple of Group 1s and we were in the mounting yard jumping around," Agresta says.

"[Bart] said, 'Don't be like those other idiots [celebrating wildly]. We celebrate in our own time.'"

Dato Tan Chin Nam and Bart Cummings were composed at Flemington after Saintly's win, but the celebrations that night included an unlikely duet. (Supplied: VRC)

But after another Melbourne Cup win, all bets were off.

"We went to Crown Casino [that night], there were about 30 of us," Agresta recalls.

"Bart and Dato Tan Chin Nam were drinking wine, and they started singing Danny Boy!

"It was a good night. Bart never worried too much about being beaten, but I could see it: the relief and the happiness on his face; it was something special [for him] to win the Cup with Saintly."

'He nearly died': Illness in Japan

The next challenge was overseas, with the Japan Cup in Tokyo, less than a month on from the Melbourne Cup. But Saintly would not get to test himself against the best.

Saintly fell ill the night before the race. Vets would not treat the horse without the trainer's permission, because it would mean Saintly could not run in the Japan Cup. Cummings gave the OK.

"The next morning I was crying," Agresta says. "Bart said, 'What's the matter with you?'

"I said, 'I'm devastated.' He said, 'Don’t worry son, it wasn't meant to be.'"

Asked how serious the illness was in Japan, Agresta pauses and says: "He nearly died."

Bart Cummings's training base in Melbourne for four decades was eventually named Saintly Place, after the "horse from heaven". (Getty Images: Vince Caligiuri)

Saintly came back to Australia, and began another campaign at Caulfield in early 1997 in the CF Orr Stakes. Once again he came from behind, still five lengths back at the 250m mark before storming home to win.

But within a week, he had bowed a tendon in training, and that race at Caulfield proved to be his last.

Joe Agresta (L) saw plenty of winning days with legendary trainer Bart Cummings (C) and stable foreman Reg Fleming (R), including Bart's 12th Melbourne Cup win on Viewed. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Agresta says Cummings denied that he had a particular love for Saintly, but his actions say otherwise.

"Living Legends wanted him [Saintly] to come there for them to look after him. He [Bart] said no," Agresta says.

"Graham Salisbury wanted him for the clerk of the course. [Bart] said no, 'He's going to live the rest of his life on my property.'"

And he did.

Saintly lived at Princes Farm, or horse heaven if you prefer, until he died in 2016 at the age of 24.

Cummings himself was already gone, dying at his home a year earlier. He had won two more Melbourne Cups, with Rogan Josh in 1999 and Viewed in 2008. Both horses ran on Derby Day.

Dato Tan Chin Nam died in 2018. He won a fourth Melbourne Cup with Bart, Cummings' final victory with Viewed in the famous chessboard colours.

A statue of Bart Cummings looks out at Flemington racecourse from an area named Saintly Place. (Getty Images: Vince Caligiuri)

Cummings' Flemington stables are also gone, turned into apartments. But there is still a Saintly Place, fittingly a section of the Flemington course Cummings made his own, complete with a life-sized statue of him.

And while no-one will ever forget the Cups King, neither will anyone who loves racing forget the "horse from heaven".

World.title: What time is the Melbourne Cup? How to watch and the weather forecast
World.content:
A strong field of Australian hopefuls and international raiders is preparing for the race that stops the nation on Tuesday.

Tuesday's Melbourne Cup will be the 166th running of the famous horse race, with rain forecast in the Victorian capital ahead of the meet.

From start time to weather forecast, below are some key things to know before the 2025 Melbourne Cup.

What time is the Melbourne Cup?

Melbourne Cup Day is held on the first Tuesday of November, which is November 3 this year.

The Melbourne Cup will be the seventh race of 10 at Flemington Racecourse.

Here are the start times for the Melbourne Cup in each state and territory, including New Zealand.

3pm AEDT: Victoria, NSW, Tasmania, ACT

2:30pm ACDT: South Australia

2pm AEST: Queensland

1:30pm ACST: Northern Territory

12pm AWST: Western Australia

5pm NZDT: New Zealand

How to watch and follow the Melbourne Cup

The Nine Network has the television rights to broadcast the 2026 Melbourne Cup.

All 10 races at Flemington will be broadcast on Channel Nine, and streamed on Nine Now.

ABC Sport will have live digital coverage of Melbourne Cup Day with a live blog. You can also listen to the live call of the Melbourne Cup on the radio, online, or via the ABC Listen app.

What is the weather forecast for the Melbourne Cup?

There is forecast to be some rain around Melbourne for Cup Day on Tuesday.

The Bureau of Meteorology has forecast between 3-15 millimetres to fall in Melbourne on Monday, with a possible morning shower on Tuesday.

There was plenty of rain in the lead-up to last year's race, won by Half Yours, with the track rated a Soft 6 for the Cup.

Who is the favourite to win the Melbourne Cup?

There will be a field of 24 for the Melbourne Cup.

The favourite to win is number 20, Point of Law.

Point Of Law showed sustained speed for an impressive win at Geelong. (Racing Photos via Getty Images: Pat Scala)

Point of Law is a UK thoroughbred, sired by the great Frankle, trained by Ciaron Maher.

The three-year-old colt has just five race starts for three wins, including the Geelong Cup last month.

World.title: Tonga and Samoa can be State of Origin for the new century
World.content:
It's not often you can feel when history is happening right around you but that is what happens when Samoa meets Tonga.

The two island nations met in the most eagerly anticipated clash of the Rugby League World Cup and in the end it was Tonga who claimed the honours with a 20-18 victory.

It sets up two classic semi-finals, where Samoa will play Australia and Tonga take on New Zealand, but that feels secondary to what happened at Parramatta on Sunday.

It took everything Tonga had and then it took a little more, with the result in the balance until the final minute of a contest that was fuelled by the power of the past and teased a golden vision of tomorrow.

As State of Origin once changed the sport by creating matches that feel as big as rugby league ever can, games like this prove Samoa and Tonga can do the same.

It can be the Origin of the new century, a rivalry without end that makes itself anew every year as a date every fan — Samoan, Tongan and otherwise, rusted-on and casual — can circle on the calendar as one of rugby league's biggest nights.

It can fill stadiums as easily as it does hearts. The crowd for this one was the highest for any sporting event at the new Parramatta Stadium and would have eclipsed last year's Lang Park total of 45,000 if only the place was bigger.

It was a mighty occasion between Tonga and Samoa in Parramatta. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

It draws in eyeballs, demands attention and adds zeroes to television deals — which means it can turn a profit, In a world where games are reduced to content on a balance sheet, that alone makes the case for more.

This was a match that delivered on its promises of blood and fire and speed and craft, and it was right that it felt timeless because rugby league is just the newest framework for something that has been happening for centuries.

What happens on the field and in the stands is the expression of a relationship that has existed between Tonga and Samoa since before either had written word.

It was already old when the colonisers came, and there are moments you can feel its power so fully and clearly you may as well be able to reach out and touch it.

It was in the steel eyes of Tim Lafai, the retired Samoan legend who grew up in a house with walls, as he led the team out dressed in traditional garb.
